translations.text: There were many whose minds urged them [?] to begin to tell the word of God, to recount the mystery that the mighty Christ worked among mankind: the glorious deeds he did with words and with works.
Many wise men then wanted to praise this, the teaching of Christ, the holy word of God, and to write it clearly with their hands in a book: how the children of men should carry out his command.
Yet among that multitude there were four for this task who had the might of God, help from heaven, the Holy Spirit, power from Christ. They were chosen for it,
so that they alone should write the gospel in a book, and the many commands of God, the holy heavenly word. No others among men, among the children of men, were permitted to do it,
except that these four were chosen for it through the power of God: Matthew and Mark (so the men were called), Luke and John. They were dear to God and worthy of the work.
The ruling God had firmly placed in the hearts of those men the Holy Spirit and a wise mind, many wise words and great understanding,
so that with holy voices they should lift up the good gospel. Nowhere in this world are there words equal to it, words that ever glorify the Ruler, the Lord, more, or strike down evil things,
wicked deeds, or withstand the hatred and the strife of fiends. For he who was the master had a strong mind, gentle and good: the noble Creator, almighty.
These four were then to write it with their fingers, to set it down and sing it and proclaim it: what they had seen and heard of Christ's great power, what he himself said,
showed and did, the many wonders that the mighty Lord worked among men, just as he, the Ruler, had spoken it from the beginning by his power alone,
when he first created this world and then enclosed it all with a single word: heaven and earth and all that they contain of things made and things grown.
All that was then firmly bound by the words of God, and after that it was determined which people should rule most widely over the land, and where the ages of the world should end.
One of those ages still lay ahead of the children of men, and five had passed. The sixth was then to come, blessedly, through the power of God and the birth of Christ,
the best of healers, of the Holy Spirit, into this middle-earth as a help to many, a benefit to the children of men against the hatred of fiends, against the deception of the hidden ones.
At that time the Lord God had granted the Roman people the greatest kingdom. He had strengthened the hearts of their army so that they had conquered every nation.
Those men, confident in their helmets, had won dominion from Rome. Their commanders were stationed in every land; they had power over the peoples, over all the foreign nations.
In Jerusalem, Herod had been chosen as king over the Jewish people, because the emperor, the ruler of the realm in Rome, had set him there among that company.
Yet he was not related by kinship to the descendants of Israel, the nobly born; he did not come from their lineage. He held the kingdom only by the favour of the emperor in Rome,

so that the warrior-retainers, the descendants of Israel, were obedient to him, though they were robbed of their courage and were very unwilling friends, as long as he held power, Herod the mighty, and held the rule of the Jewish people.
Then there was an aged man there, a wise old man, who had a devout mind. He was of the people of Levi's kin, the son of Jacob, a good nation. Zechariah was his name.
He was a very blessed man, for he always served God gladly and acted according to his will. His wife did the same. She was an aged woman:
no heir had been granted to them in their youth. They lived without sin, gave praise to God, were very obedient to the King of Heaven, and honored our Lord.
They did not want to do anything wicked among mankind, or commit any crime, any quarrel or sin. Yet their minds were sorrowful because they could not have an heir, but were childless.
Then he had to carry out God's command there in Jerusalem, as often as his turn came, when the times clearly reminded him.
Then he was to tend the holy service at the temple of the Ruler, the King of Heaven, and do God's service. He was very eager to carry it out with a devout mind.
Then the time came, as wise men had reckoned it in words, when Zechariah was to tend God's temple.

Then many of the Jewish people gathered there at Jerusalem, a host at the temple, where they were to beseech the ruling God very humbly for the Lord's favor, so that the King of Heaven would set them free from evil.
The people stood around the holy house, and the venerable man went inside the temple.
The rest of the host, the Hebrew people, waited outside around the temple until the wise man had done the Ruler's will.
When the old man then carried the incense through the temple and went around the altar with his censers, the mighty servant, devoutly serving his Lord,
doing God's service very gladly with a pure mind, as one ought gladly to carry out a lord's service, terrors came upon him, fear in the temple.
After that he saw an angel of God there inside the temple. The angel spoke to him with his words. He told the old man not to be afraid and told him not to fear:
"Your deeds," he said, "are worthy in the eyes of the Ruler, and your words likewise. Your service pleases him, because you put such trust in his power alone.
I am his angel. Gabriel is my name. I always stand before God, present before the All-Ruler, unless he wishes to send me somewhere on his errand.
Now he has commanded me to travel on this journey and told me to make known to you that a child, born of your aged wife, would be granted to you in this world, a child wise in words.
Never in its life shall it taste strong drink or wine in its world. So fate has arranged for him, the Measurer and the might of God.

He told me to tell you that it would be a companion of the King of Heaven. He told you both to keep it well and raise it faithfully, and said that he wished to give him a great deal of glory in God's kingdom.
He said that the good man should have John as his name. He commanded you both to call the child so when it came,
said that he would become Christ's companion in this wide world, the companion of His own Son, and said that they would both soon come here on His mission."
Then Zechariah spoke and addressed the Lord's angel himself, and began to wonder at these things, at the words:
"How can that happen so," he said, "so late in life? It is far too late for the two of us to gain this, as you say with your words.
For we were fully twenty winters old in our world before this woman came to me;
and now we have been together seventy winters, sharing bench and bed, since I chose her as my bride.
Since in our youth we could not get what we longed for, an heir of our own to raise in our hall,
now that we are so aged — old age has taken our strength from us, so that our sight is dulled and our limbs are slow;
our flesh has fallen away, our skin is unlovely, our looks have faded, our bodies have shrunk, our faces have changed, and so have our minds and our strength —
since we have already been in this world so many a day, it seems a wonder to me how it can happen as you say with your words."

Then the messenger of the King of Heaven was angry in his mind that Zechariah should wonder so at God's work, and would not consider that holy God Himself could make him as young as he was at first, if He so wished.
Then he imposed a punishment on him: he could not speak a single word or talk with his mouth,
"until a son is born to you, a boy borne by your aged wife, a child of good family, a fine one, born into this world."
Then you shall speak words again and have power over your voice; you will not have to be mute any longer."
Then it was soon fulfilled and came true, just as the angel of the All-Ruler had said there in the sanctuary: the old man lost the power of speech, though he bore a wise mind in his breast.
All day the people waited before the sanctuary, and they all wondered why the praiseworthy man, the very wise man, needed to serve his Lord there so long,
longer than any thane had ever done there when they made the Ruler's offering with their hands at the sanctuary. Then the wise man came out of the temple.
The men crowded much closer: they were very eager to learn what true thing he would tell them, what he would show them truly.
He could not then speak a word or say anything to the gathering, except that with his right hand he signed to the people that they should carry out our Ruler's teaching.
The people understood that he had himself plainly seen something divine there, though he could not say anything about it or show it truly.
Then he had made our Ruler's offering, just as his turn had been assigned among men. Soon after that God's might, His great power, was made known:
the wife became pregnant, the woman in her old age: they were to be granted an heir, a truly godly man, a child in the town.
After that the woman waited for what fate had decreed. The winter passed by, and the count of the year went on.
John came into the light of men: his body was beautiful, his skin was fair, and his hair and nails too; his cheeks were comely.
Then wise men, the closest kinsmen above all, hurried there together. They marvelled at the work and asked how it could ever have come about
that a child should be granted in birth to two people so old, unless it were the command of God himself. They clearly perceived that it could not otherwise have happened in this way.
Then an aged man spoke there. He knew many wise words and had great understanding, and he asked eagerly what the boy's name should be in this world:

"It seems to me from his manner and from his bearing that he is better than we are. So I believe that God himself has sent him straight to us from heaven." Then soon after this the mother of the child spoke. She was holding the boy, the child, in her lap:
"God's command came here," she said, "a year ago. In its first words it commanded that he should be called John, according to God's teaching.
I do not dare to change that in my mind in any way, if I have any say in it."
Then a high-spirited man who was her kinsman spoke: "Nobody was ever called that before," he said,
"of our noble-born family or kin. Let us choose another, pleasing name for him. May he enjoy it if he can."
Then the aged man who could speak so well spoke again: "I advise no man to do that," he said, "to begin to change the word of God.
Instead, let us ask his father, who sits there so old and wise in his hall. Though he cannot speak a single word, he can still write a letter in written characters
and write down the name." Then he went nearer, laid a book in his lap, and asked him earnestly to write wisely in written signs what they should call the holy child.
Then he took the book in his hand, and in his mind he thought very gladly of God.
He wisely wrote the name John, and afterwards he also spoke it aloud very wisely. He again had control of his speech, of his understanding and of his wisdom.
The punishment had now passed, the hard affliction that holy, mighty God had laid on him so that he would not forget God in his heart when God next sent his messenger to him.
Then it was not long afterwards before everything was fulfilled just as God almighty had promised mankind for a long time:
that he would send his heavenly child, his own son, here into the world, so that he might redeem all peoples here, the human host, from torment.
Then his trusty messenger, Gabriel, the angel of the All-Ruler, came to the land of Galilee, where he knew of a woman, a lovely maiden. She was called Mary, and she had grown into a young woman.
She was betrothed to a thane, Joseph, a man of good family. She was the daughter of David, a very precious woman, a devoted woman.
There, in the town of Nazareth, the angel of God greeted her face to face, calling her by name, and spoke to her on God's behalf: "Hail to you, Mary," he said,
"you are dear to your Lord and worthy in the Ruler's sight, because you have understanding, woman full of grace. You shall be blessed above all women.
Do not lose heart, and do not be afraid in your spirit. I have not come here to bring you any harm, and I bring no deception.
Among men you shall be the mother of our Lord, and you shall bear and raise the boy, the son of the high King of heaven.
He shall have the name "Healer" (Heliand) among men. Never will there come an end to his wide kingdom, which he shall rule, the glorious king.
Then the maiden, the most beautiful of women, the loveliest of all wives, answered him in turn, answering the angel of God:
"How can that come about," she said, "that I should bear a son? I have never known a man in all my life."
Then the angel of the All-Ruler again had his words ready in answer to the woman: "The Holy Spirit shall come upon you from the meadows of heaven through the power of God.
From that a child shall be granted to you in this world. The power of the Ruler, from the highest King of Heaven, shall overshadow you with its radiance.
There was never a more beautiful birth, nor one so famous among men, for it comes into this wide world through the might of God."
Then, after that message, the woman's mind was turned entirely to God's will. "Then I stand here ready," she said, "for whatever service he wishes to have of me.

I am the handmaid of the God of the peoples. Now I put my trust in this matter. Let it be done to me according to your words, just as is the will of my lord. My mind is not in doubt, nor are my words or my ways."
So I have heard that the woman received God's message very gladly, with a bright mind, with good faith and with pure loyalty.

The Holy Spirit became the child in her womb. And she understood it herself, in her breast and in her heart, and told those she wished to tell that the power of the All-Ruler, holy from heaven, had made her pregnant.
Then Joseph's mind was troubled, his spirit disturbed. He had earlier taken the maiden as his betrothed, a woman of noble lineage whom he had bought to be his bride.
He perceived that she had a child within her. He did not suppose at all that the woman had kept herself so faithfully for him. He did not yet know the Ruler's joyful message.

He no longer wished to take her as his bride, to bring her home as his wife. Instead he began to think in his mind how he might leave her in such a way that no harm at all, no hardship, would come to her.
Nor did he wish afterwards to denounce her before the crowd. He feared that the children of men would take her life.
For such was then the custom of the people, under the old law of the Hebrew people: whatever woman took a mate unlawfully always had to pay for that bed-sharing, the woman with her life.
No woman was ever so good that she might go on living among the people, or remain among the host.
The wise man Joseph, a very good man, began to ponder these matters in his mind: how he might shrewdly leave the maiden.
Not long after that, the Lord's angel, the messenger of heaven's King, came to him there in a dream. He told him to treat her well and to love her in his heart. "Do not be," he said,
"angry with Mary, your maiden. She is an excellent woman. Do not despise her so harshly. You must treat her well and protect her in this world.
Keep up your loving loyalty to each other as you have done before, and keep your friendship well!
Do not let her become any more hateful to you because she carries within her body a child in her womb.
It comes by the command of God, of the Holy Spirit from the meadows of heaven: it is Jesus Christ, God's own child, the Ruler's son.
You shall keep her well and in a holy way. Do not let your mind fall into doubt, or your thoughts be troubled.
Then the man's mind was turned again by those words, so that he took the woman to himself, the maiden, in love: he recognized the power of God, the Ruler's command.
He had a great desire to keep her in such holiness: he cared for her in his household, and she bore the holy spirit so purely, all in God's favour, the goodly man,
until God's mighty decrees reminded her that she was to bring him into the light of men, the best of all children.
Then from the city of Rome, from a powerful man over all this great people, Octavian, a decree and message came over his broad dominion from the emperor to every one of the kings
who sat at home, as widely as his dukes ruled the peoples over all that land.

It was commanded that all men living abroad should go to their homeland, the warriors to their native seat of assembly before their lord's messengers; each was to come to the kindred from which he was descended, born of its cities.
That command was carried out over this wide world. People gathered in every city. The messengers who had come from the emperor travelled everywhere,
men learned in books, and they wrote down in a document very eagerly every name, both land and people, so that no man could escape the tax that every man had to pay for his head.
Then Joseph the good also set out with his household, as God the mighty, the Ruler, willed:
he went to the shining home, the city of Bethlehem, where the native seat of both of them was, of the man and also of the holy maiden, Mary the good.

There in former days was the throne of the famous one, the noble king, David the good, for as long as he, a nobleman among the Hebrews, was allowed to possess the lordship there and hold the high seat.
They were of his household, come from his kindred, of good family, both of them by birth.
There, I have heard, the bright decrees and the power of God reminded Mary that on that journey a son was granted to her, born in Bethlehem, the strongest of children, the most powerful of all kings:
the famous one had come, mighty, into the light of men, as for many a day before there had been omens and many signs in this world.
Then it was all fulfilled just as wise men had foretold long before: with what humility he, the protector of many, wished by his own power to come here to this earthly kingdom.

Then the mother, fairest of women, took him, wrapped him in clothing, in fair adornments, and with her two hands lovingly laid the little man, the child, in a manger, though he had the power of God, the Lord of men.
There the mother sat before him, the woman keeping watch; she guarded him herself and held the holy child. Her mind was not doubtful, the maiden's heart.
Then it became known to many over this wide world. The watchmen found it out, who were outside there as grooms, men on watch tending the horses and the cattle in the field:
they saw the darkness split in two in the air, and the light of God came shining through the clouds and surrounded the watchmen there in the field.
Then the men grew afraid in their minds: they saw a mighty angel of God come there, who spoke to them and told the watchmen not to fear any harm from the light:

"I will tell you," he said, "a dearer thing; I will say it very truly and make known a great power: now Christ is born, on this very night, the blessed child of God, in the city of David, the good Lord.
He is a joy to mankind and a blessing to all people. You can find him there in the town of Bethlehem, the mightiest of children. Take this as the sign that I can tell you in true words:
the child lies there wrapped in a manger, though he is King over all the earth and heaven and over the children of men, the Ruler of the world." Just as he spoke those words,
a countless number of angels came to join that one angel, a holy host from the fields of heaven, the fair people of God. They said much, with many words of praise for the Lord of peoples.
Then they raised a holy song, as they turned back to the plains of heaven through the clouds.
The watchmen heard how the host of angels praised almighty God with very worthy words: "Glory be now," they said,
"to the Lord himself in the highest kingdom of the heavens, and peace on earth to the children of men, to people of good will who acknowledge God with a pure mind."

The shepherds understood that they had been told of a mighty thing, a joyful message. They set out from there to Bethlehem, journeying by night; they had a great longing to be allowed to see Christ himself.
The angel of God had shown them everything with bright signs, so that they could go to him, to the child of God; and they soon found the Lord of the peoples, the lord of men.

Then they spoke praise to God, to the Ruler, with their words, and made known far and wide throughout the bright city what holy sign had been shown to them there from the plains of heaven, fair in the field.
The woman kept all that in her thoughts, the holy maiden, the virgin, in her mind: whatever she heard the men say.
Then the mother, out of love, nurtured him beautifully, the fairest of men, the Lord of many, the holy heavenly child.
On the eighth day men spoke together, many men, very wise men, with the maiden of God, deciding that he should have the name Saviour (Healer),
just as God's angel Gabriel, the Lord's messenger, had said it with true words and commanded the woman when she first conceived the radiant child for this world.
She had a great desire to be allowed to keep him in such a holy way; she served him very gladly.
The year moved on until the peace-child of God had reached forty days and nights.
Then they had to carry out a rite there: they had to present him at Jerusalem to the Ruler at the temple.
That was their custom then, the custom of the people of that land: no woman among the Hebrews could neglect it, if a son was born to her first; she always had to present him there at God's temple.
Then the good pair set out, Joseph and Mary both, from Bethlehem. They had the child with them, holy Christ, and went to the house of God in Jerusalem.
There they had to make his offering to the Ruler at the temple and fulfil the custom of the Jewish people.
There they found a good old man at the temple, nobly born, who had lived so many winters and summers in the light at the temple.
Often he gave praise to God there with a pure mind. He had the Holy Spirit in him, a blessed spirit. He was called Simeon.

The Ruler's power had shown him for a long while that he would not give up this light and turn away from this world until his wish was fulfilled: that he might see Christ himself, the holy King of Heaven.
Then his mind grew very glad in his breast when he saw the child come into the temple. Then he gave thanks to the Ruler, almighty God, that he had seen him with his own eyes.
Then the old man went toward him and gladly took him in his arms. He fully recognized the sign and the token, and also the child of God, the holy King of heaven. "Now, Lord," he said, "I must
gladly ask you, now that I have grown so old, to let your loyal servant now depart from here and go into your peace, where my forefathers went before me,
men of this world. For my wish has now been fulfilled, on the dearest of days: I have seen my Lord, my gracious Master, as I was promised long ago."
You are a great light to all the foreign peoples who did not know the power of the All-Ruler before.
Your coming is for glory and honour, my lord and master, to the descendants of Israel, your own nation, your beloved people."
Then the old man skilfully told the good woman in the sanctuary, and said truly, how her son would become, over this middle-world, for many people: for some a fall,
for some a comfort among the children of men, a joy to the people who would listen to his teachings, and a harm to those who would not listen to Christ's teachings.
"You will yet," he said, "receive sorrow, grief in your heart, when the sons of men punish him with weapons.
That will be a great trouble for you, a hardship to endure." The maiden understood all the wise man's words.
Then an old woman also came walking into the sanctuary. She was called Anna, the daughter of Phanuel. She had served her Lord well, to his satisfaction; she was an excellent woman.
After her maidenhood, once she belonged to a man, a nobleman, in marriage, that noble maiden was permitted to keep a home with her bridegroom for seven winters together.
Then, as I have heard, sorrow came to her there, for the great might of the Measurer, cruel fate, parted them.
After that she was a widow at the sanctuary of peace for eighty-four winters of her life, and she never left the temple, but served her Lord, God, well there day and night.

She too came walking there at that same time. At once she recognized the holy child of God, and made known to the men, to the people throughout the temple, great good news. She said that the Saviour's salvation had drawn near to them, the help of the King of Heaven:

"Now the holy Christ, the Ruler himself, has come into this temple to redeem the people who have waited here so long in this middle-world, for many a while, a needy people. So now mankind can rejoice in this."
Many people rejoiced throughout the temple. They heard great good news told about God.
Then the woman had made the offering in the sanctuary, just as their law commanded them and as the books in the bright city directed, the handiwork of holy men.
Then Joseph and Mary, the holy household, went home from Jerusalem. They always had the King of Heaven with them as their companion, the Son of the Lord,
the protector of many. So it never became known any more widely in this world than his will allowed, the mind of the King of Heaven.
Though here and there a holy man recognized Christ, it was never made known at the king's court to the men who were not loyal to him in their hearts,
but it was kept hidden from them in word and deed until men came from the east, three very wise men, bold thanes, travelling to that people on a long road across the land:
they followed a bright sign and sought the child of God with a pure mind. They wanted to bow down to him and declare themselves his followers; God's decree drove them on.
Then they found Herod there, the powerful one, sitting in his hall, the cruel-spoken king, proud among his men

(he was always eager for murder). They greeted him courteously, in a manner fit for a king, gracefully in his hall, and he asked at once what errand had brought them from abroad, these men on their journey through foreign lands:
"Are you bringing twisted gold as a gift for some man? Why have you come here like this on foot, travelling with provisions?
Indeed, you are men from somewhere far away, from other peoples. I can see that you are of noble birth, of a good family and lineage:
never before have such visitors come here from other peoples, not since I was granted rule over this people and this wide kingdom.
You must tell me truly, before the people here, why you have come to this land."
Then the men from the east, men wise in words, answered him: "We can truly," they said,
"easily tell you our errand and say truthfully why we have made this journey here from the east to this land."
Long ago there were men of noble birth in our country, men of good speech, who promised us a great deal of good, help from the King of Heaven, in true words.
Among them was a wise man, old and very learned (that was long ago), our ancestor, east of here. Since then there has never been any man so wise in speech.

He could tell God's message, because the Lord of peoples had granted that, here on earth, he could hear the words of the Ruler from above. Because of this that thane's understanding and thinking were great.

When he had to leave this world, give up his dwellings and the company of his kinsmen, leave the joy of people and seek the other light, he told his followers, his heirs, to come closer, and then he told his men truthfully
(all of it later came to pass in this world): he said that a famous wise king, great and mighty, of the very best birth, would come here into this middle-world;
he said that it would be the child of God, and that he would rule this world forever, earth and heaven alike.
He said that on the very day his mother bore him, the blessed one, into this middle-world, a bright star of heaven would shine in the east,
such as we had never had before, between earth and heaven or anywhere else: never such a child and never such a sign.
He ordered three men of the people to stay there waiting for it. He told them to watch carefully for the moment they saw it rise in the east,
God's sign moving. He told them to make ready at once, and ordered that we follow it wherever it went before us, westward across this world.
Now it has all come true, come about through God's power: the king has been born, brought forth bold and strong.
We have seen his sign shine brightly among the stars of heaven, so that I know that the holy Lord, the mighty one, marked it out himself.
Every morning we saw the bright star gleam, and we followed the sign here, sometimes over roads and sometimes through forests.
The greatest of all our wishes would be to see him ourselves, and to know where we should look for this king in this empire.
Tell us which of these clans he has been born into."
Then grief came into Herod's breast and pain to his heart. His mind began to seethe, and his spirit with sorrows.
He heard it said that he would have a superior there, a mightier king from a good family, more blessed among the companions.
Then he ordered that all the good men in Jerusalem be gathered together, those who were the wisest of speech and who truly knew the most book-learning in their hearts.
And he questioned them with words, very eagerly, the hostile-minded man, the king of the people: where in the earthly kingdom Christ, the best of men of peace, was to be born.
Then the people spoke back to him, the company answered truthfully, saying that they knew for certain that he was to be born in Bethlehem:
"So it is written in our books, wisely recorded, as the prophets, very wise and very learned men, spoke long ago through God's power,

that from Bethlehem a shepherd of the cities would come into this light, a beloved guardian of the land, a mighty giver of counsel, who shall rule the people of the Jews and be generous with his gifts over the middle world to many nations."
Then I have heard that soon after this the cruel-minded king told the words of the prophets to the strangers, the men who were there in a foreign land, having travelled from far away.
And after that he asked them when, on the eastern ways, they had first seen the king's star come, the sign shining brightly from heaven.
They did not want to hide anything of it from him, but told him truthfully.
Then he told them to go on their journey and to find out everything about their errand concerning the child's coming. And the king himself, the lord of the Jews, gave a very strict command
to the wise men, before they travelled on westward, that they should come back and tell him where he could seek out the king in his dwelling.
He said that he wanted to go there with his companions to worship the child. But he intended to become his slayer by the edges of weapons.
But the ruling God had other thoughts about these plans: he could accomplish more and carry it out in this light. That is still evident long after: God's power made known.
Then the signs went forth again, splendid beneath the clouds. Then the wise men were eager to travel. They left that place, bold in their mission: they wanted to seek out God's child himself.
They had no more companions from there; there were just the three of them. They understood the difference between things; they were wise men who carried the gifts.

Then they watched very wisely beneath the sheen of the clouds, up to high heaven, to see how the white stars travelled. They recognized it as God's sign, which had been made and sent here into this world because of Christ.
The men went after it and followed wisely (the Power helped them) until the travel-weary men saw the bright beacon of God, the gleam in the sky, standing still.
The bright star shone white over the house where the holy child dwelt contentedly and where the woman held him, the excellent maiden.
Then the thegns' hearts became glad in their breasts. By the beacon they understood that they had found God's child of peace, the holy King of heaven.
Then the men from the east, travel-weary men, went into the house with their gifts. At once the men recognized the ruling Christ.
The wanderers fell on their knees before the child and greeted the good one in the manner due to a king. They brought him the gifts as signs of God: gold and incense, and myrrh with them.
The men who were loyal to their lord stood ready, and at once they received the gifts gracefully with their hands.
Then the wise men, the travel-weary men, went off to their lodging, to a guest-hall.

There, as they slept at night, God's angel showed them a dream. He made them dream, just as the Lord himself, the Ruler, willed, so that it seemed to them that a man commanded them with words that they
should travel from there by another way, the noblemen, and journey to their land, and not seek again the hateful man Herod, the proud king. Then morning came, shining, into this world.
Then the wise men began to tell their dreams. They themselves recognized the Ruler's word, for they carried great wisdom in their breasts.
They prayed to the All-Ruler, the high King of heaven, that they might [?] his favour henceforth and do his will. They said that they had turned their thoughts, their minds, to him every morning.
Then the men, the noblemen from the east, travelled away from there, just as God's angel had directed them with words. They took another way and followed God's teaching.
The messengers from the east, the travel-weary men, would not tell the king of the Jews anything about the child's birth. Instead they turned back, as they wished.

Then soon after that, God's angel, the Ruler's messenger, came to speak to Joseph. The Lord's messenger told him in a dream, as he slept at night, that the cruel king wanted to seek out God's child and take his life:
"Now you must lead him away into the land of the Egyptians and stay among that people with God's child and with the good maid-
-en. Live among that people until word comes to you from your lord that you may lead the holy child, your Lord, back again to this land."
Then Joseph sprang up from the dream in his guest-hall and at once recognized God's command.
The thegn set off on the journey from there with the maiden and sought another people over the broad mountains. He wanted to carry God's child away from enemies.
Then after that, Herod the king learned, where he sat in his kingdom, that the wise men had turned from the west, east to their homeland, and had gone another way.

He knew that they did not want to come back to his hall and tell him about their errand. Then his heart became sorrowful and his mind mournful. He said the men, the heroes, had done this to him as an insult.
Then, as he sat so troubled and raged in his breast, he said that he could think of a better plan, another one:
"Now I know his age, how many winters he has: now I can bring it about that he will never grow old on this earth, here among this people."
Then Herod gave his harsh command across his kingdom: the king of the people ordered his warriors to go out,
and ordered them to cut off the heads of all those children with their own hands, all the boys around Bethlehem, as many as had been born there within two years.
The king's companions did this evil. So many little boys had to die there, free of sin.
Never before or since has there been a more terrible passing of young people, a more wretched death. Women wept, many mothers, as they saw their children destroyed:
a mother could not protect her child at all. Though she held her own child, dear and little, in her two arms, the boy still had to give up his life in front of his mother.

The killers did not shrink from crime or wickedness: with the edges of their weapons they did a great and evil deed. Many young boys fell. The mothers wept over the slaughter of their little children.
There was mourning in Bethlehem, the loudest wailing: even if someone had cut their hearts in two with a sword, no more painful thing could ever have happened in this world
to the many women, the young wives in Bethlehem: they saw their children in front of them, little boys, die in agony, bloody in their laps.
The killers punished an innocent band: the men did not hold back at all from wicked deeds. They wanted to kill the mighty one, Christ himself.
But mighty God had saved him from their hatred, so that men led him away from there by night into the land of Egypt,
men with Joseph, to the green plain, the best of lands, where a river flows, the great stream of the Nile, north to the sea, the fairest of waters.
There the peace-child of God lived as he wished, until fate carried off Herod the king, so that he left the children of men and the proud joy of men.
Then his heir was to hold power over the realm. He was called Archelaus, war-leader of helmet-bearing men: he was to rule the people of the Jews, the host around Jerusalem.
Then word came there in Egypt to the noble man [Joseph]: God's angel, the Lord's messenger, spoke there to Joseph and told him to lead the child back from there to his own land.
"Now Herod the king has given up this light," he said; "he wanted to hunt him before and put his life in danger.
Now you can lead the child in peace among your people, now that the king, that overproud man, is no longer alive."
Joseph understood God's sign completely. The good man quickly made himself ready with the maiden, since they both wanted to leave there with the child:
they carried out the bright decrees, the Ruler's will, just as he had told them before in his words.
Then Joseph and Mary, the holy household of heaven's King, went back to the land of Galilee; they lived in the town of Nazareth.
There Christ the Savior grew up among the people and became full of wisdom, and God's grace was upon him. He was dear to all his mother's kin. In his goodness that man was not like other men.
When he was twelve years old, the time came when the Jewish people were to serve their God there in Jerusalem and do his will.
Then a great crowd of Jews gathered there in the temple in Jerusalem. Mary herself was there among the company, and she had her son with her, God's own child.
When the men had performed the offering in the temple, as it was commanded in their law, carried out according to the custom of their land, then the people went back from there,

the men, as they wished; and the mighty Child of God stayed behind there in the temple, so that his mother did not truly know he was there; she thought instead that he was going on with the company, travelling with their friends.
Then afterward, on the next day, the woman of noble lineage, the blessed maiden, learned that he was not among the companions.
Then Mary's heart was full of sorrow, grieving in her heart, when she did not find the holy child among the people: the maiden of God mourned greatly.
Then they went back to Jerusalem to look for their son. They found him sitting there inside the temple, where the wise men,
very learned men, read and studied God's law, how they should give praise with their words to the one who created this world.

There in their midst sat the mighty Child of God, Christ the All-Ruler, in such a way that those who were supposed to guard the temple could not recognize him at all, and he questioned them eagerly with wise words.
They all wondered how such a childlike person could ever utter such sayings with his mouth.
There his mother found him sitting among the company, and she greeted her son, wise among the people, and spoke to him with her words:
"Why did you want to bring such sorrow on your mother, dearest of men, that I, so sad at heart, a grieving woman, had to search for you among these townspeople?"
Then the child answered her with wise words: "Why, you know well," he said,
"that it is right for me to be where I am meant to dwell, as is my wish, where my mighty Father has power."
The people, the men in the temple, did not understand why he spoke that word and uttered it with his mouth:
Mary kept it all and hid it in her breast, whatever wise words she heard her child speak.
Then Joseph and Mary went back from Jerusalem. They had with them as their companion the Son of the Lord, the best of all children who were ever born, a son from a mother:
they loved him with a pure mind, and he, God's own Child, was so obedient through his humility to his kinsmen, his parents:
in his childhood he did not yet want to make his great strength known to people, that he had such might and power in this world, but he waited willingly, obedient among the people, for thirty years,
before he wanted to show any sign there, or tell his companions that he himself was the Lord of men in this middle world.
So the holy Child of God had kept to himself words and wisdom and the greatest of all understanding, a very wise mind:
no one could tell from his speech or his words that he had such understanding, that the young man had such thoughts, but he waited obediently in this way for bright signs.
The time had not yet come for him to make himself known throughout this middle world and to teach the people how they should keep their faith and do God's will.
Yet many people throughout the land knew that he had come into this light, though they could not clearly recognize him until he himself chose to tell them.

Now John had grown up from his youth in a wilderness. There were no other people there; he alone served the all-ruling God there as His thane. He had left the company of people, the fellowship of men.
There in the wilderness a mighty word came to him from heaven, the good voice of God, and it commanded John to proclaim Christ's coming and His great power over this middle-earth.
It told him to say truly in words that the kingdom of heaven had come near to the children of men in that land, had drawn close to the people, the most delightful of good things.
Then he had a great desire to be allowed to speak of such blessings.

Then he set off walking along the course of the Jordan, its waters flowing freely. All day long he made it known to the people throughout the land that they should atone with fasting for their many wicked deeds, their own sins,
"so that you may become clean," he said. "The kingdom of heaven has come near to the children of men."
Now let your own sins grieve you in your hearts, the evil things you have done in this light, and listen to my teachings, and turn according to my words.
I shall baptize you worthily in water, though I cannot forgive your deeds, your own sins, so that through my handiwork you become clean of evil deeds.

But there is one who has come into this light, mighty among men, and who stands in your midst, though you do not want to see Him yourselves. He shall baptize you in the name of your Lord, in the Holy Spirit.
He is Lord over all. He can free each and every man from evil thoughts and from sins, whoever is so blessed in this world
as to have the will to carry out what the Child of God wishes and commands of these people.

I have come here into this world as His messenger, and I am to clear the way for Him and teach these people how they should hold to their faith with a pure mind, so that they need not go to hell, into the hot fire.
A man will be glad in his heart for this at many times, whoever gives up that wickedness, willingly gives up the service of the Fiend.
In this way whoever keeps pure loyalty up to the almighty God can win for himself what is good, the favour of the King of Heaven."
Because of these teachings many men, the people, then truly believed that he was the Ruler Christ Himself, because he spoke so much truth, such true words.
Then this became widely known throughout that given land to every man, to warriors in their dwellings.
Then messengers of the Jewish people came there from Jerusalem, from the city, to seek him, and they asked whether he was the child of God,
"of whom people here long ago," they said, "men truly said that he was to come into this world."
Then John spoke and answered the messengers boldly: "I am not," he said, "the Child of God, the true Ruler Christ. Instead, I am to clear the way for Him, my Lord."
"The heroes asked, the men who were there on the errand, the messengers from the city:
"If you are not the child of God, are you then Elijah, who was here in former days among this people? He is to come again into this middle-world. Tell us what man you are!
"Are you one of those wiser prophets who were here before? What shall we truthfully tell the people about you?
Never before has another such man come here into this middle-world, so famous for his deeds.
Why do you perform baptism here among this people, if you are not any one of the prophets?" Then the good John had a wise answer ready in return:
"I am the forerunner of my lord, my beloved master; I am to prepare this land, this people, according to his will.
From his word I have a strong voice with me, though many people here in this wilderness will not understand it.
I am in no way like my lord. He is so strong in his deeds, so famous and so mighty that it will become known to many
men throughout this world that I am not worthy to untie the straps on his shoes, though I am his own servant, the servant of so powerful a lord.
So much better is he than I. There is no equal of this messenger anywhere on earth, nor shall there be one hereafter in this world.
Turn your will toward him, people, and your faith; then your mind will be glad for a long time,

when you leave behind the torment of hell and the revelry of the hateful ones, and seek for yourselves God's light, the home of heavenly riches, the eternal kingdom, the high field of heaven. Do not let your minds doubt!"
So the young man spoke then about God's teachings, making them known to people.
Many of the children of Israel gathered there at Bethany. Companions of kings came there to John, people came for the teachings, and they received their faith.
He baptized them every day and condemned their deeds, their wicked desires, and praised to them the word of God, his lord:
"The kingdom of heaven," he said, "will be ready for any man who turns his thoughts to God and
will believe purely in the Savior and carry out his teachings." Then it was not long before God's own child, the precious son of the Lord, set out from Galilee to seek baptism.
The Ruler's child was then at his full growth, since he had lived thirty winters among the people in his world.
Then he came, as he willed, to where John was gloriously baptizing many people in the river Jordan all the long day.
As soon as he saw his lord, his gracious master, his mind grew glad, because his wish had come true. Then he spoke to him in words, that very good man, John to Christ:
"Now you come to my baptism, my lord and master, best of men. I ought rather to come to yours, because you are the mightiest of all kings."
"Christ himself, the Ruler, truly commanded that he should speak no more of those words: "You know that it befits us thus," he said,
"to fulfil every righteousness, now from this time on, according to God's will." John stood and baptized a great host of people all day long, men in the water, and also the Ruler Christ,

the lord, the king of heaven, with his own hands, in the best of all baths, and there he bowed to him in prayer, mighty, on his knee. Christ went up, fair, out of the water, the peace-child of God, the dear guardian of the people.
As he stepped onto the land, the doors of heaven opened, and the Holy Spirit came down from the All-Ruler above to Christ.
It had the likeness of a swift bird, a precious dove, and it sat upon our Lord's shoulder and stayed over the Ruler's child.
Then a word came there from heaven, loud from the high firmament, and greeted the Savior himself, Christ, the best of all kings.
It said that he himself had chosen him from his kingdom, said that the Son pleased him best of all men ever born, said that he was the dearest of all children to him.
Then John was allowed, just as God willed, to see and hear that. Soon after that he made it known to people that they had a mighty lord there:
"This," he said, "is the son of the king of heaven, the one Ruler of all: I will be a witness of this in this world,
because the word of God, the voice of the Lord, told me, when he commanded me to baptize men in water, that wherever I truly saw the Holy Spirit
come down with power from the plain of heaven upon any man in this middle-earth, that one, it said, would be Christ, the precious son of the Lord.
He shall baptize in the Holy Spirit and heal many people's wicked deeds.
He has power from God to release every one of the people from guilt and sins. This is Christ himself, God's own child, the best of men, a protection against enemies.
Well may your minds be glad of this in this world, that your wish has been granted, so that while you are living you have seen the Guardian of the land himself.
Now many a soul may quickly go free of sins into God's will, released from evils, if it will work faithfully toward its Friend and believe firmly in the Ruler Christ.
That will be to the benefit of any man who gladly does so."
So I have heard that John then commended the teaching of Christ, his Lord, to each and every one of the people, and the winning of heaven's kingdom, the greatest of goods, blessed eternal life.
Then after the baptism the good Lord himself went into a wilderness, the Ruler's Son; the Lord of men stayed there in the solitude a long while.
He had no more people, no men as companions, just as he himself had chosen. He wanted to let powerful beings tempt him there, Satan himself, who always lures people into sin, men into wicked works.
He knew Satan's mind, his hostile will, how in the beginning he first deceived this world, the great nations, with sins,
when through treachery and lies he led astray the married couple, Adam and Eve, so that after their passing away the children of men, the souls of men, went to hell.
Then mighty God, the Ruler, wished to reverse this and to give this people high heaven's kingdom; therefore he sent his holy messenger here, his son.
That grieved Satan deeply in his mind: he begrudged mankind heaven's kingdom. He then wished to do the mighty Son of the Lord the same wrongs
with which in earlier days he had secretly deceived Adam, so that Adam became hateful to his Lord; he had led him astray with sins. That is what he then wanted to do to the Savior Christ himself.
But the Ruler's child had set his mind firmly against the evil-doer, his heart so hardened: he wished to give heaven's kingdom to the people.
The Guardian of the land, the Lord of men, kept a fast there for forty nights, so that he tasted no food there.

For all that time the hidden beings, the fiend with his hateful mind, did not dare to come nearer to him or address him face to face. He thought that he was simply God, mighty, without anything of mankind in him, the holy Guardian of heaven.
Then, when he let himself go hungry, so that in his human nature he began to long for food after the forty days, the fiend came nearer, the dark evil-doer:
thought that he was certainly just a simple man; then he spoke to him with his words, the spear-enemy addressed him: "If you are God's son," he said,
"why then, if you have the power, best of all children, do you not command bread to be made from these stones?
Cure your hunger." Then the holy Christ spoke in reply: "The children of men," he said, "cannot
live, these people, on bread alone, but they must live in this world by the teaching of God and must do the works that are proclaimed by the holy tongue, by the voice of God:
that is life for every one of men, of people, who is willing to carry out what is commanded by the word of the Ruler."
Then the monstrous fiend began to try again and came nearer a second time, and tested his Lord.
The peace-child put up with the will of the hostile one and gave him power to test him about his great strength; then he let himself be led by the harmer of people,
so that he set him up in Jerusalem at God's temple, at the very top, on the highest of all houses, and the hostile one spoke mocking words with great boasting:
"If you are God's son," he said, "glide down from here to the earth."
It was written long ago, set down in books, how the almighty Father has commanded his angels to be your guardians on every way and to hold you up in their hands.
Indeed, you need never strike your feet against a rock, against hard stone." Then the holy Christ, best of all sons, spoke in reply:
"It is also written in books," he said, "that you shall not test your Master, your Lord, too hard: that brings you no benefit at all."
Then for the third time he let the harmer of people bring him up onto a high mountain:
there the evil-minded one let him look out over all the mighty nations, delightful wealth and worldly kingdoms, and all such riches
as this earth holds of fair goods, and then the fiend spoke to him and said that he would give him all of it, so good, the high lordships,
"if you will bow to me, fall at my feet and have me as your lord, and pray at my bosom.
Then I will let you fully enjoy all this wealth that I have shown you here."
Then the holy Christ would no longer listen to the words of the hateful one. He drove him away from his favour and swept Satan away,
and soon afterwards the best of all children spoke. He said that people should pray up to the almighty God and serve him alone very humbly, many thanes, warriors seeking his favour:
"There help is ready for every man." Then the wicked foe, Satan, very sorrowful in mind, went away from there, the fiend down into the deep valleys.
Then a great host of God's angels came there from the All-Ruler above to Christ. Afterwards they were to give him discipleship and service, and serve him humbly:
so should one do for the God of the peoples, the Lord, to win his favour, the King of heaven.
The blessed Child of God stayed there in the great wilderness for a long while, until he came to prefer making his great power known, to the joy of the people.
Then he left the shelter of the forest, the land of the wilderness, and sought again the company of men, the great people and the joyful throng of men. He went then along the bank of the Jordan.
There John found him, that peace-child of God, his Lord, the holy King of heaven. When John saw him walking, he said to the men, his disciples:
"This is the Lamb of God, who shall free this wide world from its wicked sins, from the crime of mankind: the glorious Lord, the mightiest of kings."
Christ, God's own child, then went on into the land of Galilee. He travelled to his friends, where he had been raised and gloriously brought up, and Christ told his kin in words,
the mightiest of kings, how they should atone for their own sins. He commanded them to repent of their many harmful deeds and give up their wicked acts:
"Now it has all been fulfilled, just as the old men here once foretold, when they promised you the kingdom of heaven for your help.
Now it has already come near through the power of the Savior. From now on, all who gladly wish to serve God and work according to his will may enjoy it."
Then many of the people were filled with delight. The teachings of Christ became very sweet to that company.
He then began to gather men as his disciples: good men, wise in words. He went then along the shore of a water, a lake that the Jordan had formed beside the land of Galilee.
There, by the river, he found Andrew and Peter sitting, the two brothers, where they were busily spreading their nets on the broad water, fishing in the flood.
There on the shore of the sea the peace-child of God himself greeted them. He told them to follow him and said that he would give them a great share of God's kingdom:

"Just as you two catch fish here in the stream of the Jordan, so you two shall yet draw the children of men into your hands, so that many people may pass into the kingdom of heaven through your teaching."
Then both brothers became eager in their minds. They recognized the child of God, the beloved Lord.
Andrew and Peter left everything they had by the river, all the gains they had won by the water.
They had a great desire to go with the child of God, together in his company, and they were to receive a blessed reward.
So it is with any man who wishes to serve for the Lord's favor and do his will.
When they came further along the shore of the water, they found an old man sitting there by the sea with his two sons, James and John, who were young men.
Father and sons sat up on a sandbank and busily wove and mended with both hands the nets they had torn in the sea the night before.
There the blessed child of God himself spoke to them. He told James and John, both of them young men, to go with him on his journey.
Then the words of Christ meant so much to them in this world that by the shore of the water they left their old father alone, the aged man by the flood, along with all the property they owned there,
their nets and nail-built boats. They chose the saving Christ, the Holy One, as their Lord, for they needed to serve him to earn his help. So it is for every thane, every man in this world.
Then the Ruler's son went on with the four, and then Christ chose for himself the fifth at a place of trade: a king's retainer, a man wise of mind.
He was called Matthew. He was an officer of noble men and had to take in tribute and tolls there for his lord's hands.
He had good loyalty and noble bearing. He gave up everything together: gold and silver and many gifts, precious treasures. And he became our Lord's man.
The king's thane chose Christ as his lord, a more generous giver of treasure than his liege lord had been before in this world. He took up other things for himself, a more lasting reward.

Then it became known to all the people, in every town, how the Child of God gathered companions. He himself spoke so many wise words and so much truth, showed so much that was bright, and worked many signs in this world.
It was plain in his words, and in his deeds as well, that he was the Lord, the heavenly Lord, and had come as a help into this middle-world for the children of men, for the people in this light.
He often made it plain in that land, when he gloriously worked so many signs there, when he healed the lame and the blind with his hands
and freed many people from infirmity, from such sicknesses as the fiends had cast on the children of men as the heaviest of all: a very long-lasting sickbed.
Then the people traveled there every day, to where our Lord himself was among his band of companions,
until a great, mighty crowd of many nations had gathered there, though they did not all come with the same faith, men with one purpose.
Some of them sought the Ruler's Child, many poor people who needed food, so that they might receive food and drink there from the people in the crowd,
for many a good thane was there who gladly gave their alms to poor men. Others in turn were of the Jewish race, a hostile people.
They had traveled there to lie in wait for our Lord's deeds and words. They had hostile minds and hateful intent.
They wanted to make Christ the Ruler hateful to the people, so that they would not listen to his teachings or turn to his will.

Others in turn were very wise men, discerning men and worthy to God, chosen among the people. They came there for the teachings of Christ, so that they might hear his holy word, learn it and carry it out.
They had held fast to him with their faith and had devout minds. They became his thanes so that, after their last days, he would bring them up into the bliss of the people, into God's kingdom.
He gladly received many of mankind and promised them protection for a long time, and he was well able to fulfill it.

Then a very great host of people gathered there around the famous Christ. Then he saw a crowd of eager people coming together from all lands, from all wide ways. His fame had spread so widely among many.
Then the Mighty One himself, the most powerful of children, went up onto a mountain to sit apart, and he himself chose twelve, counted out:
faithful men, good men, whom he as Lord wanted to have always in his company as his disciples, every day from then on.
Then he named them by name and commanded them to come nearer to him: first of all Andrew and Peter, two brothers, and with them both James and John.
They were dear to God; he was gracious to them in his heart. By birth the two of them were sons of one man. The Child of God chose them as good disciples, and many other men, famous men:
Matthew and Thomas, two Judases, and the other James, his own cousin. Christ and James came of the kin of two sisters; they were good kinsmen.
Then the rescuing Christ had counted out nine of the men there, faithful men. Then he himself also commanded the tenth to come with the companions:
he was called Simon. He also commanded Bartholomew to come up onto the mountain, away from the other people, and Philip with him, faithful men.
Then the twelve went together, the warriors, to the private council where the Ruler sat, the protector of many, who wished to help all mankind against the oppression of hell
and to protect against the inferno anyone who is willing to carry out the beloved teachings that he meant to show the people there through his great wisdom.
Then the companions he himself had chosen, the Ruler among the host, came nearer around the rescuing Christ.
Wise men stood around the Son of God, men very eager and willing.
They longed for his words. They thought and were silent, waiting for what the Lord of peoples, the Ruler himself, would make known to them in words for the good of these people.
Then the Shepherd of the land, God's own Child, sat facing the men. With his speech he wanted to teach the people many wise sayings: how they should give praise to God in this worldly kingdom.
He sat there, silent, and looked at them for a long while. The holy Lord was gracious to them in his mind and kind in his heart. Then he unlocked his mouth.

The Son of the Ruler showed many glorious things in words. With wise words he told the men whom he, Christ the All-Ruler, had chosen to come there for that speech which of all mankind, of the race of men, would be the most worthy to God.
He told them then in truth. He said that blessed were those people in this middle-earth who here in their hearts were poor through humility:
"To them is given the eternal kingdom, very holy, everlasting life in the meadow of heaven."
He said that the meek were also blessed: "They will possess the glorious earth, that same kingdom."
He said that those who here weep for their wicked deeds were also blessed: "In return they will receive what they long for, comfort in their Lord's kingdom."
Blessed also are the men who here long for what is good, so that they judge rightly. For this they will be filled in the kingdom of the Lord because of their righteous deeds.
Such good things will those men receive who here judge rightly and do not want to deceive people in secret when they sit at the assembly.
Blessed also are those in whose breasts a merciful mind grows here: to them the holy Lord, mighty himself, will be merciful.
Blessed also, among these many people, are those who have cleansed their hearts: they will see the Ruler of heaven in his kingdom.
He said that blessed also were "those who live peaceably among this people and will not stir up any fight or quarrel by their own deeds:
they shall be called sons of the Lord, for he will be gracious to them; for that they may long enjoy his kingdom itself."
He said that blessed also were the men who wanted what is right, "and for that endure the hatred and insults of powerful men:
to them also God's meadow in heaven is given afterward, and spiritual life ever after, forever, whose end never comes: the wealth of the delightful one."
So then Christ the Ruler had counted out eight blessings there for the men and proclaimed them;
with them anyone may always win the kingdom of heaven if he wishes to have it. Otherwise he will forever afterwards lack wealth and joy, once he gives up this world,
his earthly life, and seeks another light for himself, pleasant or hateful, according to what he has done here among these people in this world,
just as Christ the All-Ruler, mightiest of kings, God's own Son, told it there in his words to his disciples: "You will also be blessed," he said,
"when people throughout this land bring charges against you and speak hostile words, mock you, do you much harm in this world and inflict punishment on you,
heap wicked speech and enmity on you, call your teaching lies, and do you much hateful harm because of your lord.
Therefore always let your mind [?], and your life, be in joy, for your reward stands ready for you in God's kingdom, for every good deed, great and manifold:
that is given to you as a reward because you endured hardship here before, punishment in this world.
It is worse for the others, grimmer things are in store for them, for those who have good things here, broad worldly wealth:
they use up their joys here and enjoy plenty of them; afterward, after their going hence, the men shall endure harsher things.

Then those who were in joys here before will weep over their misery there, those who live in every pleasure and will not give up any of it, the evil-minded ones, nor the hateful deeds that it entices into their minds.
Then their reward comes to them, evil hardship; then they must see its end in sorrow.
Then their minds become sore, because they followed the will of this world so much, men in their hearts.

Now you must rebuke them for that wickedness, restrain them with words, just as I can now show you and tell you truly, my companions, with true words: that from now on you shall be the salt of this world,
of sinful men, to amend their evil deeds, so that the people take hold of better things and abandon the fiend's work, the devil's deeds, and seek their Lord's kingdom.
So you shall turn many people with your teachings, in accordance with my will.
But if any one of you then goes bad and abandons the teaching he ought to carry out, then it is with him as with the salt that is scattered widely by the shore of the sea:
then it is good for nothing, but the children of men trample it with their feet, people on the sand. So it will be for the one who is to proclaim God's word to men:
if he lets his mind waver, so that he will not, with a pure heart, draw people toward the kingdom of heaven with his speech and tell God's message, but turns away from the words,

then the Ruler becomes angry with him, the mighty one, the stern of mind, and so do the children of men as well; he becomes loathsome to all the great nations, to the people, if his teachings are worthless."
So he spoke then wisely and told God's message; the guardian of the land taught his people with a pure mind. The men stood, the warriors around the Son of God, very eagerly, the men willingly:
they had a longing for the words; they pondered and were silent; they heard the Lord of the peoples tell God's law to the children of men; he promised them the kingdom of heaven and spoke to the men:
"I can also tell you, my companions, with true words, that from now on you shall be the light of this world for the children of men, fair among humankind over many a people, radiant and delightful:
your great works, by which you make your mind known, cannot be hidden, any more than the city which stands on a mountain, high on a sea-cliff,
can be hidden, the gigantic work; no more can your words, your deeds, be hidden from men in this middle-world.
Do as I teach you: let your great light shine for the people, for the children of men, so that they understand your mind,
your works and your will, and with a pure mind praise the ruling God, the heavenly Father, for it in this light, because he gave you such teachings.
No one who has a light shall hide it from people or cover it up too closely, but he shall set it up high in the hall, so that all who are inside there may see it alike, the men in the hall.
Likewise you shall not hide your holy word from the people in this land, nor conceal it from the race of men, but you shall spread it high, the command of God,
so that each and every one of the children, the people over all this land, may understand it and carry it out, as very wise men spoke it in words in former days,
when men kept the old law; and also, as I can now tell you, every one of all men shall serve God even more strongly than the old law commanded there.

Do not think in any way that I came into this world for this, that I wish to overturn the old law, to bring it down among this people, or to reject the words of the prophets, which such truthful men openly proclaimed here.
Sooner shall both pass away, heaven and earth, which now stand enclosed, than any of the words which they truly proclaimed here to these people should remain unfulfilled in this light.
I did not come into this world in order to cast down the words of the prophets, but I shall fulfil them, increase and renew them for the children of men, for the benefit of this people.
That was written long ago in the old law—you often heard men wise in words say it—:
whoever in this world does this, that he deprives another of life, robs him of life, the children of men shall sentence him to death.
Now I want to take it deeper for you, further: whoever out of enmity, one man against another, becomes angry in his mind, in his breast—because they are all brothers,
the blessed people of God, bound by kinship, men joined by family—then if anyone becomes so angry in his mind with another that he would want to rob him of life, if he could accomplish it:
then he is at once outlawed and must forfeit his life, under the same judgment as the other man who, by the strength of his hand, took another man's head.
It is also written in the law in true words, as you all know, that a man shall love his neighbor eagerly in his heart, be loyal to his kinsmen, good to his relatives,
be generous with his gifts, gladden every one of his friends, and shall hate his enemy, withstand him with strife and with a strong mind, and defend himself against the hostile.
But I tell you truly now, more fully, before this people, that you shall love your enemies in your heart, just as you do your kinsmen, in God's name.
Do them much good, show them a pure mind and loyal faithfulness, love in return for their hostility.
That is a lasting counsel for any man whose mind strives to do this toward his enemy.
Then you may have the benefit that you may be called sons of the King of Heaven, his joyful children. You cannot gain a better counsel for yourselves in this world.
I also tell you truly, each of the children, that with an angry mind you cannot give any of your goods to the Ruler at God's houses
in such a way that it is worthy for him to receive, as long as you harbor any enmity, any malice of mind, against another man.

First you must always reconcile yourself with your adversary and speak with him in agreement; afterwards you may give your treasures at God's altar. Then they are worthy to the Good One, the King of Heaven.
You must serve more for his favor and fulfill God's will more than other Jews do, if you wish to possess the eternal kingdom and see everlasting life.
I shall also tell you further how the old law commands there that no man shall seduce another's wife, a woman, into wickedness.
But I also tell you truly that a man's eyes can lead him badly astray into dark sin, if he lets his mind entice him so that he begins to desire what is not to be his.
Then he has already committed sin within himself, and has fastened hell-torment in his heart.
If, then, a man's eye or his right hand wants to lead any of his limbs astray onto a hateful path, then it is better for every man, for the children of men,
that he throw it away and cut that limb off his body and come up to heaven without it, than that he go to the inferno with all of them, turn whole like that into hell's abyss.
This maiming means that no one among the people shall follow his friend, a dear man, if he entices him into crimes and wrongdoing:
however closely he may be related to him by kinship, however great their kinship may be, if he entices him into murder and urges him to evil deeds,
it is better for him to do otherwise: to cast that friend far away from him, avoid that kinsman, and have no love for him,
so that he alone may climb up to the high kingdom of heaven, rather than both of them having to seek hell's oppression, broad and baleful torment, evil hardship.

It is also written in the law in true words, as you all know, that every one of mankind shall avoid false oaths and not perjure himself, for that is too great a sin; it leads people onto a hateful path.
But I will tell you further that no one of the children of men shall swear any oath at all, not by high heaven, for that is the Lord's throne,
nor by the earth beneath, because that is the All-Ruler's fair footstool; nor should any of the children of men swear by his own head,
because he cannot make any hair black or white except as holy God, the Mighty One, has marked it out. Therefore men must strictly avoid oaths.
Whoever does it often keeps getting worse, because he cannot guard himself.
Therefore I shall now command you with true words that you never swear stronger oaths, or greater ones among men, beyond what I here very truly command you with my words:
if a man brings a charge against anyone, let him tell the truth. Let him say yes if it is so, and affirm what is true; let him say no if it is not, and let that be enough for him.
Whatever people do beyond that all comes from evil to the children of men: that a man, through faithlessness, will not believe another's words.
Then I also tell you truly how it is commanded there in the old law:
whoever takes another man's eyes, cuts them out of his body, or takes any of his limbs, must soon pay for it with his own, with the same limbs.
But now I want to teach you not to avenge hostile deeds in that way. Instead, in humility, endure all punishment and harm, whatever anyone does to you in this world.
Let every man give another man help and support in the way he would wish the children of men to do good to him in return. Then God will be gracious to whoever among the people is willing to do that.
Honor the poor. Share your wealth among the needy people. Do not care whether you receive any thanks or reward for it in this transitory world,
but look to your dear Lord to repay the gifts, so that God, the mighty protector, may reward you for whatever you do for love of him.
If you want to give fair treasures to good men when you expect to receive more benefits back, why should you have any reward for it from God, or payment in his light? That is only lent wealth.
So it is with everything you do for other people out of kindness when you expect to get the same back, whether in words or in deeds:
why should our Ruler thank you for that, when you just hand over what is yours and take it back again when you want?
Give your wealth to the poor, who do not repay you in this world, and strive toward your Ruler's kingdom.
Do not do it too loudly when you give your alms to the poor man with your hands. Give to him gladly and humbly, for God's sake:
then you will receive repayment again, a very lovely reward of fairer benefits, where you will need it for a long time.
Whatever you give out secretly in this way with a sincere mind (that is pleasing to our Lord), do not boast too much about your gifts,
and neither should any man, so that the gift is not miserably lost to him through empty boasting. Then you will receive a reward for good works before God's eyes.
I shall also command you this: when you want to bow down in prayer and ask your Lord for help, so that he may release you from what is harmful,
from the crimes and sins that you yourselves have wickedly committed here, do not do it in front of other people:
do not proclaim it before the crowd so that people praise you for it and glorify the deeds, so that you do not lose all your prayer to your Lord through that empty fame.
But when you wish to ask your Lord for help, begging humbly (you have great need of this) that the Lord of victory free you from your sins, then do it secretly:
your Lord himself, holy in heaven, still knows it, because nothing is hidden from him, neither words nor deeds.
Then he will let everything happen just as you ask him, when you bow down to prayer with a pure mind."
The warriors stood, the men around the Son of God, very eager, men full of goodwill:
they longed for the words. They thought and kept silent. They had great need to remember afterwards what the holy Child had told them, the first time, in many bright words.
Then one of the twelve, one of the wise men, spoke in reply to the Child of God:
"Good Lord," he said, "we need your favour to do your will, and we need your words just as much, best of all who were born,
so that you teach us, your disciples, how to pray, as John does, the precious Baptist, who every day teaches his company with words how they should greet the Ruler, the Good One.
Do the same for your disciples: reveal the mystery to us." Then right after that the mighty one, the Son of the Lord, had a good answer ready:
"When you men wish," he said, "to greet God, the Ruler, the most powerful of all kings, with your words, then say what I teach you:
Our Father, Father of the children of men, you are in the high kingdom of the heavens. Hallowed be your name in every word.
May your mighty kingdom come.
May your will be done over all this world, the same on earth as it is up there in the high kingdom of the heavens.
Give us each day's provision, good Lord, your holy help, and forgive us, Guardian of heaven, our many sins, just as we do for other people.
Do not let hateful creatures lead us astray into doing their will as much as we deserve, but help us against all evil deeds.
That is how you men must pray with your words when you bow down to prayer, so that the Ruler God forgives you the harm you have done among humankind.

If you are willing to forgive every person the offences and sins that they commit with hostility against you yourselves here, then the Ruler God, the Father almighty, will forgive you great wicked deeds and many sins.
But if your heart becomes too hard, so that you will not forgive other people, other men, their misdeeds,
then the Ruler God will not forgive you your cruel deeds either. Instead you will have to take payment for them, a very hateful reward for a long time, for all the wrong
that you do to others here in this light, if you do not settle your quarrels with the children of men before you men go on that journey out of this world.
I shall also tell you truly how you are to carry out my teachings: when you wish to fast in order to lessen your wicked deeds, do not make it known to many, but hide it from other people:
mighty God, the Ruler, still knows your intention, even if other people, the children of men, do not praise you.
Your holy Father in the kingdom of heaven will repay you the reward for it afterwards, men, because you serve him with such humility, so devoutly among this people.
Do not seek to win wealth wrongfully, men, but work up toward God for a reward: that is a greater thing than for a man to live rich here on earth, used to worldly treasure.
If you are willing to hear my words, then do not gather great treasure of silver or gold here in this middle-world, hoards of riches,
