for here it rots in rust, and mighty thieves steal it, worms destroy it, the clothing wears out, the wealth of gold perishes.

Carry out your good works, gather for yourselves in heaven the greater hoard, fair treasures of wealth: no enemy can take that from you or change it at all, for the wealth stands ready, waiting for you,
whatever good of the hoard you gather there in the kingdom of heaven, men, through your gifts from your hands; and keep your mind fixed firmly there;
for every man's thoughts, his mind and heart, are where his hoard lies, his treasure gathered.

There is never a man so blessed that he can achieve both in this broad world: both to live rich on this earth and be among all worldly pleasures, and also to serve the ruling God in a way that pleases him.
Instead, he must always give up one of the two in all things: either the pleasures of the body or eternal life.
Therefore do not fret about your provisions, but keep your thoughts firmly on God, and do not worry in your mind about what you will eat or drink tomorrow, or what you will wear as clothing, men:
the ruling God knows everything that those people need who serve him well here and follow their lord's will.
Look, you can truly understand this from these birds that are here in this world and travel in their coats of feathers:
they cannot earn any wealth, yet the Lord God gives them help against hunger every day.
You can also notice in your minds, men, regarding your clothing, how beautifully adorned the plants are that stand here in the field, brightly in bloom:
the guardian of the city, King Solomon, who had great treasure, the greatest hoards of riches that any man owned, had won wealth and the best of all clothing, could not—
yet he could not, in his whole life, though he had power over all this land, obtain clothing such as the plant has
that stands here in the field, beautifully adorned, the lily with such a lovely bloom: the lofty Ruler of the land clothes it from the plain of heaven.
Yet he cares more about this race of men; people, whom the Ruler made in this land according to his will, are much dearer to him.

Therefore you need not worry about your clothing, nor fret too much about your provisions: God will take care of it all and help from the plain of heaven, if you are willing to serve in a way that earns his favor.
Always seek God's kingdom first, and after that do his good works and strive for what is right:
then the mighty Lord will give you every good thing, if you are willing to follow him in this way, as I truly tell you here in words.

You must not harshly pass any unjust judgment on any man, because the judgment comes back upon that same man, where it will be to his sorrow and become a punishment for him who here speaks wrong against others with his words.
Nor should any of you men in these dwellings, in payment or in trade, make an unjust, false measure for another man,
because it will always meet every person: just as he does to another, so it comes back against him, where he will not gladly see his sins.
I shall also tell you more about where you must guard yourselves against the greatest punishments and many evil deeds:
Why should you criticize any man, your brother, because you see a straw in his eye under his brows, and you will not remember the heavy beam that you have in your own sight, hard and heavy wood?
Let it come into your mind how you may first remove that. Then light will shine before you, and your eyes will be opened;
then afterwards you can heal the sight of the dear man, cure it in his head.

So it may be more in the mind of every man in this middle world, while he is in this world, that he himself does wrong here, than that he should concern himself with another man's offences and sins when he himself has committed more wicked deeds.

If he wants to do good, then he must first free himself from sins and release himself from evil deeds. Afterwards he can become a help to people with his teachings, once he knows himself to be pure, cleansed of sins.
You must not put your pearls before swine, or treasures of jewels, holy necklaces, because they kick them into the filth and soil them in the sand:
they do not know the difference of what is clean, of fairer ornaments. Many people here are like that, who will not listen to your holy word or follow God's teachings:
they do not know the difference of what is good, but empty words, needless things, are much dearer to them than the work and will of the God of the people.
So they are not worthy to hear your holy word, if they will not think about it in their minds, or learn it, or carry it out.
Do not tell them anything of your teachings, so that you do not waste God's speech and many messages on those people who will not believe in them, the true words.
You must also guard yourselves very cleverly among these people, as you travel through this land, so that the liars cannot deceive you with their teachings, either by words or by works.
They come to you in such clothing, fair ornaments, yet they have treacherous minds:
you can recognize them at once when you see them coming. They speak wise words, though their works are no good, the thoughts of those men.
For you know that grapes will never grow on thorns, or any wealth of fairer fruits, nor do people gather figs from briars.
You can well understand that the evil tree, where it stands on the earth, never gives good growth, nor did God create it so
that the good tree should bear anything bitter for the children of men. Instead, from every tree such growth comes into this world as is drawn to it from its root, either bright or bitter.
But this means the thoughts of the breast, the minds of many of mankind: how every man shows for himself and declares with his mouth what kind of mind he has, what thoughts lie around his heart.
He cannot hide any of this. From the evil man come malicious counsels and bitter, baleful speech, just as he holds them fastened in his breast around his heart.
His mind is always made known, and his will through his words, and his works follow accordingly.
So from the good man come wise answers, wise ones from his understanding, so that he always speaks with his words, the man with his mouth, what he has in his mind, the hoard around his heart.
From there come the holy teachings, very pleasing words, and his works shall then prosper for the people and become a delight to many thanes, just as the Ruler himself grants it to good men,

God almighty, the heavenly Lord. For without his help they cannot accomplish anything good in these dwellings, either in words or in works. Therefore the children of men shall all believe in his power alone.
I shall also show you how two ways lie here in this light, which the children of people travel, all mankind.
One of them is a wide and broad street. A great part of the host travels it, many of mankind, because men spend their minds there on worldly pleasures. It leads people to the worse side,
where they become lost, men in hell, where it is hot and black and terrible within. It is easy for the children of men to travel there, though it does them no good in the end.
Then there lies another way in this world, much narrower. Few of the host travel it, a small number of people.
The children of men do not want to walk it gladly, though it leads men to God's kingdom, into eternal life.

So take the narrow one for yourselves. Though it is not so easy for men to travel, it shall still be to the benefit of whoever goes through it. He shall receive his payment: a very lasting reward and eternal life, precious joy.
You must always ask the Lord for this and pray to the Ruler that you may take that way from the start and go on along it into God's kingdom.
He, the God of life [?], is always ready to give in return what one eagerly asks of him, what the children of men ask.
Seek your Father up in the eternal kingdom. Then you may find him afterwards to your benefit.
Make your journey known there at your Lord's doors. Then the gates of heaven will be opened and unlocked for you, so that you may go into the holy light, into God's kingdom, and see eternal life.
Before all this host I shall also tell you a true parable: whoever among all people wants to hold these teachings of mine in his heart and will think on them in his mind,
and carry them out in this land, does like a wise man who has understanding and keen thoughts. He chooses a site for his house in firm ground and builds the walls upon a rock,
where neither wind nor wave nor current of water can harm it at all. It can stand there upon the rock against all storms, because it was set so firmly on the stone.
The foundation holds it up from beneath and braces it against the wind, so that it cannot give way.
But any man who does not want to hear these teachings of mine, or carry out any of them, acts like the unwise man,
…are foolish, those who want to build a hall for themselves on sand by the water's shore, where the west wind and the current of the waves, the billows of the sea, tear it apart;
sand and grit cannot hold out against the wind. Instead it is thrown down and collapses into the flood, because it is not built on firm ground.
In the same way, every man's work will prosper to the degree that he carries out these words of mine and keeps the holy command.
Then the great multitude began to wonder in their minds. They had heard the loving teachings of mighty God. In that land they were not used to hearing such things said before, in words or in deeds.

Wise men understood that the Lord of the people taught with true words, as one who had authority, and that he was unlike all those who in earlier days had been chosen from among that people, from that race, to be teachers.
The words of Christ, which he spoke before the multitude and commanded on the mountain, had no equal among men.
Then he entrusted them with two things. First, they were to tell with his words how one could reach the kingdom of heaven, that wide and broad wealth. He also gave them power
to heal the lame and the blind, people's infirmities, many a sickbed and grievous diseases. He himself also commanded them not to take any reward from anyone, no precious treasures:

"Remember," he said, "that this power to act has come to you, along with understanding and wisdom, and that the Father of all men gives you this authority. You did not have to buy it with any property

or pay for it with any treasures. So from now on be generous in your hearts in helping people. Teach the children of men counsel that lasts, benefit for the future. Rebuke sinful works and grievous sins.
Do not let silver or gold, fair treasures of wealth, be worth anything to you, or let them ever come into your possession. They can never be of any benefit to you anywhere, nor bring you any joy.
You men shall not own more clothing than what you have on as your outfit when you are to go out among the crowd.
Do not worry about your food or about your livelihood, for the people shall feed the teacher. The benefits that he proclaims to the people, that lovely reward, are worth it.
The worker deserves to be fed well with food, that man who must care for so many souls and draw them onto that journey, spirits into God's meadow.
It is a greater thing to care for many souls, how one may save them for the kingdom of heaven, than to worry about food for the bodies of the children of men.
Therefore people should treat kindly the one who shows them the way to the kingdom of heaven, who fights against the evil-doers, the fiends, and rebukes sinful works and grievous sins.
Now I must send you through this land like lambs among wolves. In this way you shall go among your enemies, among many peoples, among men of every kind.
Keep your minds as wary against them as the yellow serpent, the speckled adder, is when she expects hostility and punishment, so that no one among that people can deceive you on that journey.
Therefore you must take care that those men cannot turn aside your thoughts and your will.
Be as much on your guard against them and their treacherous deeds as one must be against enemies.
Then be like doves again in your deeds. Have a simple mind toward every man and a gentle heart, so that no one there is deceived by your deeds or betrayed through your sins.

Now you must set out on that journey, on that errand. There among the people you will have to endure a great deal of hardship, and oppression just as great and of many kinds, because you teach the people in my name.
Therefore you will suffer much harm there before the kings of the world, and receive punishments.
Often you will have to stand there bound before the powerful because of these true words of mine, and endure both mockery and abuse. Do not let that make your minds doubt or your hearts waver:
you need not be anxious anywhere in your minds when you are ordered to go forth before the assembled host into the guest-hall,
about what good and wise words you should say to them in reply, for success will come to you, help from heaven, and the mighty Holy Spirit will speak from your mouths.
Therefore do not dread the hatred of those men, and do not fear their hostility:
even though they have power over your life, so that they can deprive the body of life and strike it down with the sword, they cannot harm the soul at all.
Fear the ruling God, fear your Father, and gladly carry out his commandments, for he has power over both: over people's life and their bodies, and likewise over their souls.
If you lose them on that journey there for the sake of these teachings, then you may find them again before you in the light of God, for your Father, holy God, keeps them in the kingdom of heaven.
Not all those men who call to me here for protection will come to heaven.
There are many who want to bow to the Lord every day and call there for help, while thinking of something else and doing wicked deeds:
those words are of no use to them then. But those who are eager to carry out here the works and the will of the almighty Father may pass into the light of heaven and enter the kingdom of God.
They need not cry out for help with so many words, for holy God knows the thoughts of every man's mind, his words and his will, and pays him the reward for his works.
Therefore, when you go on the journey, you must take care how you bring the errand to completion.
When you have to travel through this land, far and wide across this world, wherever the roads lead you, the broad streets to the town,
always seek out at once the best man among the crowd, and make your heart known to him with true words.
If they are worthy of it, so that they gladly carry out your good works with a pure mind, then stay with them in that house as long as you like and reward them well:
repay them with good, consecrate them to God with your own words, and proclaim to them sure peace, the holy help of the King of heaven.
But if, through their own deeds, they cannot become so blessed that they do your works and carry out your teachings, [?]
then you shall go away from those people, depart from that folk (your peace will come back to you on your own journey), and leave them in their sins
to live with their evil deeds. Seek out another city for yourselves, a great crowd of people, and do not let any of the dust follow on your feet
from the place where people will not receive you. Shake it off your shoes instead, so that it turns back on them as a shame, a witness against that people that their will is not good.
Then I tell you truly: whenever this world ends and the great day comes over mankind, the city of Sodom, which was cast down here into the abyss because of its sins by the power of fire,
brought down by fire, will then have greater peace and milder protection than those people who reject you here and will not carry out your words.
Whoever receives you with a devout heart and a gracious spirit has thereby done my will, and has also
received the ruling God, your Father, the Lord of men, the mighty Counselor, who knows all that is right.

The Ruler himself knows it, and he rewards the good will of every man for whatever good he does here, even if for the love of God he willingly gives some man a drink of water, cold water from a spring, to ease the thirst of a man in need.
These words will come true: it will never fail that he receives a reward for it, payment before God's eyes, rewards many times over, for whatever he does for love of me.

But whoever among the children of men, among the warriors, denies me before this host, I will do the same to him myself up in heaven, before the almighty Father and before all the power of his angels, before that great multitude.
And whoever of the children of men in this world will not keep silent about it, but declares before the people that he is my disciple,
him I will also acknowledge before the eyes of God, before the Father of all men, where many people will all go before the Almighty to give an account to the Mighty One.
There I will truly be a gracious protector to whoever listens to my words here and does the works that I have commanded here on this mountain."
So the Ruler's Son had truly taught the people how they should give praise to God. Then he let the crowd go from there in every direction, the host of men making their way to their homes.
They had heard the word of the King of heaven himself, his holy teaching. As long as the world lasts there will be, of words and deeds,
many among mankind across this middle-earth who are the wiser in speech, whoever has learned the sayings that the mightiest of children spoke there on the mountain.
About three nights after that, the Lord of these peoples went to the land of Galilee, where the Child of God had been invited to a feast:
a bride was to be given away there, a lovely maiden. Mary was there herself with her son, the blessed virgin, the mother of the Mighty One.
The Lord of many, God's own Child, then went with his disciples into the high house where the company, the Jews, were drinking in the guest hall.
He was at the feast with them, and there he also made it known that he had the power of God, help from the heavenly Father, the Holy Spirit, the wisdom of the Ruler.
The company rejoiced. The people were gathered there in delight, glad-hearted men. Servants went about, cupbearers with bowls, carrying clear wine in pitchers and in ale-vessels;
The men had fine merriment there in the hall. The people there on the benches had started their festivities among themselves as well as they could, and they were full of joy.
Then the people ran short of wine, of strong drink. Nothing was left anywhere in the house that the cupbearers could carry out to the gathering; the vessels were emptied of drink.
It was not long before the most beautiful of women, Christ's mother, noticed it.
She went to speak with her child, with her own son, and told him in words that the hosts had no more wine for the guests at the feast.
Then she eagerly asked the holy Christ to devise help for the people, as they wished. Then the mighty Son of God again had his word ready and spoke to his mother:
"What is it to me and to you," he said, "about these men's drink, about this company's wine? Why do you say so much about it, woman, and urge me in front of this crowd?
My times have not yet come." Even so, the holy maiden trusted firmly in her mind that after those words the Ruler's Son, best of saviours, would help.

Then the most beautiful of women commanded the servants, the cupbearers and the stewards who were to serve the company, that they should not neglect any word or deed that holy Christ might command them to carry out before the people.
Six stone jars stood there empty. Then the mighty child of God gave his command so quietly that many men there did not truly know how he spoke it with his word.
He commanded the cupbearers to fill the jars with clear water. Then with his fingers, with his own hands, he blessed it himself and made it into wine, and he commanded that some be drawn into a cup,

scooped out with a bowl. Then he spoke to the cupbearers and commanded that it be put, full, into the hand of the highest of the guests at the feast, the one who had authority over the people there after the host.
As soon as he had drunk of the wine, he could not hold back, but spoke before the crowd to the bridegroom. He said that every man always ought to serve the best drink first at his feast:
in the meantime the men's spirits are roused by the wine, so that, cheered and drunk, they make merry. After that, lighter drink may be brought: such is the custom of this people.
"But now you have arranged your feast in a strange way before this crowd: you commanded your servants to bring the worst of all your wine before this company of men first, to serve at your feast.

Now your guests are full, your lords are very drunk, and this people is [?] well refreshed. Now you have the most praiseworthy of all drinks brought out here, of any I ever saw anyone have anywhere in this world.
You should have given us this earlier today and feasted us with it. Then every man would have received it gratefully."
After these words, once they had drunk of the wine, many a warrior there became aware that holy Christ had worked a sign inside the house.
From then on they trusted all the more in his protection, believing that he had the might of God and power in this world.
Then it became widely known across the land of Galilee among the Jewish people how the Son of the Lord himself had turned water into wine there:
that was the first wonder of the signs that he showed there in Galilee to the Jewish people.
No one can count up or truly tell how many wonders happened afterward among the people, where the ruling Christ taught the Jewish people all day long in God's name,
promised them the kingdom of heaven and with his words warded off the torment of hell, and told them to seek God's protection, the everlasting life:

there is the light of souls, the joy of the Lord and the brightness of day, the goodness of God; there many a spirit lives in delight, whoever thinks rightly here, so that here he keeps the command of the King of heaven.
Then Christ went with his disciples away from the feast to Capernaum, he the mightiest of kings, to the famous city.
A crowd gathered, men coming to meet him, a blessed company of good people: they wanted to hear his sweet, holy words.
There a centurion came toward him, a good man, and earnestly begged the holy one for help. He said that in his household he had someone who had long been sick and lame, lying ill in his house:
"no man can heal him with his hands. Now he needs your help, my good lord."
Then the peace-child of God himself answered him right away, saying that he would come there and save the boy from that distress.
Then the man came closer, in front of the crowd, to exchange words with one so mighty: "I am not worthy of this," he said,
"good lord, that you should come into my house and visit my dwelling, for I am such a sinful man in words and in deeds.
I believe that you have the power to make him healthy from here, ruler, my lord:
if you speak it with your words, then at once the sickness will be undone and his body will become healthy and clean, if you give him your help.
I am an official. I have plenty of wealth, riches I have gained. Though I am under the authority of a noble king, I still have a troop of men, loyal warriors who are so obedient to me
that they leave undone no word or deed that I command them to carry out in this land; instead they go and do it and come back to their master, loyal to their lord.
Though I have wide-reaching wealth at my house and plenty of people, stout-hearted warriors, still I do not dare ask you, who are so holy,
Child of God, to come into my home and visit my dwelling, for I am so sinful; I know my misdeeds."

Then the ruling Christ, that man, spoke to his disciples. He said that nowhere among the Jews, among the descendants of Israel, had he found this man's equal, anyone in that land who had ever had more faith in God or a purer faith toward heaven:
"Now listen, as I tell you this truly in words here: many foreign peoples of mankind will yet come together from the east and from the west, God's holy people, into the kingdom of heaven:
they will be allowed to rest there in the bosoms of Abraham and of Isaac and also of Jacob, good men, and to receive both wealth and delight, and a pleasant life, good light with God.
Then many of the Jews, the sons of this kingdom, shall be bereft, deprived of such glory, and they shall lie in dark valleys in the very farthest hell.
There one may hear the men speak, where they gnash their teeth over their great anger; there is grim gnashing of teeth and greedy fire, the hard oppression of hell, heat and darkness,
black endless night as the reward for sins, for evil deeds, for whoever does not have the will to free himself before he gives up this light and departs from this world.
"Now you may go forth as you wish to your hall; there you will find the young man healthy at home:
his mind is full of joy, the child is healed, as you asked of me: it will all be done just as you hold faith firmly in your heart."
Then the official gave thanks to the King of Heaven, the all-ruling God, before the people, because he had helped him in such need.

He had then delivered his message as he wished, blessedly; he went away from there on his journey, turned as he wished to where he owned wealth, dwelling and halls: he found the child healthy, the young man.
Christ's words were then fulfilled: he had the power to show signs, so that no man over this earth can tell or reckon
what glorious deeds he performed in this middle world by his own power, what wonders he worked, for everything stood in his power, heaven and earth.
Then holy Christ went forth on his way, the Almighty, doing ⟨good⟩ every single day, the good Lord, dear to the children of men; with words he taught men God's will.
He always had many disciples as companions, the blessed people of God, a mighty force of men from many peoples, a holy host; he was good in his help, gracious to men.
Then he came with the crowd, with that splendid ⟨host⟩, the Child of God, the Savior, to the high city, to Nain: there his name was to be made famous among men.
Then the mighty Savior Christ went on until he had come near, the best of healers:
then they saw a corpse being carried there; the people were bearing a lifeless body, carrying it on a bier out through the city gate, a young man.
The mother walked behind, sorrowful in her heart, and beat herself with her hands; she lamented and mourned her child's death, the wretched woman; he was her only child:
she was a widow and had no other joy; she had placed all her joy and desire in her only son alone, until fate took him from her, the mighty decree of the Creator.
A crowd followed, a throng of townspeople, where they carried him on a bier, the young man, to the grave.
Then the Son of God showed himself there, mighty and gracious, [?] to her, and spoke to the mother; he told the widow to stop weeping and grieving for the child:
"You shall see power here, the work of the Ruler: here your wish shall be granted, comfort before this people: you need not grieve for the life of your child."
Then he went to the bier, and he himself, the Son of the Lord, touched him with holy hands, and spoke to the man; he told him, so very young, to stand up and rise from his resting place.
The man sat up, the child on the bier: the spirit came back into his breast through God's power, and he spoke in reply, the man to his kinsmen.
Then Christ the Healer gave him back into his mother's hand. The woman's heart was comforted and filled with joy, because her wish had been fulfilled there.
Then she fell at Christ's feet and praised the Lord of the people before the crowd of people, because he had protected the life of someone so dear to her against the decree of fate.
She understood that he was the mighty Lord, the holy one who rules heaven, and that he could help many, all the great nations.
Then many began to think about the wonder that had happened among the people. They said that the Ruler himself, the mighty one, had come there to visit his multitude,
and that he had sent them so famous a prophet in the kingdom of the world, one who had done them such a kindness there.
Then many a man there was seized by terror, and the people grew afraid. They saw him alive, seeing the light of day, the one whom death had taken before, who had died on his sickbed:
afterwards he was healthy again, the youth brought back to life. Then this became known among all the descendants of Israel.
Just as evening came, all the sick people were gathered there, the lame and the crippled, whoever was anywhere there, living among the people,
and they were led there and came to Christ. Through his great power he helped them and healed them, and let them go away from there healed again, as they wished.
Therefore one should praise his work and glorify his deeds, because he is the Lord himself, the mighty protector of mankind, for any of the people who believe in his word and his works.
Then a great many people of all foreign nations had come there to the glory of Christ, to the protection of one so mighty.
Then he, the Son of God, the Ruler, wished to sail across a lake there with his disciples, beside the land of Galilee, across a stream of waves.
Then he ordered the rest of the crowd to travel on ahead, and he, the Saving Christ, went with a few into a boat, to sleep, weary from the journey.
Men wise about the weather raised the sail and let the wind drive them over the sea, until he, the Ruler, came to the middle with his company.
Then the power of the weather began: a storm rose up and the waves grew. Black darkness came in among them. The sea was in turmoil; wind and water fought each other.
The men were in distress; the sea became so wild that none of the men expected to live any longer.
Then they woke the Guardian of the land with their words and told him of the force of the storm. They begged Christ the Saviour to be merciful to them against the water:
"or else we must die here a terrible death in this sea."
The good Son of God himself rose up and spoke to his disciples. He told them not to fear the fury of the weather at all. "Why are you so afraid?" he said.
"Your mind is not yet firm; your faith is too small. It will not be long now before the waters become calmer and this weather pleasant."

Then he spoke to the wind, and to the sea as well, and ordered them both to behave gently. They carried out the command, the Ruler's word: the weather grew still, and it became calm and fair on the water.
Then the people, the crowd, began to marvel among themselves, and some said in words: what kind of man could be so mighty that the wind and the wave both obeyed his word, his command?

Then he, the child of God, had saved them from that distress. The vessel glided on, the high-horned ship. The heroes, the people, came to land. They gave praise to God and proclaimed his mighty power.
A great many people came there to meet the Son of God. He gladly received them, all who sought help there with a pure heart.
He taught them their faith and healed their bodies with his hands. No man was ever so badly afflicted with sicknesses,
not even if Satan's treacherous followers had him in their hands by the fiend's power, and his mind and his wits were turned aside, so that he went about raving among the people,
but the Healer Christ always gave him life if he came into his hands. He drove the devils out of him by the Lord's power, with true words, and gave him back his wits.
Then he let him be healed against the hateful ones and gave him peace from the fiend, and the man went on to whichever land he liked best.
So the Lord's Son did good works with his disciples every day. Yet the Jews never believed any the more for this in his great power, that he was the ruler of all, of land and people.
For this they still receive their reward, exile far and wide, because they waged that strife against the very Son of the Lord.
Then he, God's own child, went with his companions back to the land of Galilee. The holy Healer went to the friends among whom he had been raised and among whose kin he had grown up from childhood.
Hosts and peoples thronged around him. Many blessed thanes were there among that company.
There men carried a sick man in their arms. They wanted to bring him before the eyes of Christ, before the child of God. He needed a cure,
for the ruler of heaven, the protector of men, to heal him. For many days he had been crippled in his limbs and could not control his body at all.
But there was so great a crowd there that they could not bring him before the child of God or push through the people to tell him of the needy man's affliction.
Then the Healer Christ went into a hall. A crowd gathered around it there, a throng of great peoples.

Then the men who had long carried the frail, lame man and borne him on his bed began to talk about how they might carry him before the child of God, into the crowd, where Christ the ruler might see him himself.

Then the companions went to work. They lifted him with their hands and climbed up onto the house. They tore open the hall from above and let him down with ropes into the building, where the mighty one was, the most powerful of kings.
As soon as he saw the man come through the roof of the house, he perceived in their minds, in the hearts of the men,
that they had great faith in him. Then he spoke before the people and said that he wished to set the sick man free of his sins.

Then the people spoke against him in turn, the fierce-hearted Jews who were watching the words of God's child. They said that it could not be so, that no one could forgive grievous deeds except God alone, the ruler of this world.
Then the mighty Son of God again had his word ready: "I will make it," he said,
"plain in this man, who lies here so sick inside this hall, terribly afflicted, that I have the power to forgive sins and also to heal a sick man without needing to touch him."
Then the famous Lord spoke to him, the lame man lying there, and commanded him to stand up before the people, fully healed, and commanded him to take his bedclothes on his shoulders, onto his back;
he quickly carried out that command before the company and went away from there healthy, whole, out of the house.
Then many heathen men, men, marveled at this and said that the Ruler himself, God almighty, had given him greater power than any other son of man, strength and skill;
yet they, the people of the Jews, would not acknowledge that he was God. They did not believe his teachings, but carried on hateful strife and fought against his words:
for this they received pain, a hateful reward, and so they still shall for a long time, because they would not listen to the heaven-king's, Christ's, teachings,
which he made known everywhere, far and wide throughout this world. He let them see his works every single day, behold his deeds, and hear his holy word,
which he spoke as a help to the children of men. And he showed so many mighty signs so that they might trust the better and believe in his teaching.
He freed so many bodies from evil sicknesses and brought them healing. He gave life to the doomed: when a man was hastening on the road to hell (death),
then the Savior himself, Christ, through his great power, made him alive again after death and let him go on enjoying the joys of this world.
So he healed the lame and likewise the crippled, and cured those who were blind, letting them see the bright light, the everlasting radiance. He loosed sins, the grim deeds of men.
Yet the faith of the Jews, of that hostile people, in the holy Christ was never any better for it; instead they had hard minds,
very stubborn strife. They would not understand that they, the people, with their faith, had been ensnared to the will of fiends.
Yet the Son of the Lord was never any slower because of it; instead he told them in words how they should win the kingdom of heaven, and taught throughout the land.

With his words he had drawn so many of the people to himself that a great host, a crowd, followed him. And the Child of God told them much in parables, which they could not understand in their breasts
or grasp in their hearts, until the holy Christ chose to tell it to them before the crowd of men in plain words, through his own power, and make known what he meant.
There a multitude, the people, thronged around him: they had great need to hear the truthful words of the heaven-king.
He then stood by the shore of a body of water. Because of the throng, he did not want to make known his teaching to the band of thegns there on the land,

but the good one, the peace-child of God, went then with his disciples nearer to the water, into a ship, and ordered it to be pushed off farther from the land, so that the people, the crowd, would not press upon him so much.
Many a thegn stood there, a host by the water, where the Ruler Christ spoke his teaching to the people:
"Listen, I can tell you, my companions," he said, "how a man began to sow clean grain on the earth with his hands.
Some of it fell on top of hard stone and had no earth, so that it could not grow there or take root, sprout or hold fast. The grain that lay there on the rock was lost.
Some of it fell on land, on earth of noble kind. Afterwards it began to grow beautifully and to take root, the shoot thriving with delight. That land was so good, splendidly prepared.
Some of it fell on a hard road, where footsteps passed, the hoofbeats of horses and the treading of men. It lodged there in the earth and came up, and began to grow on the way;
then the great passing of the crowd, the people's traffic, destroyed it, and birds picked it up, so that nothing of what fell there on the road could afterwards turn out as its owner wished.
Some of it fell where many thick thorns stood that day. It lodged there in the earth and came up, sprouted there and took hold.

Then weeds sprang up among it and hindered its growth. The cover of the forest had overgrown it from the start, so that it could not come to any profit, since the thorns were allowed to choke it like that."
Then Christ's companions, men wise in words, sat and kept silent. They wondered greatly by what images the Child of God had begun to tell such a true story.
Then one of the men began to question his gracious lord, and he bowed toward him with great reverence: "Truly, you have power," he said,
"both in heaven and on earth, holy Lord, above and below. You are the all-ruler of the souls of men, and we are your disciples, loyal in our hearts.
Good Lord, if it is your will, let us hear the meaning of your words there, so that after you we may make it known to all Christian people.
We know that a true meaning follows from your words, and we have great need to learn your word and your work from you here in this land, because it comes from such wisdom."
Then the best of men gave him an answer in return: "I did not intend in any way," he said,
"to hide any of my deeds, words or works. You shall all know this, my disciples, because the Ruler of this world has granted you
that you may know the heavenly mystery in your minds. To the others, God's command must be shown in words through parables.
Now I will truly explain to you here what I meant, so that you can better understand my teaching throughout this whole land.
The seed I told you about is his own word, the holy teaching of heaven's King, and how it is to be proclaimed over middle-earth, far and wide throughout this world.
Men are of different minds, people in various ways. One man has such a mind, hard thoughts and a cruel heart, that he does not care to act according to your words,
or to follow this teaching of mine. Instead my teaching, God's message and the words of you men, are lost there in the evil man,
just as I told you before that the grain perished which could not take firm root with its sprouts on the stone.
In the same way all the speech of the noble ones is lost, God's message, whatever is taught in words to the evil man, and he chooses his path to the worse side,
among the host of fiends, against God's will, to the glory of the hostile ones, and into the surge of fire. From then on he must heat the broad flame with the thoughts of his heart.
Never be any slower to point out my teaching with words in this land, for there are so many people in this host, so many men across this earth.
Another man stands there who is young and quick-witted, and who has a good mind. He is skilled in speech and understands the meaning of your sayings.
He then thinks about it in his heart and listens very eagerly with his ears, and he stands closer. He takes God's command into his breast, learns it and carries it out.
His faith is so good that he works out how he can in turn convert another man, a wicked one, so that this man's mind may hold pure faith in the King of Heaven.

Then God's command, the beloved faith, spreads in his breast, just as the grain spreads with its shoots in the land, where it has its natural place, where fate has favored it, and where the course of the weather, rain and sun, gives it what it needs.
God's teaching does the same in the good man, day and night. The devil, that hostile creature, goes far away from him, and God's guardian comes much nearer, night and day,
until they bring him to the point where both things happen: the teaching that comes from his mouth becomes a benefit to the children of men, and the man himself comes to God.
So in this time in the world, by his way of thinking, he has gained in exchange a share of the kingdom of heaven, the greatest of riches. He goes into God's power, free of troubles.
Faith is so good for every man that no hoard of gold is equal to such faith. From now on, be generous to mankind with your teachings.
The thoughts of men are very different from one another. One man has a harsh, quarrelsome nature, a hostile will and a fickle mind. He is full of deceit and wicked deeds.
When he stands among the people and hears God's teaching there with great attention, it begins to seem to him that he will gladly carry it out from now on.
Then God's teaching begins to take hold in his mind, until wealth for his own gain and other people's treasure come into his hands again.

Then hostile creatures lead him astray, when he gets caught up in greed for wealth, and he puts out his faith. It then did him little good that he ever thought about it in his heart, if he will not keep it.
That is like the growth that began to sprout on the path, on the land: the people walking along it destroyed it again.
The great sins in a man's mind do the same to God's teaching if he does not watch over it well.
Besides that, they throw him far down to the bottom, into hot hell, where he is no longer of any use to the King of Heaven. Instead, fiends will punish him with torments.
Always keep teaching with words in this land. I know the minds of these people, how different the minds of mankind are, and how changeable their ways.
One man has turned his mind wholly to this, and he has worried more about how he can hold on to his hoard than about how he can do the will of the King of Heaven.
So God's holy command cannot grow there. It may take hold there and put out roots, but the wealth chokes it.
Just as the weeds and the thorns catch hold of the grain and keep it from growing, wealth does the same to men.
It ties up the man's heart so that he cannot think in his mind about what he needs most, about how he can achieve it, for as long as he is in this world,
so that afterwards he may have the kingdom of heaven forever, through his Lord's grace, such endless wealth that no man in this world can know it.
No thegn can ever think so widely in his mind that a man's heart could hold it, so that he might truly know what good the ruling God has prepared,
all of which stands ready for any man who loves him well here and keeps his own soul for it, so that he may go into God's light."
So he taught with words. A great crowd stood around the child of God and heard him tell many parables in words about the turning of this world.
He said that a nobleman once sowed pure, clean grain in his field with his own hands. He wanted to grow a pleasant crop there for himself, fair fruit.
Then his enemy went there after him with a secret purpose, and sowed darnel over it all, the worst of weeds. Then both grew, both the grain and the weed.
Then his servants came walking to the house and told their lord, the thegns told their chieftain with bold words:
"Look, good lord, you sowed pure grain, unmixed, in your field. Now no one sees anything but more weeds growing. How could that have happened?"
Then the noble man spoke again to the men, the lord to his thanes. He said that he could well understand that a hostile man had sown after him there, a fiend sowing wicked weeds:
"He begrudged me the fruits and spoiled my crop."
Then the friends, his followers, spoke back to him and said that they wanted to go there, come with strength and pull the weeds out from there, take them out with their hands.
Then their lord answered them: "I do not want you to weed it," he said,
"because you cannot watch out and take care as you walk, even if you do not mean to do it, that you do not ruin too much of the grain and the sprouts, and trample them under your feet."
Let them both grow on from now until the harvest time comes and the fruits in the field are ripe and ready in the field.
Then we will all go there, take it with our hands, gather the clean grain together carefully, bring it into my hall and keep it there,
so that nothing anywhere can ruin it. And we will take the weeds, bind them into bundles and throw them into the bitter fire, and let the hot flame, the insatiable fire, take them there."
Then many a man stood there, thegns keeping silent, wondering what the man of the people, the famous mighty Christ, the most powerful of children, meant, what he signified by that parable.
Then they eagerly begged the good Lord to unlock the teaching, so that the people might go on to hear the holy things.
Then their lord, the famous and mighty Christ, answered them: "That is," he said,
"the Son of Man: I myself am the one who sows there, and these blessed people are the pure, clean grain, who listen to me well here and do my will;
This world is the field, this broad land where the children of mankind live. Satan himself is the one who sowed such hateful teaching there after me.
He has led so many of these people, so many of the host, astray, so that they commit crimes and act according to his will.
Yet they shall grow on here, the damned men, just the same as the good men, until the might of Muspell comes over mankind, the end of this world.
Then every one of all the fields in this kingdom is ripe: the children of men must fulfil the fates decreed for them. Then the earth passes away, which is the broadest of all dwelling-places;
then the bright Lord comes from above with the host of his angels, and all the peoples who ever saw this light come together, and then they shall receive the reward for evil and for good.

Then the angels of God go out, the holy guardians of heaven, and gather the pure men together apart, and bring them into everlasting splendour, the high light of heaven; and the others into the depths of hell: they throw the sinful into the surging fire;
there, bound, they shall suffer the bitter flame and torment, and the others shall have great bliss in the kingdom of heaven, shining like the white sun.
Such is the reward men receive for their deeds. Whoever has understanding, let him think about it in his heart; or whoever can hear, a man with his ears, let this be a concern to him within,
in his mind: how he must stand on that great day before the mighty God and give account for all the words and works that he does in this world.
That is the most terrible of all things, the most fearful for the children of men, that they must speak before their Lord, men before the good Lord:
then everyone would gladly be, every single man, free of wickedness and of grievous crimes.
Therefore every person who wishes to possess perfect glory then, the high kingdom of heaven and the favour of God, must take care beforehand, before he gives up this light."
So I have heard that the Lord's own Son, the best of all children, then told in parables what in the kingdom of this world, among the race of men, was like the kingdom of heaven;
he said that often something small became more splendid and raised itself up so high: "So does the kingdom of heaven: it is always greater than any man in this world expects.
That work is also like it, when someone casts a dragnet into the sea, a fishing net into the water, and catches both bad and good,
draws them up to the shore, brings them to land, then picks out the good ones on the sand and lets the others go back to the bottom, into the wide waves.

So the ruling God will do with the children of men on that great day: he brings the great people, all together, and picks out for himself the pure ones for the kingdom of heaven, and lets the damned go down to the depths of hell's fire.
No man among the heroes knows anything to compare with the punishment that men, the peoples, receive there in the inferno.
Nor can any man ever find anything equal to the reward, the wealth and the joy that the Ruler allots there,
that God himself pays to any man who keeps it here, so that he may go into the kingdom of heaven, into the lasting light."
So he taught them then with skill. Then the people travelled there from all over the land of Galilee to see the Child of God:
they wondered where such words could come to him from, so wisely spoken, that he could ever tell God's message so truly and speak it so powerfully:
"He is from this family here," they said, "the man, by kinship; his mother is here with us, a woman among this people.
Why, we who are here all know it; his descent and every one of his kin are well known to us;
and also among this people: where could such wisdom have come to him, and greater power than other men here possess?"
So the people begrudged him and spoke scornful words to him. They despised him, holy as he was, and would not listen to his message.
Nor would he show them many miracles there, bright signs, because of their unbelief, for he knew their doubting minds
and their hostile will. There were no other men among the Jews as fierce as those around the land of Galilee, so hard-minded:

though the holy Christ was there, the child of God by birth, they still would not receive his message faithfully. Instead the people, the men, began to plot among themselves how they might bring harm on the mighty Christ.
Then they summoned their people, their companions, together. With wrathful will they were eager to charge the Son of God with sins.

They had no desire for his words, his wise sayings. Instead they began to discuss among themselves how they might throw him, powerful as he was, from a cliff, over the wall of a mountain. They wanted to take the life of the child of God.

Then he went gladly along with the people. His mind was not afraid, for he knew that because of his divinity the children of men, the Jewish people, could do him no harm or hostile deed before his time had come.

So he climbed up the stony height together with the people, until they came to the place where they meant to throw him down from the wall and fell him to the ground, so that he would lose his life and his days would come to an end.

Then the minds of the men, the bitter thoughts of the Jews up on the mountain, came to nothing, so that none of them had a spirit fierce enough or a will wrathful enough to recognize Christ, the Ruler's Son.
He was not known to any of them, so that they then [?] him. So he could stand among their crowd, walk through the middle of their throng, and go among their people.

He himself made his own peace and protection against the multitude, and went away from there through the middle of that hostile people. Then the Ruler's Son, mightiest of kings, went where he wished, into a wilderness.
He had the power to choose where in the land he would most like to be in this world.
Meanwhile John, God's servant, went another way with his disciples. He taught the people lasting counsel and commanded them to do good and give up crimes, wickedness and murderous deeds.
Many good men there held him dear. Then he went to see the king of the Jews, the war-leader, at his home. This king was called Herod after his ancestors, and he was an arrogant man.
He was living with the bride who had earlier been his brother's wife in wedlock, until the brother went elsewhere and departed this world.
Then the king took that woman as his queen. She had earlier been granted children, offspring by his brother.

Then the good John began to rebuke him over the bride. He said that it was against God and hateful to the Ruler for any man to do such a thing: to take his brother's bride into his bed and have her as his wife.
"If you will listen to me and believe my teachings, you shall not keep her any longer. Shun her in your heart, do not hold such love for her, and do not sin so greatly.
Then the woman's mind grew anxious at these words. She feared that he would entice the ruler of the world with his speech and wise words, so that he would leave her.
So she began to give him much harmful advice in secret, and ordered warriors to seize him, the sinless man, and lock him up in a prison with fetters and limb-shackles.
Because of the people they did not dare take his life, for the people were all his friends. They knew him to be so good and so worthy of God, and held him for a prophet, as well they might.
Then, in the count of years, the time of the king of the Jews had come, as the wise men of the people had reckoned it, the day when he was born and came into the light.
Such was the custom of the people, that every one of the Jews was to celebrate it with feasting.
Then a great host of men, of army leaders, gathered in the guest-hall, in the house where their lord sat on his royal throne.
Many Jews came into the guest-hall. Their minds grew glad there, joyful in their breasts: they saw their ring-giver in good spirits.
Clear wine was carried into the hall in bowls. Cup-bearers went about, going around with golden vessels. There was loud merriment inside the hall; the warriors drank.
The shepherd of the land was eager to see what he could do that would most delight the company.
Then, as he sat on his bench flushed with wine, he ordered the merry girl, his brother's child, to come forward, and he spoke to the woman.
He greeted her before the company and eagerly asked that she should put on entertainment there before the guests, beautifully in the hall:
"Let this people see how you have learned to delight the many people on the benches. If you grant me this request, my word before this company,
then I will truly declare it here, clearly before these people, and also fulfil it, so that afterward I will honour you with whatever you ask of me before these ring-friends of mine:"
even if you ask me for half of this dominion, of my kingdom. Even so I will make sure that no man can change it with words, and so it shall be."

Then the girl's mind was turned by this, her thoughts toward her lord, so that inside the house, in the guest-hall, she started the entertainment, just as was the custom of the people's land, the usage of the nation.
The girl danced lively through the hall. The thoughts of many were full of delight, their hearts glad.
When the girl had served to the satisfaction of the king of the people and of all the company of good men who were inside, the girl then wanted to have her reward in front of the crowd.
So she went to speak with her mother and asked her eagerly what she should ask of the guardian of the city.

Then the mother advised her according to her own will. She told her to ask for nothing at all in front of the gathering except that she be given, there inside the hall, the head of John, cut off from his body.
That grieved all the people, the men in their hearts, when they heard the girl say it. So it did the king as well.
He could not go back on his promise or change his word. So he ordered his weapon-bearer to go out of the guest-hall, and ordered him to take the life of the man of God.
Soon after, the man's head was brought into the hall and given there to the girl, the maiden, in front of the crowd. She carried it out to her mother.
That was the last day of the wisest of all men who ever came into this world, of all the children a woman ever bore to a man. The one exception, always, is the one whom the maiden bore,
who never knew a man in her life, except that the Ruler God from the heavenly plain mightily marked him out by the Holy Spirit. He had no equal anywhere, before or after.
The men turned to it, the men around John, his many disciples, blessed companions, and buried him in the sand, the beloved body.
They knew that he would possess God's light, precious joy together with his Lord, and would be blessed to reach the home on high.
Then the companions went away from there, John's disciples, sad at heart and holy in spirit. Their lord's death was a great sorrow to them.

Then they went to seek the Ruler's Son, mighty Christ, in the wilderness, and told him of the good man's death: how the king of the Jews had cut off the head of the most famous of men with the edges of a sword.
The Son of the Lord would say nothing harsh about it. He knew that the soul was kept holy against its enemies, in peace from its foes.
Then, when the best of teachers became known throughout the lands in the wilderness, a host gathered and people came in crowds. They had a great longing for wise words.
He, the Son of the Lord, also had the same wish: that he might invite such a band of companions into God's light and win them over gladly.
The Ruler taught many people, foreign men, all the long day, until in the evening the sun sank to its seat.
Then his twelve companions, the men, went to the Child of God and told their good lord what hardship the people were living in there. They said that the men in the desert land needed his kindness:
"They cannot sustain themselves here with anything, the warriors, because of the pressure of hunger. Now, good lord, let them go where they can find lodging."
Many towns with large populations lie near here. There the men will find food to buy in the villages."
Then the Ruler Christ, Lord of peoples, spoke again. He said there was no need for this: "that through lack of food they should abandon my loving teachings.
Give these people enough; feed them here gladly." Then Philip, the wise man, had his answer ready. He said that there was such a great multitude of men there:
"Even if we had food here ready to give them, as much as we could at most pay for, if we paid out two hundred silver coins here all together,
it would still be doubtful that any of them would get even one bite. That would be so little for these people."
Then the guardian of the land, the Lord of men, spoke again and asked them eagerly what food they had obtained there as provisions.
Then Andrew answered him with his words before the men and told the Almighty himself that they had no more provisions in their company
"except five barley loaves in our party and two fish."
"But what good is that for this multitude?" Then mighty Christ, the good Son of God, spoke to him again and ordered the crowd of men to be divided and separated, and ordered the groups to be seated,
the men across the ground, the great people on the green grass. Then he spoke to his disciples, he the best of all who were ever born, and told them to fetch the bread and bring the fish forward.
The people waited quietly; a great company sat there. Meanwhile the Lord of men blessed the food by his own power,
the holy King of heaven, and broke it with his hands and handed it to his disciples, and ordered them to carry it among the crowd and share it out.
They carried out their Lord's word and gladly brought his gifts, holy help, to every man. It grew under their hands, food for every man:
the great people had life in delight. The people all became full, a blessed people, all who had gathered there from every wide road.
Then Christ the Ruler told his disciples to go, and told them to take good care that the leftovers were not lost there. Then he told them to gather them up where many of mankind had eaten their fill.
There was so much food, so much bread left over, that they gathered twelve baskets full:
that was a great sign, a great power of God, for the men counted there, not including women and children, came to five thousand of the host altogether.
All the people, the men, understood in their minds that they had a mighty lord there.
Then the people praised the King of heaven. They said that no wiser prophet had ever come into this light, nor anyone who had more power with God in this middle-earth, or a more sincere mind.
All said that he was worthy of every good thing, that he ought to possess the earthly kingdom, the wide throne of the world,
"now that he has such wisdom and such great power with God." All the men agreed that they would raise him up as highest lord and choose him as king:
to Christ that was worth nothing at all, for he himself, by his own power alone, made this kingdom of the world, earth and heaven above, and has held it ever since, land and people,
– though the hostile adversaries did not believe it at all – so that everything stands in his power: the might of kingdoms and of empires, the assembly of great peoples.
Therefore the holy Lord did not want to have any lordship through the words of those men, or the name of a worldly king;
nor did he stir up any further strife with words against the people. Instead he went off where he wanted to go, up onto a mountain:
the Child of God fled the boasting talk of the arrogant. He ordered his disciples to travel across a sea, and he himself told them where they should come to meet him again.
Then the crowd of people scattered over the whole land, and the great host went away, after their lord, the mightiest of all who were ever born, the Ruler, had gone up onto the mountain as he wished.
Then Christ's companions, the twelve of them, whom he himself had chosen for their good loyalty, gathered at the shore of the water:
they had no doubt at all that they wanted to travel across the sea in God's service, and gladly.
Then they let the high, horned ship cut through the strong current, the clear waves, the bright water.
The daylight slipped away and the sun went down. Night wrapped the seafarers in mist. The men pressed onward over the flood;
Then the fourth watch of the night had come — the saving Christ was watching over the seafarers —: then a great wind arose, a storm lifted up high: the waves roared, the current against the prow;
the men steered hard against the wind; their minds were troubled, their hearts full of sorrows: the seafarers did not expect to reach land themselves through the strife of the weather.
Then they saw the Ruler Christ walking on the sea itself, going on foot: he could not sink into the flood, into the sea, because his own holy power held him up.
Their minds were in fear, the men's hearts: they were afraid that a mighty fiend was doing this to deceive them.
Then their Lord, the holy King of heaven, spoke to them and told them that he was their lord, famous and mighty:
"Now you must take hold of firm courage; let your mind not be afraid, act boldly: I am the Child of God, his own Son, who shall protect you against this sea, against this great ocean current."
Then one of the men answered him over the side of the ship, a most worthy man, Peter the good (he did not want to suffer pain, the torment of the water): "If you are the Ruler," he said,
"good lord, as it seems to me in my mind, then command me to go there to you across this current of the sea, dry over the deep water, if you are my Lord, the protector of many."
Then mighty Christ commanded him to come towards him. He was ready at once, stepped off the prow and went forth vigorously to his Lord.

The flood held the man up through the power of God, until he began in his mind to fear the deep water, when he saw the waves driven by the wind: the waves surged around him, the high current encircled him.
Just as he doubted in his mind, the water gave way under him, and he went into the waves, sank into the sea-current,
and right after that he cried out quickly to the Son of God and earnestly begged him to save him, since he was in distress, the thane in danger.
The Lord of peoples caught him in his arms and asked at once why he had doubted:

"Why, you could well have trusted and known as truth that the power of the water in the sea could not hinder your journey, nor could the ocean current, as long as you held firm faith in me in your mind."
Now I will be a help to you, save you in this distress." Then the Almighty, the Holy One, took him by the hands:

then the clear water became firm under his feet again, and they both went together on foot until they stepped from the current over the side of the ship, and the best of all children sat down at the prow.
Then the broad water, the currents, became still, and they came to the shore, the seafarers reaching land together after the strife of the water; then they gave thanks to the Ruler,
glorified their Lord with deeds and words, fell at his feet and spoke many wise words, saying that they knew well

that he himself was truly the Son of the Lord in this world and had power over middle-earth, and that he could save the life of every man, just as he had done for them on the flood against the strife of the water.
Then the Ruler Christ, the Son of the Lord, the only Child of God, went on his way from the sea.
Foreign people, men, came to meet him: his good works were known far and wide, and that he spoke so many true words.
It was his great wish to bring about such a people that they would always gladly serve God, and that many of mankind would be obedient to the King of Heaven.
Then he went across the borders of the Jews and sought out the city of Sidon. He had companions with him, good disciples.
There a woman from other peoples came to meet him. She was of noble birth, of the race of the land of Canaan.
She asked the mighty Lord, the holy one, to give her help. She said that harm had befallen her, sorrow over her own daughter; she said that her daughter was gripped by sickness:
"Hidden creatures have deceived her. Now her death is at hand; the hostile ones have robbed her of her wits.
Now I ask you, Ruler, my lord, son of David himself, to release her from such sicknesses, and in your mercy to protect her, so wretched, from the evil harmers."
Christ the Ruler did not yet give her any answer. She went after him and followed him boldly until she came to his feet, and greeted him weeping.
The disciples of Christ asked their lord to be merciful in his heart to the woman. Then the Son of the Lord again had his word ready and spoke to his companions:
"First I must be of benefit to the descendants of Israel, to the people, so that they may have a devout mind toward their Lord:
They are in need of help. The people are lost; they have abandoned the Ruler's word; the host is in doubt; they harbor a secretive mind;
the nobility of Israel will not obey their Lord; the warriors are unbelieving toward their lord. Yet from there help shall come to all foreign peoples."
The woman kept on pleading with her words, that Christ the Ruler would become gentle in his heart toward her, so that she might from then on have her child and have her healthy.
Then her lord spoke to her in answer, glorious and mighty: "It is not," he said,

"right for a man, nor good for any man to do, that he should take bread away from his children, refuse it to them against their will, let them suffer torment and fierce hunger, and feed his dogs with it."
"That is true, Ruler," she said, "what you speak with your words and truly say.
Yet often inside the hall, under their master's table, the puppies scurry about, full of the crumbs that fall down from their lord's table."
Then God's child of peace heard the woman's wish and spoke to her with his words: "It is well for you, woman, that you have a good will!
Great is your faith in the power of God, in the Lord of peoples. Everything concerning your child's life will be fulfilled just as you asked of me."
Then she was healed at once, just as the holy one had spoken it with truthful words. The woman rejoiced that she could have her child from then on.
Christ the Healer had helped her. He had protected her, who had been seized by the power of fiends, from the evil harmers.
Then the Ruler, the best of children, went on and sought out another city, which was very densely settled with the people of the Jews, with southern people.
There, I have heard, he spoke to his companions, the disciples he had chosen for himself for his good, who gladly stayed with him, men drawn by his wise speech:
"I will ask all of you in words, my disciples," he said: "what do these Jewish people, this famous great nation, say about what sort of man I am?"
His friends, his disciples, answered him eagerly: "This Jewish people, these men, are not of one word.

Some say that you are Elijah, the wise prophet, who was here long ago, good among this human race; some say that you are John, the precious messenger of the Lord, who once baptized people here in water.
All of them say in words that you are one of the noble men, the prophets, who once taught these people here with words, and that you have come back into this light to guide this people."
Then the Ruler Christ spoke again: "Who do you say that I am," he said, "my disciples, my dear men?"
Then Simon Peter was not slow: he answered at once, alone before them all. He had good courage and bold thoughts, and he was loyal to his lord:
"You are the true Son of the Ruler, of the living God who created this light, Christ, the eternal King. So we all wish to say, your disciples, that you are God himself, the best of healers."
Then his Lord answered him in turn: "Blessed are you, Simon," he said, "son of Jonah. You could not have thought this up yourself or worked it out in the thoughts of your mind,
nor could any man's tongue have shown it to you in words; rather, the Ruler himself did it for you, the Father of all the children of men, so that you spoke out so profoundly about your Lord.
You shall receive a precious reward for this. You have pure faith in your Lord; your thoughts are like stone, you are as firm as the hard rock.
The children of men shall call you Saint Peter. Upon that stone my hall shall be built, God's holy house;
there his household shall gather in blessedness. The gates of hell shall not be able to hold out against your strong power.
I give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that after me you may have power over all Christian people. All the souls of men shall come to you.

You shall have great power: whichever of the children of men here on earth you choose to bind, to him both things are done: the kingdom of heaven is closed, and hell, the burning fire, is open to him.
Whomever you choose to unbind again, to loosen his hands, to him the kingdom of heaven is opened, the greatest of lights, and eternal life, God's green meadow.
With such things I will reward your faith. I do not want you yet to make it known to these people, this multitude, that I am the mighty Christ, God's own Son.
The Jews shall yet bind me, a guiltless man; they shall torment me terribly and inflict many torments on me in Jerusalem with spear points, seek my life with sharp blades, and deprive me of life.

Through our Lord's power I shall rise from death into this light on the third day." Then the best of thanes, Simon Peter, was very sorrowful; his mind was grieved, and the warrior spoke privately to his Lord:
"The good Ruler of the kingdom," he said, "shall not will that you should ever suffer such great torment among this people. There is no need for that at all, holy Lord."
Then his lord spoke to him in answer, the glorious, mighty Christ (he was gracious to him in his heart): "What, now you are opposed," he said,
"to my will, best of thanes! You know only the human ways of these people. You do not know the power of God that I am to carry out.
I can tell you much in true words: here among this company stand companions of mine who will not die, will not turn on their journey hence, before they see the light of heaven, God's kingdom.
Soon after that he chose from among his disciples Simon Peter, James and John, the two men, both of them brothers,
and then the blessed child of God, the Lord of peoples, the Ruler of this world, went up the mountain apart with the companions, with the three thanes:
there he wished to show them many wonders and signs, so that they would trust the better that he himself was the Son of the Lord, the holy King of heaven.
Then the men climbed the high wall of stone and mountain until they came up toward the clouds, to the place where the Ruler Christ,
mightiest of kings, had chosen to show his divinity to his disciples through his own power, a bright sign.
When he bowed down there to pray, his appearance and his garments became different up there: his cheeks grew bright, shining like the bright sun.
So the child of God shone, his body gave off light: rays of splendour streamed from the Ruler's child; his clothing became as white as snow to look at.
Then after that a wondrous thing was shown there: Elijah and Moses came there to Christ to exchange words with one so mighty.
There was such delightful speech, such good words among the men, when the Son of God wished to talk with the famous men; so joyful it became upon the mountain:
the bright light shone; there was a fine enclosure and a green meadow there, like paradise. Then Peter spoke, the bold-hearted hero, and spoke to his lord, addressing the Son of God:
"It is good to be here, if you will choose it, almighty Christ, that someone should build a house for you here on this height,
splendidly made, and another for Moses and a third for Elijah. This is a home of bliss, the most delightful of riches."
Just as he spoke that word, the air split in two: a bright cloud shone, a gleaming radiance, and enveloped the good men in its beauty.
Then from the cloud came the holy voice of God, and he himself told the heroes there that this was his Son, the dearest of the living:
"in him I am well pleased in my thoughts. You shall obey him; follow him gladly."

Then the disciples of Christ, the men, could not withstand the brilliance of the cloud and the word of God, his great might, but they fell forward on their faces: they did not expect to keep their lives, to live any longer.
Then the guardian of the land went to them, the best of healers touched them with his hands, and told them not to be afraid:
"Nothing that you have seen here, wondrous and glorious things, shall harm you in any way.

Then courage came back into the hearts of the men, their spirits were healed, and there was comfort in their breasts: they saw the child of God standing alone; the rest was gone then, the light of heaven hidden.
Then holy Christ went down from the mountain; after that he commanded his disciples not to tell the vision among the people of the Jews:
"before I myself rise here most gloriously from death, arise from my rest. After that you may tell it forth, proclaim it across middle-earth to many peoples, far and wide throughout this world."
Then the ruling Christ went back into the land of Galilee; he sought out his kinsmen, the mighty one went to the home of his relatives, and there he told many bright parables,
and the Child of God did not hide the sorrowful tidings from his blessed companions, but he told them all openly, his good disciples, how the Jewish people would torment him terribly.
At this the wise men there became very sorrowful; their minds were sore, their hearts grieving:
they then heard their lord, the Son of the Ruler, recount in words what he would have to suffer among that people, willingly, among that host.
Then the ruling Christ went on, the man from Galilee; he sought out a city of the Jews, and they came to Capernaum.
There they found a king's thane, proud among the people; he said that he was a powerful messenger of the noble emperor.
After that he greeted Simon Peter and said that he had been sent there to remind every man there of the head-taxes which they had to pay as tribute to the court:
"There is no doubt about it: every single man pays it promptly with choice treasures; only your master has neglected it.
That will not please my lord well, the noble emperor, when it is made known to him at his court."
After that Simon Peter went and wanted to tell it to his lord then; but the ruling Christ was already aware of it in his mind:
no word could be hidden from him; he knew the thoughts of every man. He then commanded his famous thane, Simon Peter, to cast a hook into the sea:
"Whatever fish you can catch there first," he said, "draw it out of the water to you and force open its jaws:
there, under the jaws, you can take golden coins, so that you can pay the man, to his satisfaction, whatever tax of mine and yours he is seeking from us."

After that he did not need to command him any further with other words: the good fisherman, Simon Peter, went and cast a hook into the sea, into the waves, and drew up a fish from the water with his two hands,
split open its jaws, and under the jaws took golden coins: he did everything just as the Son of God had instructed him with words.
There the Ruler's mighty power was made known, showing how every man must very willingly and gladly pay his worldly lord the dues and taxes that are assigned to him:

he must not neglect him in any way, nor disregard him in his mind, but be gracious to him in his heart and serve him humbly; in that way he can do the will of the God of the peoples and also keep the favor of his worldly lord.
So the holy Christ taught his good disciples: "If any man," he said,
"sins against you, then take him aside, the man in private, and give him your counsel, instruct him with words.
If he then does not consider it worth listening to you, bring other good men there with you, rebuke him for his grim deeds, and accuse him with truthful words.
If after that his sins, his wicked deeds, are still not hateful to him, make it known to other people: proclaim it before the multitude and let many men know of his misdeeds.
Then perhaps he will begin to regret his deeds and repent in his heart, when many men hear of it, the children of men take note of it and reproach him for his evil deed with words.
If he still will not turn back, but scorns such a gathering, then let that man go. Count him as a heathen and let him be hateful to you in your mind,
avoid him in your mind, unless the merciful God, the King of heaven, the Father of all the children of men, grants him help here again." Then Peter, the best of all thanes, asked his lord:
"How often, dear Lord, must I forgive the men who have done me harm? Shall I forgive them their sins seven times,
their wicked deeds, before I take any vengeance for it, as payment for the harm?" Then the guardian of the land, the Son of God, spoke again in answer to the good thane:
"I do not tell you seven times, as you yourself say and speak with your mouth; I add more to that:
seventy times seven times you shall forgive every sin and every harm. This is the teaching I will give you, in truthful words.
