Now that I have given you such power, that you are to be the highest in my household, over much of mankind, you must be kind to them and gentle to the people."
Then a young man came to the teacher there and asked Jesus Christ: "Good master," he said, "what must I do, of all the many things, so that I may obtain the kingdom of heaven?"
He had gained all kinds of wealth for himself, many treasure-hoards, though he carried a generous mind in his breast. Then the Child of God spoke to him:
"Why do you speak about the good? There is no man who is good except the One who created everything, the world and its joys.
If it is your will to be allowed to go into God's light, then you must keep the holy teachings that are commanded in the old law: that you do not kill anyone,
and that you do not swear falsely. Give up adultery and false witness, strife and theft. Do not be too harsh in mind, or envious, or hateful, and do not commit robbery.
Give up all envy. Be good to your parents, your father and mother, and loyal to your friends, and gracious to your neighbours.
Then you may enjoy the kingdom of the heavens, if you will keep this and fully follow God's teachings." Then the young man spoke again: "I have fulfilled all of that," he said,
"as you now teach me and instruct me with words, so that I have never neglected any of it since my childhood." Then Christ began to look at him with his eyes:
"One thing is still lacking in those deeds," he said. "If you have the will to be able to serve your lord perfectly,
then you must take your hoard, must sell all your wealth, your precious treasures, and have it distributed to poor people:
Then afterwards you will have treasure in heaven. Then come to me and you will be kept safe. Follow my way, and afterwards you will have peace."
Then Christ's words caused the young man great sorrow. His mind was sore, and his spirit was heavy around his heart.
He had gained many treasures and much wealth. He turned away from there, uneasy within his breast and heavy in his spirit.
Then Christ, the All-Ruler, looked after him and spoke there, as he wished, to his disciples who were present. He said that it would be hard for a rich man to come up into God's kingdom:
"It would be easier to make a camel pass through the eye of a needle, though the camel is enormously large and the eye is very narrow,
than the soul of the rich man can come to heaven, the man who here has turned all his will and the thoughts of his mind to worldly treasure, and gives no thought to the power of God."
The honored man, Simon Peter, answered him and asked his dear lord to tell them:

"What shall we receive in return for this," he said, "as a reward for good, since for the sake of following you as disciples we have left all our property and inheritance, our farmsteads and households, chosen you as lord, and followed in your company?
"What shall become of benefit to us for this, as a lasting reward?" The Lord of the people himself then said to them: "When I come to sit," he said,
"in the great power on the glorious day, when I shall pronounce judgments on all the great nations, then you may sit there yourselves with your Lord and may have authority over the case:
you may judge the noble peoples of Israel according to their deeds; in this way you will be honored there.
And I tell you truly: whoever does this in this world, that for love of me he leaves behind the dear dwelling of his kinsmen,
he shall receive a reward for it here ten times tenfold, if he does it faithfully, with a pure mind. Beyond that he will also have the light of heaven, eternal life open to him."
Then after that the best of all children began to tell him a parable. He said that in days of old there was a rich man among the people:

"He had plenty of wealth and had gathered treasures. He was always dressed in gold and fine cloth, beautiful finery. He had a great many good things in his courtyards, and every day he sat at feasting:
he lived a splendid life, with merriment on his benches. And there was also a beggar, crippled in his body; his name was Lazarus.
Every day he lay in front of the doors, where he knew the rich man was inside in his guest-hall, enjoying the feast and sitting at the banquet, and he always waited there outside in his poverty:
he was not allowed to come in, nor could he get anyone by begging to bring him the bread that fell down from the table under their feet:
no help could come to him there from the master who ruled the house, except that the man's dogs came over and licked his sores where he lay suffering hunger;
nothing at all came from the powerful man to help him. Then, I have heard, the poor man's destiny, his last day, pressed upon him with great force, so that he had to leave the joy of men.
God's angels received his spirit and led him away from there, and they set the poor man's soul in Abraham's bosom: there he could be in joy forever after.
Then fate also came to the rich man, the hour of death, so that he left this light:
hateful creatures sank his soul into black hell, into the fire, as the fiends wished, and buried him in the home of the hostile ones.

From there he could look on the good man, see Abraham, where he was up above in the delights of life, and Lazarus sat happy in his bosom and received a bright reward for all his poverty. And the rich man lay burning in hell and cried up from there:

"Father Abraham," he said, "I am in dire need that you become merciful to me in your heart, kind to me in this flame: send Lazarus here to me, so that he may bring me some cold water into this inferno.
I am burning alive here, hot in this hell: now I need your help, so that he may cool my tongue with his little finger, since it now bears the mark of evil torment.
For malicious counsels and hateful speech, for all of that the payment has now come to me."
Then Abraham, who was the patriarch, answered him: "Remember in your heart," he said, "what wealth you once had in the world.
Indeed, you used up all your joys there, the good things in your dwellings, whatever was to be granted to you.
Lazarus suffered torment in the light. He had much hardship there, punishment in the world.
Therefore he shall now have wealth and live in delight, and you shall endure the flame, the burning fire. No relief can come to you from here into hell:
holy God has fastened it so with his arms that no man can travel there through the darkness. It is so thick here between us."
Then the man spoke back to Abraham from hot hell and begged for help, asking that he send Lazarus himself into the joyful world of men:
"so that he may tell my brothers there how I suffer burning torment here. They are there among the people, five of them among the folk.
I am afraid that they will do wrong there, so that they too must come into this torment with me, into so greedy a fire."
Then Abraham the patriarch answered him again. He said that the people there in the land had God's law, the command of Moses, and also the words of many prophets:
"If they are willing to keep it, then they need not go into hell, into the inferno, if they act as those people command who read the books to the people for teaching.
If they will not carry out any of that, then they will not listen either to one who rises from here, a man from death.
Let them choose in their own minds which seems sweeter to them to gain while they are in this world, so that afterwards they will have either evil or good."
So he taught the people with bright words, the best of all children, and the mighty Lord told mankind many a parable. He said that a blessed man began to gather men to himself in the morning,
"and the head of the household promised them a reward, a very gracious payment." He said that he would give each of them a silver coin.
"Then many men gathered in his vineyard early at dawn, and he assigned them work.
Some also came there at mid-morning, some came there at midday, men coming to the work, and some came there at nones, which was the ninth hour of the summer day.
Some came there later still, at the eleventh hour. Then evening came on, and the sun went to its setting.
Then he himself, the lord of men, ordered his stewards to pay each of the men his reward, the wages for the men's labour. He ordered that it be given first to those [?]

those who had come there last, the people who had come, the men, to the work. And with his words he commanded that the men be paid their wages, last of all those who had come first, willingly, to the work.
They fully expected that a greater reward had been set aside for them for their labor; but then everyone was given the same, all the people alike.
That was very hateful, a grievance to all of those who had come first: "We came here in the morning," they said,
"and endured many labors here through the day, at times the immeasurably hot, shining sun:
Now you give us no more money than you give the others, who were here at your work only a short while."
Then the master of the household again had his answer ready. He said that he had not promised them any more pay than that for their work.
"Well," he said, "I have the right to pay you all alike your reward, the worth of your work."
But Christ the Ruler meant something greater, even though he spoke to the people in these words about the vineyard, and about how the men came to the work at different times.
In the same way the children of mankind will go from this world into the glorious light, people into God's meadow.

One person begins to prepare himself right away in his childhood. He has chosen a right mind and a good will for himself, avoids worldly wrongdoing and gives up his lusts. His body cannot lure him into misfortune.

He learns wisdom, God's law, and rejects the will of the hostile, wrathful ones. He goes on like this through his life, keeps it up in this light, until the evening of his life, of his days, comes to him.
Then he departs on the upward way. There all his labor is rewarded and repaid with good things in God's kingdom.
That is what the workers meant who began their hard work early, at dawn, in the vineyard and kept at it, those men, until evening.
Another came there at midmorning. He had been delayed and had missed the morning hours of the day's work. Many foolish, witless people do this.

In his youth such a man eagerly pursues all kinds of things. He has learned hateful boasting and many lying words, until his childhood has passed and, after his youth, God's grace gladly urges him in his heart.
He turns to better things in word and deed, and lives his life that way, all his days, to the end. Then the full reward for his good works comes to him in God's kingdom.

Another man gives up wickedness and grievous sins in the middle of his life. He takes up blessed things and through God's power begins to do good works. He makes amends for his evil speech and lets himself regret his bitter deeds in his heart.
Help comes to him from God so that his faith holds as long as his life lasts. With that he goes on his way and receives his wages, a good reward from God. There are no better gifts.
Another begins even later, when he has grown older and is declining in years. Then his evil deeds begin to become hateful to him in this light, when God's teaching urges him in his mind.
His heart grows gentler. He carries on with good, and when he leaves this world he receives his payment, the high kingdom of heaven. His wages turn out to be the same as those
the men received who came to work in the vineyard at nones, the ninth hour of the day.
Some man becomes so very old that he will not atone for his sins, but instead adds every kind of evil to them, until his evening draws near and he has worn out his world and his joys.
then he begins to dread punishment, and his sins become a sorrow in his heart. He remembers how much evil he himself did for as long as he could enjoy his youth.
He cannot make up for the deeds he did so wickedly with other good works. Instead, every day he beats his breast with both hands and weeps over those deeds with bitter tears.
He mourns them loudly with lamentation and begs the holy Lord, the Mighty One, to be merciful to him. After that he does not let his mind waver. So merciful is the one who rules over all:
he will not refuse any human being what he wishes for. The Ruler himself grants him the holy kingdom of heaven, and from then on he is saved.
All of them, the human race, shall receive honour there, even though they do not all come there at the same time. Yet the mighty Lord wishes
to reward everyone of all peoples who accepts his faith here. He gives one heavenly kingdom to all nations, to people as their reward.
That is what mighty Christ, the best of children, meant when he told the parable of how workers came to the vineyards, men at different times. Yet each of them received his full wages from his lord.
In the same way the children of men shall receive their payment from God himself, a very lovely reward, even though some of them come so late.
Then he told his good disciples, the twelve, to come closer to him. They were the most loyal men he had on earth.
The Mighty One himself told them a second time what hardships lay ahead of him there. "There can be no doubt about this," he said.

He said that they were now to travel to Jerusalem, among the Jewish people: "There everything will be fulfilled and carried out among the people, just as wise men spoke about me in words in former days.
There they shall sell me among that powerful people, the men to the army. There my hands will be bound, and my arms will be fastened.
I shall endure much there and hear mockery and insults, scornful speech and many threatening words.
They will wound me terribly with the edges of weapons and take my life. Through the Lord's power I shall rise from death to this light on the third day.
I did not come here among these peoples so that the children of men should labour for me, or so that this people should serve me.
I do not want to accept that from them now or demand it of this people. Instead I shall be of benefit to them, serve them humbly, and give my soul for all these people.
I myself will now redeem them with my life, the many of mankind who have waited here so long for my help."
Then he travelled onward. The Lord's child had a firm mind and a glad heart. He wanted to go to Jerusalem and face the will of the Jewish people.
He knew very well the hate-filled mind of that people, their harsh hostility and their hostile will. The company travelled on past the city of Jericho. God's Son was there, mighty among the crowd.
Two men sat there by the road, and both of them were blind. They needed help: they needed the Ruler of heaven to heal them, because they had been deprived of light for so long, for a great while.
Then they heard the great crowd passing, and at once the two stone-blind men asked eagerly which powerful man among the people was the foremost there, the highest in rank.
Then a man answered them and said that Jesus Christ from Galilee, the best of healers, the highest, was travelling there with his people.

Then the minds of both blind men became glad, when they knew that the child of God was among the crowd. They called out to him with their words, loudly to the holy Christ, and asked that he provide them help:
"Lord, son of David, be merciful to us with your deeds, save us from this distress, as you do for many of mankind: you are good to many, you help and heal."
Then the people began to hold them back with words, telling them not to shout so loudly to Christ the Ruler.
They would not obey them in this, but kept shouting loudly, more and more, over the crowd of people.
The Healer stood still, the best of all children. He then commanded that they be brought to him, led through the people, and spoke to them wisely and kindly before the multitude:
"What help of mine do you two want to have here?" he said.
They asked the Holy One to open their eyes and grant them this light, so that they might see the joy of people, the bright shining of the sun, the beautiful world.

The Ruler did it. He touched them with his hands and gave his help to it, so that the eyes of both blind men were opened, and through the power of God they could make out earth and heaven, light and people.
Then they gave praise to God and glorified our Lord because they could enjoy the light of day. Both of them went with him and followed him on his journey.
The benefit was granted to them, and the Ruler's work was also made known far and wide and proclaimed to many.
A very powerful symbol was shown there, where the blind men sat by the road, suffering torment, deprived of light.

Yet it stands for the children of men, all humankind: how mighty God, in the beginning, by his power alone, himself made the two spouses, Adam and Eve, and gave them the way upward, the kingdom of heaven.
But then the hateful one came too near them, the fiend with his malice and wicked deeds. He deceived them with sins, so that they lost eternal beauty, the light.
They were cast into a more hateful place. Human beings were thrown out into this middle world. Here they suffered slavery in darkness, endured the paths of exile, and went without wealth.
They forgot God's kingdom and served enemies, the children of fiends. In return, those enemies paid them wages of fire in hot hell.

Therefore the children of men were blind in their minds in this middle world, because they did not recognize him, the mighty God, the heavenly Lord, who had created them with his hands and made them according to his will.
This world was then so far turned aside, forced down into darkness, into slavery, into the valley of death.
They sat then by the Lord's road, sorrowful in mind, waiting for God's help. It could not come to them until the ruling God, the mighty Lord, chose to send into this middle world
his own Son, so that he might unlock the light for the children of men and open eternal life to them, so that they could truly know the All-Ruler, the mighty God.
I can also tell you, if you will turn your minds to it and listen, so that you may recognize the power of the Savior: how his coming became a help to many in this middle-world,
yes, what the Lord himself meant by many of his deeds, and why the famous city that stands there in the land of the Jews, built with walls, is called Jericho:
it is named after the moon, after the bright heavenly light. The moon cannot escape its times; every single day it does one or the other: it wanes or it waxes.
So do the children of men here in this world, in this middle-world: they go and follow one another; the old die, and young ones come again after them, grown men, until fate takes them away in turn.
That is what the child of God, the good one, meant when he went out of the city, out of Jericho: that the blindness could not be healed for the children of men before then,
so that they might see the bright light, the eternal beauty, until he himself here in this middle-world took on humanity, flesh and body.
Then the children of men in this world became aware of it, those who had sat here before in torment, in sins, without sight, suffering in darkness
— they perceived that a Savior had come to this people as a help from the kingdom of heaven, Christ, the best of all kings; they could recognize him at once and sense his coming.
Then the men cried out a great deal to the mighty God, that the Ruler would afterwards be merciful to them.
But the heavy sins which they themselves had committed before held them back strongly and hindered them from that faith.
Yet the sins could not keep the people from their desire; instead they cried loudly to the ruling God until he granted them their healing, so that they might see eternal life,

the open, everlasting light, and go into the bright dwellings. That is what the blind men signified who cried loudly there by the city of Jericho to the child of God, asking him to grant them their healing, light in this life:
though the people travelling on the road in front and behind tried hard to stop them with words. That is what wicked sins do to mankind in this middle-world.
Hear now how the blind men acted after they had been healed, so that they could see the light of the sun:
they went off together with their Lord, followed his journey, and spoke many words in praise of the shepherd of the land.
So the children of men still do far and wide throughout this world, since the ruling Christ enlightened them with his teachings and granted to good men eternal life,
God's kingdom, the high light of heaven, and his help besides, to whoever acts so that he may follow his way.

Then Christ the Savior, the good one, drew near to Jerusalem. Many people came out there to meet him, gladly and with good will. They received him warmly and strewed the road before him with their garments and also with plants,
with bright blossoms and with branches of trees, and the field with lovely palms, all as befitted his journey, since the Son of God meant to go to the famous city.
A great crowd of people thronged around him in joy, and the multitude gladly raised a song of praise. They gave thanks to the Ruler that the son of David himself had come there to visit the people.

Then the good Ruler Christ, the best of men, saw the wall of the city of Jerusalem gleaming, and the dwellings of the Jews: the high gabled halls and also the house of God, the most delightful of all sanctuaries.

Then his mind welled up within him, against his heart. Then the holy child could not hold back his weeping; he spoke many words sorrowfully (his mind was pained): "Woe has come upon you, Jerusalem," he said,
"because you do not truly know the fates that are yet to befall you: how you will yet be surrounded by the might of an army, and cruel-minded men will besiege you, enemies with their troops.

Then you will have no peace anywhere, no protection among men. Many will bring spear-points and blades against you here, the word of war. They will destroy your people with the flames of fire, lay waste these dwellings, and fell the high walls to the ground.
Not one stone of rock will be left standing on another. These places around Jerusalem, of the Jewish people, will become desolate,
because they do not recognize that their time has come upon them. They have doubting minds, and they do not know that the power of the Ruler is visiting them."
Then the Lord of men went with the crowd into the bright city. When the child of God moved into Jerusalem with the multitude of people, with his companions,
there arose the greatest of all songs, loud voices raised in holy words. The multitude of people praised the guardian of the land, the best of children.
The city was in an uproar, the people were afraid, and at once they asked who it was who had come there with the host, with the great multitude.
Then a man answered them and said that Jesus Christ, the Savior, had come there from the land of Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, a wise prophet, to help the people.
Then the Jews who had been hostile to him before were resentful in their minds and grieved in their hearts that the people made so many songs of praise for him and glorified their Lord.

Then they went, in their recklessness, to speak to Christ the Ruler. They asked him to order his company to be silent and to restrain the people, so that they would not give him so much praise with their words:
"It is hateful to this crowd," they said, "to these city-people." Then the child of God spoke again: "If you hinder them," he said,

"so that the children of men may not glorify the Ruler's power with words here, then the hard stones, the strong rocks, shall cry it out before this people, before it should ever be left undone, rather than that no one should speak his praise far and wide throughout this world."

Then he went into the temple, into the house of God. There he found many Jews, men of various kinds, many of them together, who had chosen it as a marketplace and were trading there in many kinds of goods.
Money-changers sat inside the temple and had their exchange money ready every day to hand out. All of this was offensive to the child of God.
He drove them out of there, far from the temple building, and said that it would be a more righteous deed for the children of Israel to come there to pray "and ask for help in this house of mine,
that the Lord of victory may free them from their sins, than for thieves to hold their assembly-place here, and for wicked men to carry on exchange: pure injustice.
You show no honor to this house of God, people of the Jews."
So then he, the mighty Lord, cleared and set in order the holy house, and he was a help to many of mankind, those who had heard of his great power from afar and came travelling there over a long way.
Many a sick person was there; the lame were healed and the crippled likewise, and the blind were cured.
So the Child of God did this, willingly, for the people, because everything concerning the life of these people, and also this land likewise, stands in his power.
Then the ruling Christ, the dear guardian of the land, stood before the sanctuary and observed the minds of the people and their intentions:
he saw a great crowd bringing treasures into the famous house, giving gold and fine woven cloth, precious ornaments. Christ the Lord watched all that wisely.
Then a widow also came there, a poor woman, and went to the temple, and she laid two brass coins in the treasure-house. Her heart was single-minded, full of good will.
Then the ruling Christ, the man, spoke to his disciples and said that she had brought a much greater gift there than any other son of man:
"If wealthy men have brought possessions here," he said, "many treasure-hoards, they have kept more of their gathered wealth for themselves at home.
This widow did not do so. She gave to this temple all the wealth she had gathered, so that she left herself no goods at all in her dwelling.
Therefore her gifts are greater and more worthy to the Ruler, because she gave them to this house of God with such good will.
For this she shall receive payment, a very lasting reward, because she has such faith."
So I have heard that there in the temple the ruling Christ, the Lord of men, taught with words every single day.
A crowd stood around him, a great people of the Jews, and they heard him speak his good words sweetly.
One man among the crowd became so blessed that he began to store it up in his mind; they learned the teachings that the guardian of the land, the Child of the Lord, spoke, all in parables.
To others, in turn, Christ's teachings, the words of the Ruler, were very hateful: their minds were hostile, all those who were highest in the host, the foremost among the people:

in their hostility they intended to set traps with their words. To help them they had brought in adversaries, men of the highest man [probably Herod], Herod's retainer, who stood present there with hostile intent,
so that he might overhear their words, and so that, if they caught him, those people might then lay fetters and limb-bonds on him, the sinless one.
Then the companions went up to him with bitter minds, so that they, hostile adversaries, spoke these words to the Child of God:
"Well, you are a prophet to all peoples," they said, "you teach so much truth: you need not avoid any man in the least because of his power,
but you always speak what is right and with your teachings lead the companies of men onto God's way. No one among this people can find fault in you. Now we must ask you,
mighty king, what right the emperor of Rome has, who seeks tribute here from this people and has reckoned what we must pay him every year as head-tax.
Tell us what you think about this in your mind: is it right or is it not? Counsel your countrymen well: we have need of your teachings."
They wanted him to speak against it, but he could recognize their hostile intent well: "Why, you liars," he said,
"do you test me so boldly? It shall not become a benefit to you that you deceivers now want to trap me secretly."
He then commanded the coins to be brought forth for viewing, "which you are obliged to give in tribute." The Jews brought forth a silver one:
many looked at how it was minted: in the middle shone the emperor's image (they could recognize that well), the likeness of their lord's head.
Then the holy Christ asked them whose likeness had been put on it.
They said that it was the world-emperor's from Rome, "who has power over all this realm in this world." "Then I will tell you truly here," he said,
"myself, that you should give him his own, the worldly lord his revenue, and give to the ruling God what is his: that shall be your souls, the spirits of men."
Then the Jews' spirit was diminished in that assembly: those wicked ones could not manage with words, as their will went, to trap him,

because the peace-child of God guarded himself against the hostile ones and told them truth in return, a true message, though they were not so blessed as to receive it in the way that would have been to their benefit.
Yet they would not let it go. Instead they had a woman brought out in front of the crowd who had committed a crime, a plain wrong.
The woman had been caught in adultery. She was liable to lose her life, so that the children of men would take her life and deprive her of it, as was written in their law.
Then they began to ask him, those bold people, hostile with their words, what they should do with the woman, whether they should kill her,
whether they should let her live, or what he would judge about such deeds. "You know how this multitude," they said,

"was commanded by Moses with true words that any woman who forfeited her life in adultery should then be stoned by the men with their hands, with hard stones. Now you can see her standing here, caught in sin: say what your will is in this."

The adversaries wanted to trap him with words. If he said that they should let her live and spare her life, then the Jewish people would say that he was speaking against the law of their ancestors, the law of the land of the people.
But if he ordered them to take the young woman's life in front of the crowd, then they would say that he did not carry in his breast the kind of merciful mind that the child of God should have.
So either way they wanted to blame holy Christ for his words, whichever answer he gave there before the crowd as his judgment.
But the Lord Christ knew those men's thoughts and their hostile intent very well. Then he spoke to the crowd, to all those men:
"Whichever of you is without cruel sins," he said, "let that man go up to her himself and be the first to throw a stone at her with his hand."
So the Jews stood there, thinking, and kept silent. No man could find any [?] answer against what he had said. Every man remembered his own wicked thoughts, his own sins.

None of them was so free of guilt that, at that word, he dared to throw a stone at the woman. Instead they left her standing there alone inside, and the fierce-hearted Jewish people went out from there,
one after another, until not one of that hostile crowd was left there who wanted to go after her life, the woman's death.
Then, I have heard, the peace-child of God, the best of all men, asked her: "Where has this Jewish crowd gone," he said, "your accusers, who accused you here before me?
Did they do you no harm at all today, those hateful people who wanted to take your life and torment you with wounds?"
Then the woman answered him. She said that, through the holy help of the Saviour, no one there had done her harm in payment for her wrongdoing.
Then the ruling Christ, the lord of men, spoke in reply: "I will not harm you at all yet," he said,
"but go away from here safe, and let it be a concern in your mind that you never become sinful after this."
So the holy child of God had helped her and protected her life.
But the Jewish people stood there ill-minded, as from the first, with hostile will, plotting how they could carry out their verbal hatred against the peace-child of God.
The people had split into two in their beliefs. The common folk were much more eager to do his will and to carry out the word of God's child, as their Lord commanded them:
they strove for what was right better than the powerful men did. They held him as their master, indeed as the King of Heaven, and followed him gladly.
Then God's son went into the temple. A crowd, a great throng of people, gathered around him.
He stood in their midst and taught the people with bright words and a loud voice. They listened closely, and many men fell silent. He told the people that whoever there was oppressed by thirst
"should come here to me to drink," he said, "every day, from the sweet spring."

I can tell you this: whoever of the children of men here among this people firmly believes in me, from his body shall flow a living flood, running water, a great spring like a river. Living springs shall come from there.
These sayings will come true and be fulfilled for people, for whoever here believes in me."

By that water the ruling Christ, the lord King of Heaven, meant the Holy Spirit, and how the children of men would receive it: light and wisdom and eternal life, the high kingdom of heaven and the favour of God.
Then the people fell to quarrelling about Christ's teaching, about his words.
Proud men stood there, arrogant Jews, boasting loudly. They mocked it and said they could clearly hear that hostile beings, evil spirits, were speaking out of him:
"Now he teaches falsely," they said, "in every word." Then the other group spoke:
"You have no need to blame the teacher," they said. "Mighty words of life come from his mouth. He works many things, wonders in this world.
That is not the deed of hostile ones or the power of fiends. It would never then lead to such benefit. It comes directly from God almighty, from his power."
You can clearly recognise this from his true words: that he has power over everything on earth.
Then his enemies wanted to seize him there on the spot or throw stones at him, but they were afraid of the crowd of men and feared the people.
Then God's child of peace spoke: "I show you so much good," he said,
"from God himself, in words and works. Now, because of your hard minds, you want to punish me here, throw stones at me, and rob me of my life."
Then the people, his hostile adversaries, answered him: "It is not because of your works," they said,
"that we want to put you to death. We do it because of your words, because you speak such wickedness."
because you glorify yourself this way and speak such blasphemy. You declare before these Jews that you are God himself, the mighty Lord, and yet you are a man as we are, born of this people."
Christ the all-ruling did not want to listen any longer to the boasting of the Jews and the wishes of those hostile men. He went away from the temple and across the river Jordan.

He had his disciples with him, his blessed companions, who always gladly stayed with him. He sought out other people and did there what he was accustomed to do, the Lord himself: he taught the people.
Whoever was willing believed in his holy word. That would always be good for any man who took it to heart.
Then, as I have heard, messengers came there to Christ from Bethany and told the child of God that two women had sent them there on that errand, Mary and Martha, noble maidens, very lovely women.
He knew them both. They were two sisters, whom he himself had loved in his heart before then because of their gracious minds, the women for their good will.

They sent him true word then from Bethany that their brother Lazarus was bedridden and that they did not expect him to live. They begged that Christ the all-ruling, the holy one, would come there to help.
As soon as he heard them speak about the sick man, he answered at once and said that Lazarus's sickness had not been inflicted on him for his death,
"but through it the Lord's praise," he said, "shall be brought about. It has not been inflicted on him for any other harm."
The Lord's Son himself then stayed there for two nights and days. The time had now drawn near when he wanted to visit Jerusalem and the Jewish people again, as he had the power to do.
Then the Lord's son told his companions that he wanted to go back across the Jordan to the Jewish people. His disciples answered him at once:
"Why are you so eager to go there, my lord?" they said. "Was it not just recently that they meant to punish you for your words and wanted to stone you with hard stones?"
And now you are eager to go back among that quarrelsome people, where there are enemies enough, arrogant men?"
Then one of the twelve, Thomas, spoke. He was a worthy man and a precious thane of the Lord. "We should not blame him for this deed," he said,
"or keep him from what he wants. Let us stay with him and suffer with our lord. That is a thane's choice: to stand firm together with his lord and die with him there at the time of judgment.
Let us all do the same and follow him on this journey. Let us not value our lives at anything against this, unless we die with our Lord, in that company with him."
Then their fame lives on after them, a good word among men." So the disciples of Christ, nobly born men, became of one mind, willing to do their lord's will.
Then holy Christ himself told his companions that Lazarus had fallen asleep from his sickness: "He has given up this light; he has been put to sleep in his dwelling.
Now let us go on that journey and wake him, so that he may see this world again, the light, living. Then your faith will afterwards be made firmer still."

Then he went away from there over the river, the good Son of God, until he came with his disciples to Bethany, the Child of the Lord himself with his companions, where the two sisters, Mary and Martha, sat sorrowful in grief of heart.
Many of the Jewish people from Jerusalem had gathered there, who wanted to comfort the women with words, so that they would not grieve so much over the young man's death, the loss of Lazarus.
As the Guardian of the land then went toward the dwellings, the coming of God's Child was made known there, that he, so mighty, was outside the town.
Then both of the women had a strong desire for this, when they knew that the Ruler, the peace-child of God, was journeying toward them.
Then the greatest of joys for the women was the coming of the Lord and the hearing of Christ's words.
Weeping, Martha went, sorrowful, to exchange words with the Mighty One, and she spoke to the Ruler, troubled in her mind:
"If you, my lord," she said, "best of saviours, had been nearer, good Healer, then I would not now have to suffer such harm,
bitter heart-sorrow; then my brother Lazarus would not now be dead, gone from this light, but could go on living at home, full of life.
Yet I, my lord, believe clearly in you, best of teachers, that whatever you wish to ask of the bright Lord, he will grant it to you at once, God almighty, and fulfil your wish."
Then the Ruler Christ spoke an answer back to the woman: "Do not let your spirit grow dark within you over this," he said.
"I can tell you with true words that there is no doubt of this: your brother shall rise from death in his body, through God's command, through the Lord's power."
"I [?] believe so," she said, "that it shall happen so, whenever this world ends and the glorious day passes over mankind,
that he will then rise up from the earth on the Day of Judgment; then every one of mankind will come alive from death through God's might and arise from rest."
Then the powerful Christ almighty told the woman in plain words that he himself was the Son of the Lord, both life and light for the children of men, for them to rise again:
"Whoever believes in me here shall never die or lose life. Even if the children of men cover him with earth and bury him deep, he is no more dead for that.
The flesh is buried, but the life is kept, and the soul is safe." Then the woman at once answered him with her words: "I believe that you are the true one," she said,
"Christ, the Son of God. One can well recognize that and know from your words that, through the holy decrees, you have power over heaven and earth."
Then, as I have heard, the other of the women came walking there, Mary, sorrowful; many of the Jewish people went after her.

Then she, sorrowful in mind, told the child of God what had brought sorrow and grief into her heart. With lamentation she mourned the loss of Lazarus, the beloved man, and wept in mourning, until the heart of the child of God was moved.
Hot tears welled up as he wept. Then he spoke to the women and told them to lead him to where Lazarus had been laid in the earth.
A rock lay over it there, a hard stone covering it. Then the holy Christ ordered them to open up the stone, so that he could see the body and look upon the corpse.
Then Martha could not hide what was in her mind in front of the crowd. She spoke to the Mighty One: "My good lord," she said,
"if anyone takes away the rock and opens up the stone, then I expect a stench will come out of there, a foul smell. For I can tell you in true words
that there is no doubt about it: he has now been buried there in the earth-grave for four nights and days."
The Ruler gave the woman an answer: "Well, did I not tell you truly before," he said,
"that if you are willing to believe, it will not be long now before you come to know here the power of the Lord, the great might of God?" Then many went up to it and lifted off the hard stone.
Then holy Christ looked up with his eyes and gave thanks to the one who created this world: "that you hear my words," he said,

"victory-Lord yourself. I know that you always do so, but I say this for the sake of this great people of the Jews, so that they may know truly that you send me into this world as a teacher for these people."
Then he called to Lazarus in a strong voice and ordered him to stand up and walk out of the grave.
Then the spirit came into the body. He began to move his limbs and stirred under the garment; he was still bound up then, wrapped in the bedding of the dead.
Then the ruling Christ ordered that he be helped. Men went up and unwound the garment.
Lazarus rose up splendidly into this light. His life had been given back to him, so that he might have his span of life and peace from then on.
Then both rejoiced, Mary and Martha. No one can truly tell another how the two sisters rejoiced in their hearts.

Many of the Jewish people were amazed when they saw him come out of the grave sound and well, the man whom sickness had carried off before and whom they had buried deep under the earth without life. Now he could go on living, healthy, at home.
In this way the great might of God, the King of heaven, can protect the life of every man and, holy, help him against the enmity of fiends, whoever it is he grants his favor to.
Then the minds of many men there were turned toward Christ and their thoughts were changed, after they had seen his holy work for themselves, for never before had such a wonder happened in the world.
But on the other hand there were very many of the people, such stubborn men, who would not openly acknowledge the might of God; instead they fought against his great power with their words.
The Ruler's teachings were hateful to them. They went to other people in Jerusalem, where the Jews had their lordly court and their capital, the great company of a grim people.
They then told them about Christ's deeds. They said they had seen alive with their own eyes the man who had been in the earth, committed to the ground for four nights and days,
buried dead, until he himself had awakened him with his deeds and with his words, so that he could see this world.

Then that was very hostile to the proud men, the Jewish people. They then ordered their retinue, the host, to gather and hold a council, the great people all together. They took counsel in secret against mighty Christ:
"It is no counsel at all," they said, "that we should put up with this: too many of this people will believe in his teachings.
Then people will march against us, a mounted host; warriors from Rome will become our overlords.
Then we shall have to live deprived of this kingdom, or we shall have to lose our lives, we men, our heads."
Then an honored man spoke there before the gathering of men. He was the bishop of the people there in the city, the high priest; he was called Caiaphas.
The people of the Jews had chosen him in that year to look after God's house and guard the sanctuary. "It seems a great wonder to me," he said,
"famous people, you who know how to tell many things apart, why do you not know truly, host of the Jews, that here the better counsel for every one of the children of men
that a single man here be deprived of life and die bloody through your deeds, giving up his life for this people, than that this whole nation be lost."
Yet it was not his own intention that he spoke so truly, so openly before the people, and proclaimed the benefit of mankind before the multitude.
Rather, it came to him from the power of God through his holy office, because he was to tend God's house there in Jerusalem and guard the sanctuary.
Therefore he spoke so truly, the bishop of the people, about how the child of God would redeem all mankind with his single life, with his body.
That was the benefit of all these peoples, because through it the ruling Christ brought heathen peoples, men, into his will.
Then the arrogant men, the people of the Jews, were of one mind. The famous people agreed in their assembly that they would not let their resolve waver:

whoever could find him among the people should seize him at once and bring him before the people's assembly. They said that they could not put up with it any longer that this one man should overcome them all, the whole host.
But the ruling Christ knew the men's thoughts very well, their fiercely hostile minds, because nothing at all in this middle-world was hidden from him.
After that he would not go openly into the crowd, among the folk of men, among the Jews.
The Son of God waited for the bright time that was coming to him, when he was willing to suffer for this people and endure torment for this host. He himself knew that appointed day well.
Then our Lord went away. The almighty Christ, the holy Lord, stayed with his band in Ephraim, in the high city, until he chose to turn back to Bethany with a great throng, with his good retinue.
The Jews spoke against him in every word when they saw such a great host following him. "There is no benefit," they said,
"in the counsel of our realm. Even though we speak what is right, nothing at our assembly succeeds. This people wants to turn to follow his will."
All this world follows him; people follow his teachings, so that we cannot do him any harm in front of this people."

Then the Child of God went into Bethany six nights before the gathering of the Jewish people was to take place there in Jerusalem at the holy days, when they were to keep the holy season, the Passover of the Jews.
The Son of God stayed there, mighty among the crowd. A great host of men, of people, was there because of his words.
Two women came there and gathered around him, Mary and Martha, with kind hearts, and served him humbly. The Lord of the people gave them a lasting reward:

he freed them from every harm and cleared them of their sins, and he himself commanded that the women should go in peace, safe from the hatred of enemies, with his good leave. They had turned their service toward his will.
Then the Ruler Christ, the Lord of men, went on with the people into Jerusalem, where the hostile, harsh city of the Jews was, where they were keeping the holy feast at the temple.
So many people were there, of powerful families, who did not want to hear Christ's words gladly and had no love in their hearts for the Child of God,

but they were very hostile toward him, an arrogant people, proud mankind. They had murderous thoughts and malice within them. They took Christ's teaching the wrong way and wanted to punish him, the mighty one, for his words.

But so many people were there around the noble one the whole long day (the common people had surrounded him in a crowd because of his sweet words) that his enemies did not dare to seize him among the multitude, and kept away from him because of the crowd.
Then mighty Christ stood inside the temple and spoke many words for the benefit of the children of men.
People were there all the long day, until the bright sun went to its setting. Then many of mankind went to their lodgings.
There was a famous mountain outside the city, broad and high, green and beautiful. The Jewish people called it Olivet by name.
The Saving Christ went up there when night overtook him, and stayed there with his disciples, so that none of the Jews knew for certain where he was. For he stood in the temple,
the Lord of the people, when light came from the east, and received the multitude and told them many true words, so that there is no one in this world,
in this middle-earth, no man so wise, none of the children of men, who could recount the teachings that he spoke there in the sanctuary, the Ruler in the temple.
And with his words he always commanded every one of them to prepare themselves for God's kingdom, so that on the great day they might receive their Lord's glory.
He told them what sins they had committed, and always commanded them to put those sins out. He told them to love God's light in their hearts and to give up wickedness
and wrongful pride, to take up humility and load it into their hearts. He said that then the kingdom of heaven would be theirs, the greatest of good things, made ready for them.
Then very many men were turned toward his will, after they had heard the holy word of God, the King of heaven,
and recognized the great power, the coming of the Lord, the help of the Master: yes, that the kingdom of heaven, the Saviour, and God's grace had come near to the children of men.
Some of the Jewish people were so arrogant. They had grim minds and cruel hearts and would not believe his word, but set up a great struggle against Christ's power:
…the people could not come, because of their hateful strife, to hold firmly to him in faith. The benefit was not granted to them, that they might possess the kingdom of heaven.

Then the Son of God left the temple, and his disciples with him, the Ruler, just as he willed, and the Child of the Lord climbed up onto the mountain. He sat there with his companions and told them a great many true words.

Then they began to talk about the temple, the men about God's house. They said that there was no finer sanctuary on earth made by the hands of men, by human work, a building raised with mighty strength.
Then the mighty one spoke, the lord, heaven's king, and the others listened: "I can tell you," he said,
"that the time will yet come when not one stone of it shall stay standing on another. It will fall to the ground and fire will take it, the greedy flame,
even though it is now so fine and so wisely built. All the created things of this world will do the same: the green plain will pass away."
Then his disciples came up to him and asked him quietly: "How long," they said,

"will this world still stand in its joys before the change comes and the last day of light shines through the cover of clouds? Or when is your coming to middle-earth expected again, to judge the race of men, the dead and the living?"
My good lord, ruling Christ, we are very eager to know when that shall happen."
Then almighty Christ himself gave the men a kindly answer:
"The Father of the heavenly kingdom, the Ruler of this world, has hidden it so well and concealed it so firmly," said the good Lord, "that no human child can know
when that famous hour will come in this world. Not even God's angels, who are always present before him, truly know it.
they too cannot say truly in words when it will happen that he, the mighty Lord, will come to this middle-earth to visit men.
Only the holy Father in heaven knows it. Otherwise it is hidden from all, the living and the dead, when his coming will be.
But I can tell you what wondrous signs will appear here beforehand, before he comes into this world on that glorious day:
first it will happen here in the shining of the moon, and in the sun likewise: they will both grow dark and be wrapped in darkness;
the stars will fall, the white bodies of heaven, and the earth will quake, this broad world will tremble (there will be many such signs);
the great sea will rage, and the stream of the ocean will cause terror to the earth-dwellers with its waves.

Then the people will wither away because of the great distress, the folk through the fear. Then there will be peace nowhere, but many a war will be hatefully raised over all this world, and armies will lead one people against another.
There will be strife among kings, great military campaigns; there will be the death of many, open war (it is a terrible thing that men must ever start such slaughter);
there will be so great a plague over all this world, the greatest dying of men that has ever been in this middle-earth through sickness:
sick men will lie there, they will droop and die and end their days, paying in full with their lives. Huge, fiercely grim hunger will travel over the children of men, the greatest of famines.
that is not the least of the torments in this world that must happen here before Judgment Day.
Whenever you see these deeds happen in this world, you may truly understand that the last day is drawing near to people, the great day, to men, and the power of God,
the shaking of the heavenly powers, and the coming of the Holy One, the Lord with his glory. Look, you can recognize a sign of these deeds in these trees:
when they burst forth and bloom and the leaves open out, the foliage unfolds, then the children of men know that soon after that summer draws near, warm and pleasant, with fair weather.
In the same way you will also know by these signs that I have told you here when the last day draws near to people.
Then I tell you truly that this people may not pass away, this nation may not perish, before my words are fulfilled in this way and made true.
Yet the end of heaven and earth will come, and my holy word stands fast from now on and will all be fulfilled in this way, carried out in this light, as I have spoken before these people.
Keep watch carefully: Doomsday, the famous day, is certain for you, and so is your Lord's power, the great mighty strength, and the famous time, the end of this world.
Therefore you must take care that he does not suddenly catch you sleeping in your bed, in wicked deeds, full of sin.
Muspilli comes in the dark night. Just as a thief goes about his deeds in secret, so the day comes to men, the last day of this light, without these people knowing it beforehand,
just as the flood did in former days, which there, with its sea-streams, destroyed people in Noah's time, except that God, the holy Lord, saved him and his household against the flood's surge:
in the same way the fire also came hot from heaven, so that the black flame, grim and greedy, seized the high cities around the land of Sodom, so that none of the men there survived except Lot alone:
the Lord's angels led him and his two daughters away from there up onto a mountain. The burning fire took all the rest: the flame destroyed both land and people.
The fire came as suddenly as the flood had come before: so too will the last day come.
Therefore every one of all people should think ahead to that judgment; every man has great need of that. So take this care into your minds.
For whenever it comes about that the ruling Christ, the famous Son of Man, the mightiest of kings, comes with the might of God, with that power, to sit in his own might, and with him all the angels
who are holy up there in heaven, then the children of men, the peoples of every land, shall all come there together, of all living people, whoever of mankind was ever born in this light.
There the famous Lord shall judge the people, all mankind, according to their deeds. Then he separates the wicked men, the sinful men, to the left hand:
In the same way he places the blessed on the right-hand side. Then he greets the good and speaks to them: "Come," he says,
"you who are chosen, and receive this mighty kingdom, the good one that stands prepared there, that was made there for the children of men from the beginning of this world.
"The Father of all the children of men has himself blessed you. You may enjoy these good things and rule this wide kingdom, because you often did my will,
followed me gladly and were generous to me with your gifts when I was gripped by thirst and hunger, caught by frost, or lay in fetters, shut up in prison.
Often help came to me there from your hands. You were kind to me in your hearts and visited me with honour." Then that host answers him in turn:
"My good lord," they say, "when were you ever so confined, oppressed by such needs as you tell of before this people, mighty one, as you declare?
When did any man see you gripped by such needs? Why, you have power over all peoples, and likewise over the treasures that the children of men have ever won in this world."
"Then the ruling God speaks to them again: "Whatever you did," he says,
"in the name of your Lord, giving of your goods for God's honour to those people who are the least here, of those who now stand among this multitude and through humility were poor men,
because they did my will — whatever of your wealth you gave them and did for them out of love, your Lord himself received it. That help came to the King of heaven.
Therefore the holy Lord will reward your faith: he gives you eternal life."
Then the Ruler, the Lord, turns to his left hand, to the wicked men, and tells them that they must pay for what they did, those men, for their wicked works: "Now you must go away from me," he says,
"go thus accursed into the eternal fire, which was prepared there for God's adversaries, the host of fiends, for their wicked deeds, because you did not help me
when hunger and thirst afflicted me terribly, or I went without clothing, sorrowful at heart; I was in great need, yet I had no help there; when I was fettered,
locked in limb-fetters, or sickness laid me low, grievous disease, then you would not visit me there in my sickness at all; it was not worth anything to you to give me a thought.
Therefore you shall suffer in hell, in darkness." Then the people speak to him in reply: "O ruling God," they say,
"why will you speak so against this host, address this multitude so? When did you ever have need of men, of good from people?
Indeed, they have it all through your gifts, the wealth in this world." Then the ruling God speaks again: "When you," he says,
"heroes, despised in your hearts the poorest of the children of men, the least of men, and let them be hateful to you in your minds,
and deprived them of your treasures, then you did the same to your Lord: you refused him your wealth.
Therefore the ruling God, your Father, will not receive you. Instead you must go into the fire, into deep death, and serve the devils, the angry enemies, because you acted this way before."
Then, after those words, the host splits in two, the good and the evil.
The damned men go into hot hell, sorrowful at heart. The men ruined by their own deeds receive torment, evil without end.
Then the King of heaven leads the pure peoples up from there into the lasting light. There is eternal life there, God's kingdom, made ready for good people.

So I have heard that the mighty Lord then told the men in words about the end of this world: how it goes on as long as the children of men may dwell in it, and how at the end it shall fall apart and pass away.
He also told his disciples there in true words: "Indeed, you all know," he said,
"that now after two nights the time has come, the Passover of the Jews, when they must serve their God, the men in the temple.
There is no doubt that the Son of Man will be sold there to the mighty people and struck on the cross, and will suffer a violent death.
Then many hostile-minded thanes gathered there, men of the southern people, the band of the Jews, where they were to serve their God.
The lawgivers all came to the assembly, the men whom they counted the wisest among the multitude of men, a powerful lineage. Caiaphas was there, the bishop of the people.
Then they plotted against the child of God, how they might kill him, though he was without sin. They said that they must not lay hands on him on the holy day among the multitude of men,
"so that this great people, the warriors, may not be stirred up, because this host will defend him by fighting.
We must seek his life so quietly that this people of the Jews does not raise a riot during these holy days."
Then Judas, a disciple of Christ and one of the twelve, went forth to where the nobles sat, the band of the Jews. He said that he could give them good advice about him:
"What will you give me here," he said, "in treasures as payment, if I hand the man over to you without fighting and without strife?
"Then the minds of the host, of the people, were filled with joy: "If you will carry it out so," they said,
"and make your word good, then you shall have the power to choose what you wish to receive from this people in good treasures.
Then the band promised him, at his own decision, thirty pieces of silver all together, and he spoke to the people with bold words, saying that he would hand over his Lord in return.
Then he turned away from the host. His mind was hostile. Faithless as he was, he kept reckoning when the time would come when he could betray him to the hostile people, to the folk of his enemies.
But the peace-child of God, Christ, the true Ruler, knew that he was to give up this world and these dwellings, seek out God's kingdom, and journey to his Father's homeland.
No child of men ever saw greater love than he then showed to those men, to his good disciples. He prepared a feast, seated them lovingly, and spoke many true words to them.
The day glided westward, the sun toward its setting. Then the Ruler himself gave the command with his words and ordered clear water to be brought for washing hands. And the holy Christ rose,
the good one at the meal, and there he washed his disciples' feet with his hands and afterwards wiped them with his cloth, dried them lovingly. Then Simon Peter spoke to his Lord:
"This does not seem a fitting thing to me," he said, "my good lord, that you should wash my feet with your holy hands."
Then his master answered him in turn, the Ruler with his words: "If you are not willing," he said,
"to accept that I wash your feet out of such love as I show to these other men here out of affection, then you have no share with me in the kingdom of heaven."
Then Simon Peter's mind was changed: "You yourself have the power," he said,
"my good lord, to wash feet and hands and my head as well, with your hands, Lord,
so that I may have your favour from now on, and such a share of the kingdom of heaven as you, Lord, will grant me through your goodness."
Christ's disciples, the men, endured that service, the thanes with patience, whatever their lord did to them, mighty out of love; and he intended to accomplish far greater things for people.
The peace-child of God then went back to sit among that company of companions and told them much lasting counsel. Then light came again, morning to men.
His disciples greeted mighty Christ and asked where they should prepare his feast on that holy day, where he himself wished to keep the holy time with his companions.
Then he told the men to go to Jerusalem: "When you come walking," he said,
"into the city (there is a great uproar there, a throng of mighty peoples), there you will see a man carrying in his hands a vessel full of clear water.
"You are to follow him into whatever dwelling you see him go into, and then say to the master himself who owns those courts that I sent you there to prepare my feast."
"Then he will show you a fine house, a high upper room, which is all hung with beautiful ornaments."
"There you are to prepare my meal. There I will surely be myself, with my companions."
Then soon after that Christ's disciples set out on their journey to Jerusalem, and they found everything just as he had said, a true sign in words: there was no deviation from it.

There they prepared the feast. The Son of God, the holy Lord, came into the house where they were to carry out the custom of the land and fulfil God's command, just as the law and ancient custom of the Jews had been in former days.
Then in the evening Christ, the all-ruler, went to sit in the hall; he commanded his twelve companions to come to him there,
who were the most loyal men to him in their hearts, in words and in ways: the holy Lord himself knew their thoughts.
He greeted them then over the meal: "I am very glad," he said, "that I may sit together with you, enjoy the feast, and share the Passover of the Jews with you, who are so dear."
"Now I must tell you your Lord's will: that in this world I may no longer partake of food with men, any further with people, until the kingdom of heaven is fulfilled."
"Torment and terrible agony are now at hand for me, which I must suffer for this host, for this people."
When the holy Lord spoke thus to the thanes, his mind became troubled, his heart grew dark, and the good one spoke again to his companions, to his disciples:

"Listen: I promised you God's kingdom," he said, "the light of heaven, and you loyally promised me your service as thanes. Now you will not carry it through like that, but you will waver from those words."
"Now I tell you truly here that one of you twelve will betray his loyalty and will sell me to this race of the Jews,"
"hand me over for silver; he will take treasure for it there, precious riches, and give his lord in exchange, his gracious master."
that it shall nevertheless turn to harm for him, become a punishment; when he sees his fate and looks upon the end of [?] his toil, then he knows it to be true
that it would have been a better thing for him, much better, if he had never been born alive into this light, than that he should receive that reward, evil toil, for his wicked counsel."
Then each of the men began to look at the other, looking about in sorrow; their minds were sore, grieving about their hearts: they heard their lord speak words of grief.
The men worried about which of the twelve he meant by this, the guilty wrongdoer who had bargained there with the people for the treasure.
It was not easy for any of the thegns to confess such malice, such wicked thoughts. Each of the men denied it. They all became afraid,
and they did not dare to ask, until a worthy man, Simon Peter, made a sign (he did not dare to say it himself) to John the good:

he was the dearest of the thegns to the Child of God in those days, the greatest in His love, and he was allowed to rest there on the lap of the mighty Christ, and he lay on His breast and leaned his head there:
There he received so many holy secrets, deep thoughts, and then he spoke to his Lord and began to ask him: "How shall that be, my lord," he said,
"that someone will sell you, most powerful of kings, among the people of your enemies? We would be very eager, Ruler, to know this."
Then Christ the Healer again had his word ready: "See to whom I here give into his hand some of my food before these men:
he has wicked thoughts and bears a bitter mind; he shall hand me over into the power of killers, to enemies, where they will seek my life and my being."

After that He took some of the food before the men and gave it to the wicked wrongdoer, into Judas's hand. He Himself spoke to him in front of His companions and told him to go quickly away from His people:
"Do as you intend," He said, "do what you must do: you cannot hide your will any longer. Fate is at hand; the time has now drawn near."
As soon as the faithless one received the food and tasted it with his mouth, the power of God left him, and fiends went into his body,
hateful creatures. Satan pressed painfully upon him, hard about his heart, since the help of God had abandoned him in this light.
So it is woe to the people who must change lords in this way under this heaven.
Then Judas went out from there, eager for malice: the thegn had a grim mind against his lord. By then it was dark night, very gloomy.
The Son of the Lord continued there at the meal with His disciples. There the Ruler consecrated both wine and bread, the King of Heaven made them holy,
broke it with His hands and gave it out among His disciples. He thanked God and gave thanks to Him who created all things, the world and its joys, and He spoke many words:
"Believe this clearly," He said, "that this is my body and likewise my blood: I give you both of them here together to eat and to drink.
This I shall give and pour out on earth, and with my body I shall redeem you for God's kingdom, into eternal life, into the light of heaven.
Always remember to carry out what I do at this meal; proclaim this before the multitude:
This is a mighty thing. With this you shall show honour to your Lord. Keep this in remembrance of me, a holy example,
so that the children of men who are in this world may carry it on afterwards, and so that all people across this middle-earth may know that it is done out of love for me, for the favour of the Lord.
Always remember how I command you here to keep up your brotherhood firmly:
have a righteous mind and love one another in your hearts, so that the children of men among all peoples may understand that you are truly my disciples.
I shall also tell you how a mighty enemy, a fierce and hostile hater, Satan himself, intends to test your minds here. He is coming here boldly to tempt your souls.
Always keep the thoughts of your hearts firmly on God. I shall stand by you in your prayer, so that the evil-doer cannot make your minds waver. I will help you against the fiend.
He also came here once before to tempt me, though nothing of what he wanted, nothing he desired, came about here in my body.
Now I will no longer hide from you what will soon come upon you here to your sorrow:
you will fail me, my companions, in your loyalty as thanes, before this dark night passes from the people and the light comes again, the morning to men."
Then the men's minds grew very dark and their hearts were sore. They were grieving in their hearts and deeply sorrowful over their lord's words.
Then Simon Peter, the thane, spoke boldly to his lord, out of loyalty to his master:
"Even if all this company of men, your companions, fail you," he said, "I will still always endure every hardship with you.
I am always ready, if God allows me, to stand firmly in support of you.
Even if these people lock you up tightly in the enclosure of a prison, I have little doubt that I will stay with you in the chains and lie there with you, my beloved.
If they then seek your life with the violence of blades, my good lord, I will give my life for you in the play of weapons.
there is nothing I would shrink from, as long as my mind and the strength of my hands protect me." Then his lord spoke to him in reply:
"What, you trust," he said, "in sure loyalty and in bold deeds: you have the spirit of a thane and a good will.
I can tell you how it will nevertheless happen: you will become so faint-hearted, though you do not think so now, that tonight, before the cock crows, you will deny your loyalty to your lord and say
that I am not your lord, and you will renounce my protection." Then the man spoke back: "If it ever in the world," he said,
"should happen that I had to die together with you, die gloriously, even then the day would never come when I would willingly deny you, dear Lord, before these Jews."
Then all the disciples said the same: that they would endure with him there in those troubles.
Then the Ruler himself, the mighty King of heaven, spoke again and commanded them not to let their minds waver. He told them not to give way to deep brooding:
"Do not let your hearts be troubled by your Lord's words, and do not be too afraid. I shall go to our Father himself and send you a Holy Spirit from the kingdom of heaven.
He shall comfort you afterwards and become a help to you. He will remind you of the teachings that I have taught you in many words.
He will give you understanding in your breast, delightful teaching, so that from now on you carry out the words and the works that I commanded you in this world."
Then the mighty one, the saving Christ, rose up inside the hall and went away from there by night with his companions. Christ's disciples went sorrowfully, deeply mourning, sad at heart.
Then he went up onto the high Mount of Olives. He was used to going up there with his disciples. Judas, the evil-minded man, knew that well, because he had often been on the mountain with him.
There the Son of God addressed his disciples: "You are now so troubled," he said,
"now that you know of my death; now you mourn and weep, and these Jews are full of delight. This multitude rejoices, they are glad in their hearts, this world is in joy."

Yet that will very soon be reversed. Then their minds will be sore, then they will mourn in their hearts, and afterwards you shall rejoice for ever, for no reversal of your blissful life will ever come.
Therefore you need not grieve over these events or lament my departure, for from it help shall come to the children of men."
Then he told his disciples to wait there on the mountain, and said that he wished to climb higher among the rocky cliffs to pray.
Then he told three thanes to go with him: James and John and the good Peter, the bold-hearted thane. They went gladly together with their lord.

Then on the mountain the Son of God told them to bow down in prayer. He told them to call on God and pray earnestly that he would ward off from them the power of the tempters, the will of the hostile ones, so that the adversary,
the wicked destroyer, could not make their minds doubt. And then the Son of the Lord himself, the mighty one, the most powerful of kings, bowed down on his knees, forward to the earth.
He called on the good Father of all peoples and spoke sorrowfully in words of grief. His mind was troubled; his spirit was shaken because of his human nature; his flesh was afraid.
Tears fell from him, and his precious sweat dripped down just as blood comes welling from wounds. Then there was a struggle within the child of God between the spirit and the body.

The one, the spirit, was eager to set out on the way forth into God's kingdom. The other, Christ's body, stood in anguish: it did not want to give up this light, but was troubled in the face of death.
He kept crying out to the Lord, and called the more on the Mighty One, the high Father of heaven, holy God, the Ruler, with his words: "If now it cannot be," he said,
"that mankind is saved unless I give my dear body for the children of men to be tormented terribly, then if that is your will, I am willing to endure it:
I take the cup in my hand and drink it to your glory, my Lord, mighty Protector."
Do not look here to the comfort of my flesh. I shall fulfil your will: you have power over all."

Then he went back to where he had earlier left his disciples to wait on the mountain. The child of God found them sleeping in their sorrow. Their minds were sore because they would have to part from their lord.
In the same way, it is a heartache to any man when he has to leave a beloved lord and give up one so good.
Then he spoke to his disciples: the Ruler woke them and addressed them with words: "Why do you want to sleep like this?" he said;
"Can you not keep watch with me for one hour? Fate is at hand, so that it must come to pass just as God, the mighty Father, has appointed it."
"There is no doubt in my mind. My spirit is ready to do God's will and eager to go, but my flesh is in sorrow and my body holds me back:
it is very unwilling to suffer torment. Yet I shall carry out my Father's will. Keep your minds steadfast."
Then the glorious Lord went away from there a second time, up onto the mountain to pray, and there he spoke many good words.
God's angel came, holy, from heaven. He strengthened his mind and gave him courage to face the bonds. He kept on praying earnestly and addressed his Father, the Ruler, with his words:
"If it cannot be otherwise now," he said, "glorious Lord, unless I suffer a deadly torment for this people of men, then I shall abide by your will."
Then he went back from there to look for his companions. He found them sleeping and suddenly greeted them.
He went away from there again a third time to pray, and the king of the peoples, the Lord's Son, spoke all the same words to the all-ruling Father
as he had done before. Christ the Saviour pleaded very earnestly with the mighty Creator of men. Then he went back to his disciples and greeted them at once:
"Sleep and rest," he said. "Soon the one who has sold me will come here with force. He has sold me, though I am free of sin."
Then after those words Christ's companions woke up and saw the troop coming up the mountain with a great uproar: hostile men carrying weapons.

Judas, a hostile-minded man, guided them, and the Jews followed after him, a host of enemies. Fire was carried among them, flames in lanterns, and burning torches were brought from the city as they climbed up the mountain ready for a fight.
Judas knew the place well, where he was to lead the people.
As they went there, he walked ahead of the people and gave them a sign, so that the men would not seize the wrong man there:
"I will go up to him first," he said, "and kiss him and greet him. That is Christ himself.
You must seize him with the force of the people, bind him on the mountain, and lead him from here to the city among the people. By his words he has forfeited his life."
Then the troop, the fierce people of the Jews, went on until they came to Christ, where the glorious Lord stood with his disciples. He was waiting for what fate had decreed, for the bright hour.

Then the faithless man, Judas, went toward him. He bowed his head to the Child of God, greeted his master, and kissed the mighty one. So he kept his word and pointed him out to the troop, just as he had promised before.
The Lord of the peoples, the Ruler of this world, bore all this patiently. He spoke to him and boldly asked him:

"Why do you come to me like this with these people? Why do you lead these people to me and speak [?] me to this hateful nation? Why do you sell me with your kiss among this race of Jews and betray me to this crowd?"
Then he went toward the men, toward the other company, and asked them with his words whom they had come seeking with that band so eagerly at night,
"as if you wanted to do harm to some man." Then the multitude spoke back to him and said that the Healer had been pointed out to them there, up on that hill,

"who stirs up this strife among the Jewish people and calls himself the Son of God. We have come here to seek him and would gladly seize him: he is from the land of Galilee, from the town of Nazareth."
When Christ the Saviour had told them truly that he himself was the one, the Jewish people grew afraid and were terrified,
so that all at once they fell backward and dropped to the earth. The crowd was thrown back: they could not stand against the word of God, his voice.

Yet they were such stubborn men that they leapt up again on the hill, steadied their minds and hardened their hearts. In their rage they came closer with hostile intent, until they had surrounded Christ the Saviour with their troop.
