There stood wise men, Christ's disciples, deeply grieved before the cruel deed, and they spoke to their Lord: "If it were now your will," they said,
"Ruler, my lord, that they might destroy us here on the points of their spears, wounded by weapons, then nothing would be as good for us
as to be allowed to die here for our Lord, pale from mortal wounds." Then the swift sword-thane, Simon Peter, grew angry; his spirit surged within him so that he could not speak a word:
It hurt him so much in his heart that men wanted to bind his lord there. Then he went in anger, the very bold thane, to stand before his chieftain, hard before his lord.

His mind did not waver, nor did the blood in his breast. He drew his blade, the sword at his side, and struck at the foremost enemy with all the strength of his hands, so that Malchus was marked by the edges of the blade, marked by the sword on his right side.
His ear was hewn off and he was wounded in the head, so that his cheek and ear burst open with the deadly wound, bloody from the sword. Blood sprang out after it and welled from the wound.
Then the foremost of the enemies had a gash in his cheek. The people stood back, because they feared the bite of the blade.
Then the Child of God himself spoke to Simon Peter and told him to put his sharp sword back in its sheath. "If I wanted to," he said, "against this troop,

against the attack of this host, to wage battle, then I would call on the great and mighty God, the holy Father in the kingdom of heaven, to send me so many angels down here from above, so skilled in war,
that men could not withstand the force of their weapons. Never could such a force of people stand together, bound into one, that their lives could be spared after that.
But the ruling God, the almighty Father, has marked it out otherwise: we must endure whatever bitter thing this people brings upon us.
We must not grow angry at all or become wrathful at their attack. For whoever is eager to practise the violence of weapons, grim spear-hatred,
will die in turn by the edge of the sword and perish covered in blood. We must not ruin anything by our deeds."
Then he went to the wounded man and skilfully joined the body together at the head wound, so that it was healed at once, the bite of the blade. And the Child of God spoke to that angry crowd:
"It seems a great wonder to me," he said, "if you wanted to do me some harm, why you did not seize me when I stood among your people inside the temple and spoke many true words there."
"When the sun was shining, the precious light of day, you would not do me any harm in that light,
and now your people lead me off into the dark night, just as one does with a thief, when one wants to seize him and he has forfeited his life, a criminal."

Then the band of the Jews, a grim people, a crowd of haters, seized the Son of God. They swarmed around him, the arrogant mob of men (they paid no heed to the wickedness), and bound his hands together with harsh bonds, his arms with fetters.
He had no need to endure such cruel torment and hardship, or to suffer such punishment, but he did it for the sake of these people, because he wanted to redeem the children of men,
to fetch them from hell into the kingdom of heaven, into its wide riches. Therefore he said nothing against what they wanted to inflict on him out of malice.
Then the proud people of the Jews grew so arrogant, and the crowd so boastful, at being able to lead the holy Christ in bonds on his limbs and to bring him along in fetters.
The enemies went back from the mountain to the town. The child of God walked among the armed band with his hands bound, sorrowing, down to the valley.
His dear companions had now deserted him, just as he himself had told them before.
Yet it was not out of any cowardice that they abandoned the beloved child of God. It had been the word of the prophets long before that it would happen so, and therefore they could not avoid it.
Then John and Peter, the two men, went after the crowd, following at a distance. They were very eager to know what the grim Jews wanted to do to the child of God, their Lord.
Then they came down from the mountain to the town, where their bishop was, the guardian of their temple, and there the proud men led him, the warriors, within the enclosure.
There was a large fire there, a fire in the courtyard, set in the middle of the people, made in front of the crowd. The Jews went there to warm themselves, and left the Son of God waiting in bonds.
There was a great noise there, the din of exultant men. John was already known to the high priest, and so he was able to push his way into the court with the people.
Peter, the best of all thanes, stood outside there. The gatekeeper would not let him follow his Lord until his friend John asked one of the Jews to let him go on into the courtyard.
There a deceitful woman came walking toward him. She belonged to one of the Jews, a servant of their lord, and then the unlovely maid spoke to the thane:
"Why, you could be one of the men," she said, "a disciple from Galilee, of the one who stands over there with his arms bound."
Then Simon Peter at once grew afraid, faint in his heart. He said that he did not understand the woman's words and that he was not that lord's thane.
Then he denied it in front of the crowd and said that he did not know the man. "I don't know what you are talking about," he said. The power of God, the steadfastness, had left his heart.
Moving about, he went forward among the people until he came to the fire, and went there to warm himself. There a woman also began to lay accusing words on him:
"Here," she said, "you can see your enemy. This is truly a disciple of Christ, his own companion."
Right after that the hostile men came closer to him, and the children of enemies eagerly asked him which people he belonged to. "You are not one of the people of this town," they said;
"so that we can see it in your bearing, in your words and in your ways, that you are not of this people, but you are a Galilean man."
He would not admit any of it, but stood there and argued, and swore a strong oath with great force that he was not one of that company.
He had no control over his words: it had to happen just as He had marked it out who watches over mankind in this world.
Then in the crowd a kinsman also came up to him, a kinsman of the man he had struck earlier with his blade, with the sharp sword. He said that he had seen him there, up on the mountain,
"where we bound your lord's hands in the orchard and tied his hands fast."
Then, out of a fearful heart, he denied his dear lord, and said that he would forfeit his life
if any man there could truly say that he was one of that company and had followed that band. Then for the first time the cock-crow was raised.
Then holy Christ, the best of children, there where he stood bound, looked himself at Simon Peter: the Son of the Lord looked at the man over his shoulder.
Then at once Simon Peter grew sore within, in his mind; there was pain in his heart and his spirit was troubled. He was in deep sorrow over what he himself had said before.
He then remembered the words that the ruler Christ had himself told him before: that in the dark night, before the cock-crow, he would deny his lord three times.
That pained him bitterly deep in his mind, in his breast, and the man went away from the crowd, angry, in heartache, in great sorrow,
and he wept over his own words, his wicked deeds, until hot tears came welling up through his heartache, bloody from his breast.
He did not think that he could ever make any amends for his crimes, or come back to his lord, to his lord's favor:
there is no man so old that he ever saw a son of man regret his own words more sorely, lament or bewail them:
"Oh, mighty God," he said, "I have so ruined myself that I have no cause to give thanks for my life in this world.
If I must now go without your favor and the kingdom of heaven forever, Lord, then I have no reason to be thankful, dear Lord, that I ever came into this light.
I am not worthy now, my ruling Lord, to walk among your disciples, sinful as I am, among your companions: I must keep away from them myself in my heart, now that I have spoken such wickedness."
So the best of men grieved, and regretted it so bitterly that he had denied his dear lord.
Yet the children of men, people, need not wonder why God wanted something so hateful to happen to so dear a man,
that he, the boldest of thanes, so shamefully denied his dear lord because of the words of a serving-girl: it was all done for the sake of these peoples, for the benefit of the children of men.
The holy Lord wanted to make him the foremost, the highest over his household: he let him learn what strength the human mind has without the might of God;
let him sin, so that afterwards he would better trust the people, knowing how dear it is to every man, when he has done wrong,
that someone should release him from the harm he has done, from his crimes and sins, just as God of the kingdom of heaven himself then did for him, the wrongdoer.
Therefore a man's boasting is of little use, a young warrior's bragging: if God's help fails him because of his sins,
then the heart in his breast soon becomes the more fearful, though he made boastful speeches before, bragging of his fighting and of the work of his hands, the man bragging of his might.
That became plain there in the famous one, the best of thanes, when the holy help of his lord failed him.
Therefore a man should not boast too much about himself, for his hope and his will often fail him if the ruling God, the lord, the King of heaven, does not strengthen his heart.
Then the best of all children waited and endured bonds for the sake of mankind.
Many of the Jewish people swarmed around him and spoke great insults. They mocked him where he stood bound. He patiently endured whatever the people did to him, whatever hateful things they did.
Then light came again, morning came to men. A great host of the Jews gathered: they had wolfish minds and malice within them.
Many of the lawmen were gathered there in the morning, angry and stubborn, eager for malice, with wrathful intent.
The men went together into the assembly to talk in secret, and then they began to plan how they might, by means of faithless men,
by means of perjurers, prove sins against mighty Christ from his own words, so that they could then condemn him to horrible torment and sentence him to death.
That day they could not find such hostile testimony that they dared to sentence him to punishment for it, or put him to death and take his life.
Then at last two faithless men came forward into the assembly and began to accuse him. They said that they had heard him say himself

that he could throw down the temple of God, the highest of all houses, and by the power of his hands, by his strength alone, raise it up again on the third day, so that no other man would need to labor at it [?].
He kept silent and endured. However much the people spoke against him with lies, he never took revenge with hateful words in return.
Then an evil-minded man rose up among the crowd, the high priest of the people, the foremost of the nation, and questioned Christ, and also made him swear by strong oaths to speak about himself.
He greeted him in God's name and eagerly asked him to tell them whether he was the Son of the living God,
"who created this light: Christ, the eternal king. We cannot recognize anything of that, either in your words or in your works."
Then the true one, the good Son of God, answered him in turn: "You say it now before these Jews; you truly say that I am he myself.
These people do not believe me in this, and for that reason they will not release me. They do not think my words are worth anything.
But now I tell you truly that you will yet see the famous Son of Man sitting at the right hand of God, in the mighty power of the almighty Father,
and coming again from there, here in the clouds of heaven, and judging the whole race of men with his words, according to their deeds."
Then the high priest grew angry and bitter-minded. He raged against those words and tore his garments, ripped them in front of his chest:
"Now you need not wait any longer," he said, "for this crowd's testimony, now that such words come from him, blasphemy from his mouth.

Many men here have now heard it, warriors in this hall: he makes himself out to be so mighty that he claims he is God. What sentence do you Jews want to pass on this? Do such words now make him worthy of death?"
The whole crowd, the people of the Jews, spoke out: he had forfeited his life and so deserved punishment.
Yet nothing he had done justified what the Jewish people there in Jerusalem did when they condemned the Lord's Son, who was without sin, to death.
Then the Jewish people were eager and proud of their deeds, of whatever harm they could do to the child of God now that he was a prisoner.

Then they surrounded him with their crowd and struck him on his cheeks, on his face, with their hands. All this was done to him in mockery. The crowd of enemies heaped wicked words on him, words of scorn.
The child of God stood firm among his enemies. His arms were bound. He patiently endured whatever bitterness the people brought him. He was not angry at all at the crowd's hostility.
Then angry men took the child of God, bound as he was, and led him to the place where the people's assembly house was.
There many thanes thronged around their commander. Their lord's representative from Rome was there, sent by the one who then ruled the empire.
He had come from the emperor. He had been sent among the Jewish people to govern the land and was the ruling counsellor there.
He was called Pilate. By birth he came from the land of Pontus. He had a great force with him, people gathered in the assembly house, a throng of men.

Then faithless men, the Jewish people, handed over the Son of God into the hands of hostile people. They said he had forfeited his life and should be punished with the edges of weapons, with sharp blows.
The crowd of Jews would not push into the assembly house. The people stood outside and spoke from there to the crowd inside.

They would not go into the gathering among foreigners, so that they would not hear unjust words there or anything wicked being judged on that day. They said they wanted to keep the holy time, their Passover, in complete purity.
Pilate received the Ruler's child, who was without sin, from the wicked men.
Then Judas's mind became full of sorrow when he saw his Lord handed over to death. After that the deed began to grieve him in his heart, that he had sold his sinless Lord.

So he took the silver in his hand, the thirty coins he had been given for his Lord. He went to the Jews and told them about his terrible deed, his sins, and eagerly offered to give the silver back to them:
"I have bought it so horribly with my Lord's blood," he said, "that I know it will bring me no good."
The Jewish people would not accept it. Instead they told him to consider such sins himself, what he had done against his lord:
"You saw to that yourself," they said. "Why do you come to us about it now?
Don't blame this crowd for it!" Then Judas went away from there to God's temple in deep sorrow and threw the silver into the temple. He did not dare keep it any longer.
Then he went off in fear, as the children of fiends, the proud ones, urged him on. The hostile ones had taken hold of the man's mind, and God was angry with him, so that he then made himself a rope,

and then he bowed into the deadly noose, into the hanging, the outlaw in the halter. He chose punishment: the hard oppression of hell, hot and dark, the deep valley of death, because he had earlier betrayed his lord.
Then the Child of God waited, enduring bonds in the court-house, until the people, the men, had all come to agreement among themselves about what deadly torment they would inflict on him.
Then the emperor's messenger from Rome rose from the benches there and went proudly to speak with the powerful men of the Jews, where the crowd stood milling around the courtyard.
They would not come into the house on the Passover day. Pilate boldly began to ask over the Jewish people by what that man had become guilty of murder and earned punishment:
"Why are you so angry with him, so full of hatred in your minds?" They said that he had done them a great deal of harm and wrong:
"These people would not have handed him over to you if they had not known him before as an evil man, guilty in his words."
He has led a great many of this people astray with his teachings. He stirs these people up and makes them doubt in their minds, so that we may not pay tribute to the emperor's court.
We can prove that against him with true testimony. He also speaks great words: he says that he is Christ, king over this realm. He claims great things for himself."
Then the emperor's messenger answered them: "If he so openly," he said,
"commits evil deeds among this crowd, then take him back among your own people, if his life is forfeit, and judge him as your elders' law commands, if he deserves death."
Then they said that they were not permitted to become the slayer of any man with weapons in the holy season, on the holy day.
Then the angry-minded man turned away from the crowd, the emperor's thane, who was the messenger from Rome over the people.
He ordered the Child of God to come nearer to him, and eagerly [?] asked him boldly whether he was king over the people of this nation.
Then the Son of the Lord had his answer ready: "Do you say that of yourself," he said, "or did other men here tell you this, speaking about my kingship?"
Then the emperor's messenger spoke again, proud and angry, as he talked with Christ the Ruler in the hall: "I am not from this kingdom," he said,

"not from the Jewish people, and I am no relative of yours or kinsman of these men. But this crowd handed you over to me. Your own kinsmen, the Jewish people, gave you to me, a prisoner, into my hands."
What harm have you done, that you must so bitterly endure bonds and torment among your own kin?"
Then Christ, the best of healers, answered him as he stood bound inside the hall: "My kingdom is not here," he said, "in this age of the world.

If it were, then my disciples would be so strong-minded against the warlike, hostile people that I would not be handed over to the Jewish people, to those who hate me, into their hands in fetters, to be cruelly tormented.
I was born into this world for this purpose: that by my coming I should make known the testimony of the truth.
"The men who have come from the truth can recognize that well: they can understand my words and believe my teachings."
Then the emperor's envoy could find no fault at all in the child of God, no deceitful word, for which he would deserve to lose his life.

Then the man who was bold of speech went back to the band of the Jews. He told the crowd openly, so that very many could hear, that he could find no such grievous crime in the captive man, before the people, that he should lose his life for it or be worthy of death.
Then the foolish-minded Jewish people stood there and accused the Son of God with words. They said that he had first started strife in the land of Galilee,

"and from there he went across Judea to here, and made men's minds, their hearts, waver. So he deserves death, and he should be punished with the edges of weapons, if ever a man can deserve death for such deeds."
So the host of the Jews accused him with words out of hateful minds. Then the governor, a cruel-minded man, heard it said what kin Christ had been raised among, the best of men:
he was of that famous people, the good people from the land of Galilee. There was a company of noble men there.
Herod held a powerful kingdom there, as the emperor, the mighty one from Rome, had given it to him, so that he should carry out every right among the people there, keep the peace and give judgments.
On that very day he too was in Jerusalem with his retinue, with his host at the temple. Such was their custom then, that they were to keep the holy feast there, the Passover of the Jews.

Pilate then commanded the men to take the captive man, the child of God, bound as he was. He ordered the warriors to bring him as a captive into Herod's hands, because he was from Herod's realm, from the people under his rule.
The warriors carried out their lord's word. They led holy Christ in fetters before the ruler of the people, the best of all children who were ever born into the light of men.
He walked in bonds on his limbs until they brought him to where King Herod sat on his bench. A force of men stood around him, proud warriors.
They had a great desire to see Christ himself there. They expected that he would show them some sign there, famous and mighty, as he had done for many of the Jewish people through his divine power.
Then the king of the people questioned him eagerly with many words. He wanted to find out more about his mind, and what benefit he might show to people.
Then mighty Christ stood there, kept silent and endured. He would not give the king of the people, Herod, or his men any answer in words.

Then the angry people, the Jews, stood there and maligned and accused the Son of God, until the king of the world and all his retinue became hostile to him in their minds. They despised him in their hearts:
they did not recognize the power of God, the heavenly Lord. Instead their minds were dark and mixed with evil.
Through humility, the Lord's child endured all their angry works, words and deeds, whatever harm they wanted to do to him then.
Then they ordered a white garment to be laid about his limbs in mockery, so that he would be all the more a laughingstock to the people there, sport for the young men.
The Jews rejoiced when they saw them hold him up to mockery, the men in their arrogance. Then King Herod sent him back from there to the other people.
He ordered bold men to lead him away. They spoke insults and hurled wicked words at him as he walked in fetters, laughed at with mockery.
His mind did not waver. Instead he endured it all through humility. He would not repay their evil words, their mockery and abuse.
Then they brought him back into the house, up into the palace, where Pilate was at the place of judgment.
The thanes gave the best of the born, the sinless one, into the hands of slayers, as he himself had chosen: he wished to free the children of men from death, to save them from distress.
The hate-filled ones, the Jews, stood before the guest-hall. The children of the fiends had urged on that crowd, so that they would not hold back [?] from any grimmer deeds.
Then the emperor's thane, the hard army-leader, went over there to speak with the people: "Listen," he said, "you sent me this captive man
into this hall and told me yourselves that he had led so many of your people astray, misled them with his teachings.
Now I cannot find, with these people, among this folk, that he has forfeited his life for this charge.
It was plain today: Herod, who knows your law, the land-law of your people, could not find out anything about his life showing that he should die here today for any sin and give up his life.
Now I will punish him here before these people with punishments [?] and with bold words, correct the thoughts of his heart, and then let him go on enjoying his life among men."

Then the people of the Jews all shouted together with loud voices. They urgently demanded that Christ's life be taken with a violent death, that he be nailed on the cross and tormented terribly [?] with wounds:
"He has deserved death by his words: he says that he is the Lord, truly the Son of God.
He must pay for that malicious speech, as it is written in our law that such blasphemy is paid for with life."
Then the one who ruled over the people became greatly afraid in his mind, when he heard the men say that they had heard him himself say, declaring before the people, that he was the Son of God.
Then the commander turned back into the house, to the place of judgment. He addressed the Son of God with bold words and asked what he was among men: "What sort of man are you?"
he said. "Why do you hide your mind from me like this and conceal your deep thoughts? Do you know that everything about the fate of your life rests on my judgment?
These people, the host of the Jews, have handed you over to me, so that I have the power either to destroy you at the spear's point or to kill you on the cross,
or to let you live, whichever seems better to me to carry out with my people." Then God's child of peace spoke in turn:
"Know this for truth," he said, "that you could have no power over me if holy God himself had not given it to you."
But those who handed me over to you out of enmity, who gave me up bound in chains, have the greater sin."
After that the hostile-minded man, the emperor's thane, would gladly have let him go, since he had power over him there before the people. But the race of the Jews opposed his wish with every word:
"You are no friend of the emperor," they said, "and not loyal to your lord, if you let him go away from here unharmed."
that it may yet become a sorrow to you and turn into a punishment. For whoever speaks such words raises himself so high that he says he may have the name of king,
unless the emperor has given it to him. He is disrupting the emperor's worldly kingdom and scorning his word, despising him in his heart.
Therefore you must punish such crime, so many mocking words, if you care about your lord and about your master's friendship. You must take his life from him."
Then the governor heard the Jewish host threaten him with his lord.
Then he went himself to sit in front of the place of assembly, where so great a crowd of people had gathered, and he ordered the Ruler Christ to be led before the people.
The Jews longed for the moment when they would see the holy child hanging, tortured on the cross.
They said that they had no other king among their host except the noble emperor from Rome: "He has power over us here.
Therefore you must not let this man go. He has spoken so much hostility against us, and he has ruined himself by his deeds.
He shall suffer death, torment and terrible torture." The host of the Jews, so many of them, charged mighty Christ with all sorts of things as sins.
He stood silent out of humility and answered nothing to their hostile words. He wanted to redeem this whole world with his life.
So he let the hateful people torment him terribly, just as they wished. He did not want to reveal openly to all the Jewish people that he was God himself.
For if they had known it for certain, that he had such power over this middle-earth, their hearts would have grown fearful in their breasts.
Then they would not have dared to lay hands on the child of God, and the kingdom of heaven, the greatest of lights, would not have been opened to the children of men.
Therefore he kept it hidden in his heart and did not let the people know what they were doing.
Then the appointed fate drew near, the great might of God, and midday, when they were to carry out the deadly torment.
Now there also lay in chains inside the city a notorious arch-criminal, who had plotted so much murder in the kingdom and committed killings. He was a notorious great thief:
there was no one like him anywhere. He too was held there in fetters for his sins. Barabbas was his name. Throughout the cities he was known to many for his crimes.

Now it was a custom of the Jewish people that every year, for the love of God, on the holy day, they were to ask for one prisoner, so that the guardian of their city, their leader, would grant him his life.

Then the governor began to ask the host of the Jews, the people as they stood before him, which of the two they wanted to decide for, to ask life for: "which of those who lie here in fetters, held captive among this host?"

The host of the Jews had by then stirred up all the poor men to ask life for the land-ravager, to plead for the thief who had often done wickedness in the dark night, and to have the Ruler Christ killed on the cross.
Then it became known everywhere how the people had given their judgment. Then they were to do the deed and hang the holy child.
That later became a sorrow for the commander: he knew the matter, that the crowd hated the saving Christ out of envy, and yet he listened to them in this and did their will.
For this he received punishment, a reward in this light and long afterward: he won woe later, after he gave up this world.

Then the hostile one, the greatest of harmful foes, Satan himself, became aware, when the soul of Judas came to the bottom of grim hell. Then he knew for certain that it was the ruling Christ, the Son of the Lord, who stood there bound;
he knew then for certain that by his hanging he meant to free this whole world from the bondage of hell and release the people into God's light.
That was painful to Satan's mind, a great grief in his heart. So he wanted to help him then, so that the children of men would not take his life or torment him on the cross. Instead he wanted
him to stay alive, so that the children of men would not be set free from hell, cleared of their sins. Then Satan went to where the governor's household was, inside the city.
There the monstrous fiend began openly to show wonders to his wife, the woman, so that she would plead in words on Christ's behalf, so that he might stay alive,

the Lord of men (he had already been sentenced to death). For he knew for certain that Christ was going to take the power from him, so that he would no longer have such great power over this middle-earth, over the wide world.
The woman then became afraid, very anxious, when the visions came to her in the light of day through the doing of the hidden one, who was concealed under a helmet of concealment.

Then the woman sent word to her lord in her own words and ordered that he himself be told truthfully what had come to her there in visions because of that holy man. She begged him to help and to spare his life:
"Because of him I have seen so many strange things here that I know the sins will turn out badly for every man, if you boldly seek his life."
Then the messenger went on his way until he found the governor sitting inside the court, on the stone pavement, where the street was laid with stone.
He went there to his master and told him the woman's words. Then the governor's mind grew troubled (it was in turmoil inside him), and the thoughts of his heart were afraid:

both choices were painful to him: either that they should kill him, though he was without sin, or that he would not dare to let the matter drop before the people, because of what the crowd was saying.
Then his mind was turned in his heart toward the host of the Jews, to do their will. He did not guard himself at all against the heavy sins that he himself was committing there.
Then he ordered clear spring water to be brought for his hands, water in a basin, where he sat before the crowd. The emperor's thane washed himself there in front of the people,
[?] the hard army-leader, and then he spoke before the crowd. He said that he declared himself free there of the sins, of the wicked deeds: "I want no part in this," he said,
"concerning this holy man. You yourselves must take all of it, both the words and the deeds, that you do to him here as punishment."
Then the whole army of the Jews shouted together, the great multitude. They said they were willing to take responsibility for the man, for the harsh deeds:
"Let his gore come upon us, his blood and his death, and on our children as well, and on our descendants after them. We are willing to answer for all of it," they said,
"for the killing itself, if we commit any sin in it!"
Then the best of all men was handed over there, before the Jews, into the hands of his enemies, closely held in the power of the fierce binders [?], where hostile-minded foes received him:
the people surrounded him, a host of wicked evildoers. The mighty Lord endured patiently whatever the people did to him.
Then they ordered him to be scourged, before they took his life, his existence, and they spat in his face; they did this to mock him, so that they struck him with their hands,
those men, on his cheeks, and took his garments from him. The cruel enemies stripped him, and out of hostility they put another garment, of red cloth, on him in its place;

then they ordered a head-band of hard thorns to be wound in a strange way and set upon the Ruler Christ himself. And the companions went up to him, greeted him as one greets a king, fell on their knees there and bowed their heads to him:
all this was done to mock him, yet he endured it all, the Lord of the peoples, mighty, for love of mankind.

Then they ordered men to make a strong cross of hard wood with their hands, with the edges of weapons. Then they ordered Christ, God's blessed child himself, to carry it. They ordered our Lord to bear it to the place where, bloodied, he was to die free of sins.
The Jews went on, men doing what they wanted, and led the ruling Christ, the Lord, to his death. There one could then hear a grievous and painful thing:
lamenting women followed behind, weeping, and the men who had come with him from Galilee mourned. They had followed him over far roads, and the death of their lord was a great sorrow to them.
Then he himself, the best of children, spoke and looked back behind him. He told them not to weep: "You need not grieve at all," he said,
"over my going hence. Rather, you may mourn your own wicked deeds, with lamenting and weeping, with bitter tears."
The time will yet come when those women will be glad, brides of the Jews, to whom no child was ever granted in their lifetime.
Then you shall pay grimly for your malice; then you will so long for the high mountains to cover you here, to bury you deep;
death would then be dearer to you all in this land than to endure such a slaughter of the people as will then come upon this nation here."
Then on the gravel they set up a gallows, on the field, the people of the Jews, a tree on a hill, and there they tortured God's child on the cross:
they drove cold iron, new nails, cruelly sharp, hard with hammers through his hands and through his feet, bitter bonds: his blood ran onto the earth, the gore from our Lord.

Yet he did not want to avenge the grim deed on the Jews; instead he asked God, the mighty Father, not to be the more wrathful toward that people of men, that host: "for they do not know what they are doing," he said.
Then the warriors, harsh men, divided up the garments of Christ, the Lord, the clothing of the Mighty One. The men could not, concerning that very garment,
come to an agreement, until they cast lots in their gathering to decide which of them should have the holy tunic, the most pleasing of all garments.

Then the commander of the troops, the governor, ordered that it be written on the cross above Christ's own head that this was the king of the Jews, Jesus from the town of Nazareth, who stood there nailed to the new gallows, to the wooden tree, out of hatred.
Then the people asked that the wording be changed. They said he should put it as Jesus' own claim: that he himself had said he had power over the people and was king over the Jews.
Then the emperor's envoy, the harsh governor, spoke again: "It is written for you over his head just as it stands, wisely written, so that I may not change it now."

Then, as a punishment, the Jewish people placed two condemned men there on crosses on both sides of Christ. They let them suffer torment on the gallows-tree as the reward for their works, their evil deeds.
The people spoke many mocking words to holy Christ and taunted him with scorn. They saw the best of all men suffering on the cross: "If you are king over all," they said,

"the son of the Lord, as you yourself have said, save yourself from this distress and free yourself from this hatred. Come down here safe and sound. Then the children of men, these people, will believe in you."
A very arrogant Jew also insulted him as he stood in front of the gallows: "Woe would have come to this world," he said, "if you were to rule it.

You said that in one day you could throw down the high house of the King of heaven, the greatest of stone buildings, and make it stand again on the third day, so that no man of this people would need to labour on it any further.
See now how you stand here fastened and badly wounded. You cannot heal yourself of any of this harm."
Then one of the thieves also spoke there in his bonds, as soon as he heard the people, with angry words. His will was not good, nor were that man's thoughts:
"If you are king of the people," he said, "Christ, God's son, then come down from the cross, slip yourself out of the ropes, and help and save all of us together.
If you are the King of heaven, the ruler of this world, then show it in your works and make yourself famous before this crowd."
Then the other man on the gallows, where he stood fastened suffering terrible torment, spoke: "Why do you want to speak such words and taunt him?
You stand here bound to the gallows, broken on the tree. We two both suffer pain here because of our sins. Our own deeds have become a punishment for us.
He stands here without blemish and free of all sins, since he himself never committed any crime. The only reason he willingly receives punishment in this world is the hatred of this people.
"I want to believe in it," he said, "and I will gladly ask the guardian of the land, the Son of God, that you remember me and be my help, best of rulers, when you come into your kingdom:
be gracious to me then." Then Christ the Savior answered him in words: "I tell you truly here," he said,
"that this very day you may see God's light together with me in the kingdom of heaven, in paradise, though you are now in such torment."
Mary, Christ's mother, also stood there, pale beneath the tree. She watched her child suffer and endure terrible torment.

There were also women there with her [?], who had come out of love for so mighty a one. John, the disciple of Christ, also stood there, grieving beneath his lord, his heart full of pain. They mourned at his death.
Then the mighty Lord Christ spoke to his mother: "Now I shall commend you here to my disciple, who stands here facing you. Be together in his company; you shall have him as a son."
Then he spoke to John and told him to look after her well and to love her as tenderly as a man should love his mother, the spotless woman.
Then John took her into his honourable keeping with a pure heart, as his lord had commanded him.
Then at midday a mighty sign appeared, a wonder worked over all this world, when the Son of God was raised on the gallows, Christ on the cross.
Then it became known everywhere how the sun was darkened. The sun's light could not shine brightly; shadow seized it, gloom and darkness and a mist so thick.
It became the gloomiest of all days, very dark over this wide world, for as long as the ruling Christ, the mightiest of kings, suffered on the cross, until the ninth hour of the day.
Then the mist parted and the gloom was driven away. The sun's light began to grow bright in the sky.
Then he called up to God, the mightiest of all kings, as he stood on the cross, fastened by his arms: "Father almighty," he said,
"why have you forsaken me like this, dear Lord, holy King of heaven, and put your help, your support, so far away? I stand here among these enemies, terribly afflicted."
The host of the Jews laughed at it then in mockery: they heard the holy Christ, the Lord, ask for a drink before his death, saying that he was thirsty.
The people did not hesitate, the hostile adversaries. They were very eager to bring him whatever bitter thing they could.
The wicked men had mixed unsweet vinegar and gall for him. A man stood ready, a very guilty criminal, whom they had chosen for this and talked into it with words,
so that for them he took a sponge with the most loathsome of drinks, carried it on a long shaft tied to a pole, and held it to the mouth of the mighty child of God.
He recognised their dark deeds and sensed their malice. He would not taste any more of such bitterness. Instead the child of God cried loudly to the heavenly Father:
"Into your hands," he said, "I commend my spirit, according to God's will. It is now ready for this, eager to depart."
Then the Lord of men bowed his head and let the holy breath go from his body.
When the guardian of the land died in his bonds, wondrous signs were worked soon afterwards, so that many things without speech would recognise the death of the Ruler, the last day of the lord:
the earth shook, the high mountains trembled, hard stones split, rocks across the field, and the many-coloured curtain tore down the middle in two,
the curtain that for many a day had hung whole inside the temple, wondrously adorned. The children of men, the people, had not been allowed to see what holy thing hung behind the curtain.

Then the Jewish people could see that treasure. The graves of dead men were opened, and through the Lord's power they rose up living in their bodies from the earth and were shown there to people as a marvel.
It was so mighty a thing that so many things which never spoke a word with men in this world were to recognize Christ's death there and feel it so deeply.
The host of the Jews saw wondrous things, but their cruel minds were so hardened in their hearts
that no sign so holy could ever be shown there that they would trust any better in Christ's power, that he was king over all, over the whole host.
Some of those who were to guard the corpse there said in their words that he was in truth the Ruler's son, God's own indeed, who had died there on the gallows, the best of children.
Many weeping women beat their breasts. The wondrous torment was a grief in their hearts, and their lord's death a deep sorrow to them.
Now it was the custom of the Jews that, because of the holy day, they would not let the prisoners hang any longer than until life departed from them and the soul sank away.
Evil-minded men came closer in their hostility to where the two thieves stood nailed in this way; both were suffering torment beside Christ.
They were still alive, until the grim people of the Jews broke their legs, so that both of them together gave up their lives and went to seek another light.
They did not need to force the Lord Christ any further toward death with any wicked deeds: they found that he had already departed.
His soul had been sent on the true way, into the long-lasting light. His limbs grew cold, and the life was gone from the flesh.

Then one of the enemies came up to him with hostile intent. He carried a nailed spear, hard in his hands, and stabbed with battle-strength. He let the point of the weapon cut wounds, so that Christ's body was opened in his own side.

The people saw blood and water both spring out from there, welling from the wound, just as his will went and as he had earlier marked out for mankind, for the benefit of the children of men. Then it was all fulfilled in this way.
When the bright sun, with the heavenly stars, had sunk closer to its seat on that troubled day, a thane of our Lord went off. He was a wise man, and had been a disciple of Christ for a long while,
though many people did not know it for certain, because in what he said he hid it from the Jewish people. He was called Joseph, and he was secretly our Lord's disciple.
He did not want to follow the wicked people in any evil deeds, but among the Jewish people he waited for the holy kingdom of heaven. He went then to speak with the governor,

to plead with the emperor's thane. He begged him earnestly that he might take down the body of Christ, who stood there tormented to death, from the cross, take the good one from the gallows, lay him in a grave and commit him to the earth.
The governor would not refuse him his wish, but gave him permission to do so.
Then he went forth from there to the gallows, where he knew God's child was, the corpse of his lord hanging. He took him there on the new cross and freed him from the nails,
received him in his arms, as a man should receive his lord, the beloved body, and wrapped him in linen. He carried him reverently, so worthy was the Lord,
to where they had the place hewn by hand inside a stone, where the children of heroes had never before buried anyone.
There, following the custom of their land, they committed the child of God, the holiest of bodies, to the earth, and closed the best of all graves with a rock.

Weeping, the wretched women sat there, who had seen all of it, the cruel death of the man. Then the weeping women went away from there, and they took heed of how they might come back to the grave again.
They had seen sorrows enough, great grief of heart. They were called Mary, those wretched women.
Then evening came, night with mist. In the morning the hostile people of the Jews, a crowd of them, gathered again and spoke in secret counsel:
"Look, you know how this whole kingdom was thrown into doubt by this one man, and the people stirred up. Now he lies sick with wounds, buried deep.
He always said that he would rise from death on the third day. These people, this crowd, believe his words too much.
Now order guards here to watch over the grave, so that his disciples do not steal him away from the stone there and then say that he has risen, the mighty one, from his resting place.
Then this people of men will be led further astray, if they begin to proclaim it here."
Then men from the band of the Jews were assigned there to the watch.
They went with their weapons to the grave, where they were to guard the corpse of God's child. The holy day of the Jews had passed.
They sat over the grave, the men on watch through the dark nights. Under their shields they waited for the time when the bright day would come over middle-earth to men, light to the people.
Then it was not long until, by God's power, the spirit came there, the holy breath, under the hard stone into the body.
Then light was opened up for the benefit of the children of men. Many a bolt was unfastened from the doors of hell, and the way to heaven was made from this world.
Radiant, God's child of peace rose up and went where he wished. The guards, those hostile men, noticed nothing of it when he rose from death and arose from his resting place.
The warriors sat outside around the grave, the Jewish people, the band with their shields. The brilliant light of the sun glided onward.
Women set out walking to the grave, women of human kind, the lovely Marys. They had given many treasures for ointments, silver and gold,
paying for spices as much as they could get, so that they might anoint the body of their beloved lord, the Son of the Lord, cut with wounds.
The women were greatly anxious in their hearts, and some of them asked who would roll the great stone away from the grave to the side for them,
the stone that they had seen the people lay over the corpse when they laid the body to rest there in the rock.
When the noble women had walked to the enclosure, so that they could see the grave itself, an angel of the Almighty came there with a rushing sound from the sky above, flying in a feathered form,
so that the whole earth shook and the ground rumbled. The men, the guards of the Jews, grew faint at heart and fell down in fear. They did not expect to keep their lives, to live any longer.
The guards lay there, the companions half-dead. At once the great stone rose up from the grave, as God's angel moved it aside, and the glorious messenger of the Lord sat down upon the mound.
In his bearing and in his face, to anyone who could look at him with his own eyes, he was as bright and as radiant as the light of lightning. His clothing was most like winter-cold snow.
Then the women saw him sitting there on the stone that had been rolled away, and from his appearance such terror came over the women:
the noble women were all seized with great fear from the horror. They did not dare go any further toward the grave until God's angel,
the Ruler's messenger, greeted them with words. He said that he knew their whole errand, their deeds and their intention and the women's minds, and he told them not to be afraid of him:
"I know that you are looking for your Lord, the Savior Christ from the town of Nazareth, whom the Jewish people tortured here, nailed to the cross, and laid in the grave, though he was without sin.
He himself is not here now. He has already risen, and this place is empty, this grave in the sand.
You may come much closer now. I know you long to look inside this stone. Here the places where his body lay can still be seen."
The pale women, beautiful in appearance, quickly found comfort in their hearts. It was very good news for them to hear what the angel of the Almighty told them about their Lord.
He told them to go back from the grave and go to Christ's disciples, and tell his companions in true words that their Lord had risen from death.

He also told them to give the great good news in words to Simon Peter in particular: the coming of the Lord, that Christ himself had gone into the land of Galilee. There his disciples, his companions, would see him again, just as he himself had told them before in true words.
Just as the women were about to leave, two angels stood before them there in all-white, beautiful garments and spoke to them with their words in a holy way:
the women's minds grew timid with terror. They could not look at God's angels because of their appearance. The beauty was too strong for them, too intense to look at.
Then the Ruler's messengers at once spoke to them and asked the women why they had come there to look for Christ, the living among the dead, the Son of the Lord, full of life.
"You will not find him here in this stone grave now, for he has now risen in his body. You must believe this and remember the words
which he himself often told you truly when he was in your company in the land of Galilee: how he, the holy Lord, would be handed over, betrayed into the hands of sinful men,
of enemies, so that they would torture him, nail him to the cross, and put him to death; and how through the Lord's power he would rise up alive on the third day, to the joy of the people.
Now he has fulfilled all of it in this way, carried it out among people. Hurry away from here now, go quickly and make it known to his disciples.
He has gone ahead of you and has gone away from here to the land of Galilee, where his disciples, his companions, will see him again."
Then soon after that it came to pass, to the women's joy, that they heard such words spoken, the power of God made known. They were still so shaken then, and so frightened [?]:
they went away from there, from the grave, and told Christ's disciples of the wondrous sight, where they were waiting in sorrow for such a comfort.
Then the guards of the Jews also came into the city, who had sat over the grave all the long night and guarded the body there, the corpse.
They told the host of the Jews what terrors had come upon them there, a wondrous sight. They told it in words, all as it had been done by the Lord's power; they did not hide it in their minds.
Then the Jewish people offered them many treasures, gold and silver, and gave them much wealth, so that they would not tell it further or make it known to the multitude:
"But say that your weary minds lulled you to sleep, and that his companions came there and stole him from the stone.
Always hold to that in dispute, and hold to it eagerly. If it becomes known to the governor, we will help you against that highest lord, so that he does you no harm and nothing hateful."

Then they took many precious treasures from the people and did all as they had begun (they did not govern their own will). They made it widely known to the people throughout the land, for they wanted to raise such lies about the holy Lord.
But the minds of Christ's disciples were healed again when they heard the good women proclaim the might of God;
then they were glad in their hearts. Both of them went to the grave: John and Peter ran quickly.
The good John arrived first and stood over the grave, until Simon Peter came soon afterwards, a man renowned for courage, and he went into the grave.
There he saw the shroud of God's child, the linen grave-clothes of his lord, lying there, in which the body had been beautifully wrapped before;
the cloth lay apart, the one that had covered the head of holy Christ, the mighty Lord, while he was in this resting place.

Then John also went into the grave to see the wondrous thing. Soon after that his faith was unlocked, so that he knew that his Lord was to come back into this light in glory, rising up from death, up from the earth.
Then John and Peter went away again from there, and Christ's disciples, his companions, came together.
Then one of the women stood sad-hearted for a second time, weeping over the grave; her mind was full of grief. That was Mary Magdalene.
The thoughts of her heart, her very mind, were mixed with sorrows. She did not know where she should seek the Lord on whom her help depended.
She could not stop her lamenting then; the woman could not leave off weeping. She did not know where she should turn; her thoughts were confused.
Then she saw the mighty Christ standing there, though she could not clearly recognize him until he wished to make himself known and say that it was he himself.
He asked why she was weeping so sorely, so grievously, with hot tears. She said that she did not know for certain about her lord, what had become of him:

"If you could show him to me, my lord, if I may dare to ask you, if you took him from this rock here, show me where he is with your words. Then the greatest of all my wishes would be that I might see him myself."
She did not know that it was the Son of the Lord greeting her with kind words. She thought it was the gardener, the keeper of his lord's estate.

Then the holy Lord, the best of saviours, greeted her by name. The woman quickly went nearer to him with good will and recognised her Ruler himself. Because of her love she could not hold back from him:

The woman wanted to take hold of him with her hands, the Lord of the peoples, but God's peace-child held her back with his words and said that she must not touch him with her hands in any way: "I have not yet ascended," he said,
"to the heavenly Father; but hurry now quickly and make it known to the men, my brothers, that I intend to go to the Father of us both, the Ruler of all, yours and mine, the true God."
Then the woman was joyful that she could make known such welcome news and tell that he was alive and well.
The woman was soon ready for the errand. She brought the men the welcome news that she had seen the Ruler Christ alive and well, and she told them what he himself had commanded her, with clear signs.
But they still would not trust the woman's words that she had brought such welcome news straight from the Son of God. Instead they sat with sorrowful minds, the men grieving.
After he had risen from death, the holy Christ, the Lord, was openly shown a second time, to the women's joy, when he met them there on the way.
He greeted them in a familiar way, and they bowed down to his knees and fell at his feet. He told them not to carry fear in their hearts:
"Instead you must tell my brothers these words: that they are to come after me into the land of Galilee. There I will meet them again."
Then on that same day, early in the morning, two of the disciples also travelled out of Jerusalem, men going on their errand. They wanted to go to the town of Emmaus.
Then many words began to pass among the men as they travelled along the road, the warriors talking about their lord. Then the holy Son of God came walking up to them there.
They could not clearly recognize him, the mighty one: he did not yet want to make himself known to them. Still, he was there in their company with them and asked what matters they were talking about:
"Why are you going along so mournfully?" he said. "You two are grieving at heart, your spirit full of sorrows." At once the men spoke to him in answer:

"Why do you ask this?" they said. "Are you from Jerusalem, of the Jewish people [?] … [?] with the Holy Spirit from the plain of heaven, with the great power of God." [The text breaks off here and resumes partway through another scene. The missing section is marked by [?].]
Then he took his disciples, the good men, and led them out from there until he brought them to Bethany. There he raised his hands, blessed them all, and consecrated them with his words.
He went up from there to the high kingdom of heaven and his holy throne.
He sits there at the right hand of God, the almighty Father, and from there Christ the Ruler sees everything that this world holds.

Then the good companions fell to prayer in that same place. From there Christ's disciples went back to the city, to Jerusalem, rejoicing. Their hearts were glad, and they stayed there at the temple. The Ruler's power [?]
